lessons.title: What a Game Is, and Why Build Games
lessons.content:
Think about a group of children in a para alley playing kanamachi, blind man's buff. Nobody pays them, nothing useful is produced, and yet they play for an hour, laughing and arguing about whether someone peeked. Then think about a teenager on a bus in Dhaka, thumbs flying over a phone, trying to beat a level for the tenth time. Both are doing the same deep human thing: playing a game. This course is about how to build games with a computer, but before writing a single line of code we need to answer a surprisingly hard question: what exactly is a game?

Why the definition matters: When you build software for a bank, the goal is clear: move money correctly. When you build a game, there is no outside goal. The only product is an experience in the player's head. If you do not understand what makes that experience work, you can write perfect code and still make something nobody wants to play. So game development is half engineering and half design, and this first lesson sets up the design vocabulary that every later lesson uses.

Four ingredients of a game: Most definitions agree on four parts. First, rules: limits on what you may do. In kanamachi the catcher is blindfolded and must stay inside the alley. Second, a goal: something to aim for, like touching another player. Third, feedback: the game tells you how you are doing, through a shout, a score or a sound. Fourth, voluntary play: people choose to take part and can stop. Remove any one ingredient and the activity starts to feel like something else.

Famous definitions: The philosopher Bernard Suits described playing a game as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles. Golf is a good example: the easiest way to get a ball into a hole is to walk over and drop it in, but the game forbids that and makes you use a club from far away. Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, in their book Rules of Play, define a game as a system in which players engage in an artificial conflict, defined by rules, that results in a quantifiable outcome. Quantifiable outcome means you can say who won, or what the score was.

Games, toys and puzzles: A toy is something you play with freely, with no fixed goal: a ball, a doll, a sandbox. A game adds rules and goals to play: kicking the ball into a goal past a keeper. A puzzle is a game with a correct solution, such as a Sudoku: once solved, it is finished. Many video games mix all three. A game might have a toy-like world you enjoy just wandering through, puzzles to solve, and competitive goals. Designers often build the toy first: if just moving the character around feels good, the game has a strong base.

Conflict and uncertainty: A game needs something standing in the way of the goal, otherwise there is no challenge. The obstacle can be another player, a computer opponent, a timer, or the player's own skill. A game also needs uncertainty: if you know the result before starting, there is no reason to play. Uncertainty can come from chance, like dice in ludo, from hidden information, like cards in a hand, or from the difficulty of performing well, like a fast reaction test.

Kinds of play: The French writer Roger Caillois sorted play into four kinds. Agon is competition, as in football or a race. Alea is chance, as in dice or a lottery. Mimicry is pretending and role-play, as when children play shopkeeper. Ilinx is the thrill of dizziness and speed, as on a swing or a merry-go-round. He also described a line from paidia, free and unstructured play, to ludus, play shaped by strict rules. Most video games mix several kinds: a racing game combines agon and ilinx, a card game combines agon and alea. Naming the kind of play you want helps you choose the right rules.

Games as systems: A game is not just a list of rules; it is a system in which rules interact. A simple rule like enemies chase the nearest player plus another simple rule like players can hide behind walls can create interesting situations no designer wrote down, such as players luring enemies around corners. This is called emergence: complex behaviour arising from simple parts interacting. Programmers love emergence because a few lines of code can create hours of variety, but it also means bugs and exploits can emerge too, which is why testing games is hard.

Feedback loops in play: Every action in a game should produce a reaction the player can notice. Press jump and the character jumps at once with a small sound. Collect a coin and the counter goes up with a sparkle. This tight cycle of action, response and understanding is what makes games feel alive. In the HCI course you met feedback as a design principle for apps; games push it much further, because feedback is the main way players learn the rules without reading a manual.

What a video game adds: A board game needs players to enforce the rules themselves. A video game moves the rules into code, so the computer enforces them perfectly, keeps hidden information truly hidden, runs opponents, and does thousands of calculations per second. That lets designers build rules no group of humans could referee by hand, such as realistic ball physics or a hundred enemies moving at once. In return, everything must be specified exactly, which is where computer science comes in.

A tiny bit of history: Early computer games were built in research labs. Tennis for Two ran on an oscilloscope in 1958. Spacewar! was written at MIT in 1962 and spread between university computers. Pong, released by Atari in 1972, helped start the arcade industry. Since then games have moved through home consoles, personal computers, the internet and smartphones. Each step was driven partly by hardware and partly by programmers inventing new techniques, many of which you will learn in this course.

Why game development is a CS course: A game touches almost every area of computer science at once. It needs computer graphics to draw the world, linear algebra for movement and cameras, physics simulation, algorithms and data structures for speed, artificial intelligence for opponents, networking for multiplayer, operating systems knowledge for threads and memory, databases or files for saving progress, and human computer interaction for menus and controls. And it must do all of it within a tiny time budget, often 1/60 of a second per frame. That is why building even a small game is excellent practice for any software job.

Real-time software: Most programs wait for the user and then respond. A game keeps running even when the player does nothing: enemies move, timers count down, water flows. This makes a game a real-time, interactive simulation. It must read input, update the world and draw a new picture many times every second. Lesson 5 is dedicated to this game loop, the heartbeat of every game.

Who makes games: In a large studio, many roles work together. Game designers decide rules and goals. Programmers write gameplay code, engine code, tools, networking and AI. Artists create characters, environments and animations. Sound designers and composers make effects and music. Producers plan schedules and budgets. Quality assurance testers find bugs. In a small indie team or a game jam, one or two people may do all of these jobs, so it helps to understand a little of each.

The development process: Games usually go through stages. Concept: a short idea and pitch. Pre-production: prototypes to test whether the core idea is fun, and a design document. Production: building content and features. Then alpha, a version with all features roughly working, and beta, a version with all content in place that is mostly bug fixing. Then release, followed by updates and patches. Because fun is hard to predict, game teams prototype and playtest early and often, a theme that returns in lesson 25.

Example from daily life, ludo with cousins: Imagine playing ludo on Eid with cousins. The rules say you need a six to bring a token out. The goal is to bring all four tokens home. Feedback comes from the dice roll, the moving tokens and the shouting when someone gets cut. Uncertainty comes from the dice. Conflict comes from cutting each other's tokens. If you turned this into an app, you would have to write code for every one of those rules, show feedback with animation and sound, and maybe add a computer player. That is game development in miniature.

Example from a phone game you might design: Suppose you want a simple game where a boy catches falling mangoes in a basket during a summer storm. Rules: move the basket left and right; mangoes fall faster over time. Goal: catch as many as possible before missing three. Feedback: a soft thud and the score rising for each catch, a splash for each miss. Voluntary play: the player can quit any time and come back. Already you can see the questions this course will answer: how to move the basket smoothly, detect a catch, make difficulty rise fairly, and save the high score.

Common mistakes: Beginners often start with a huge dream game: an open world with hundreds of characters. That almost never gets finished. Experienced developers start with the smallest version that tests the core idea. Another mistake is thinking good graphics make a good game. Many well-loved games use simple shapes; what matters is rules, feedback and challenge. A third is ignoring feedback: if the player cannot tell what happened, the game feels broken even when the code is correct.

What exams ask: Expect questions such as: define a game and name its essential elements; distinguish a game from a toy and a puzzle; explain why games are called real-time interactive simulations; list the stages of game development; list the CS areas a game uses. When asked to define a game, give the four ingredients with one example each; it shows understanding rather than memorisation.

How this course is organised: Lessons 2 to 4 cover design: core loops, the MDA framework, balance, motivation, genres and platforms. Lessons 5 to 7 cover the technical skeleton: the game loop, engines and how game objects are organised. Lessons 8 to 16 cover the maths, rendering, input, physics and collision that make things move and touch. Lessons 17 to 19 cover AI and procedural generation. Lessons 20 to 24 cover audio, interface, saving, performance, 3D and multiplayer. Lesson 25 covers business, ethics, testing and publishing, and lesson 26 designs a small original game called Rickshaw Rush from start to finish.

Recap: A game is a voluntary activity with rules, a goal, feedback, and some conflict and uncertainty. Toys have no fixed goal, puzzles have a solution, games have challenges and outcomes. Video games move rules into code and run as real-time simulations, which is why they draw on nearly every part of computer science. Keep the four ingredients in mind: every technical topic in this course exists to serve them.
key_points: A game has four core ingredients: rules, a goal, feedback and voluntary play, plus conflict and uncertainty.
Bernard Suits: playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles.
Toys have no fixed goal, puzzles have a correct solution, games add rules, challenge and outcomes.
Uncertainty comes from chance, hidden information or the difficulty of performing well.
A video game is a real-time interactive simulation: it keeps updating even when the player does nothing.
Games combine graphics, maths, physics, AI, networking, OS, storage and HCI under a tight time budget.
Typical stages: concept, pre-production with prototypes, production, alpha, beta, release, updates.
Start small: prototype the core idea and test whether it is fun before building content.
lessons.tip: Whenever you play any game this week, pause and name its rules, goal, feedback and source of uncertainty. Doing this for ten games trains the designer's eye faster than reading theory.
lessons.task: Pick a traditional Bangladeshi game such as kanamachi, gollachut, kabaddi or ludo. On paper, write its rules, goal, feedback and sources of uncertainty. Then change one rule and predict how the play would feel different.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the core ingredients of a game discussed in the lesson?
quiz.explain: Rules, goal, feedback and voluntary play are the core ingredients. Graphics are optional; many great games use simple shapes.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes a puzzle from a toy?
options: A puzzle has a correct solution; a toy has no fixed goal
A toy always needs a computer
A toy always has a score
quiz.explain: A toy is for free play with no fixed goal; a puzzle is a game with a solution, finished once solved.

quiz.q: Why is a video game called a real-time interactive simulation?
options: Because it only runs when the player presses a key
Because it keeps updating the world many times per second while responding to input
quiz.explain: The world keeps changing even without input, and the game must read input, update and draw many times per second.

quiz.q: In ludo, which element mainly provides uncertainty?
quiz.explain: The dice introduce chance, so nobody knows the result in advance.

quiz.q: In which development stage are prototypes mainly built to test whether the core idea is fun?
quiz.explain: Pre-production uses quick prototypes and a design document to check the core idea before full production.

lessons.title: Game Design I: Verbs, Mechanics, Core Loops and MDA
lessons.content:
Watch someone play carrom. They line up the striker, flick it, watch the pieces scatter, see whether a piece went in, and line up again. Flick, watch, judge, repeat. That small cycle is the heart of carrom, and everything else, the board, the rules about the queen, the scoring, exists to make that cycle interesting again and again. Game designers call such a cycle the core loop. In this lesson you will learn the basic tools designers use to think about games: player verbs, mechanics, loops, the MDA framework, prototypes and the design document.

What game design is: Game design is deciding the rules, goals, choices and feedback of a game so that playing it creates a particular experience. It is not the same as drawing art or writing code, although designers must understand both. A designer asks questions like: what does the player do every few seconds? What choices do they face? How do they win or lose? What should they feel? The answers become a specification that programmers and artists then build.

Player verbs: A useful first step is to list the verbs of your game: the actions a player can take. In a platformer the verbs might be run, jump and stomp. In a farming game: plant, water, harvest, sell. In carrom: aim and flick. Strong games often have few verbs that combine in many ways. If your game has twenty verbs, players will struggle to learn them; if it has one verb, it must be very rich. Writing the verbs on a sheet of paper is the quickest way to see what your game really is.

Mechanics: A mechanic is a rule that defines how the game world responds to a verb or how the world changes by itself. Jump is a verb; the mechanic says you rise with a certain speed, gravity pulls you down, and you can only jump while standing on ground. Other mechanics include health that drops when you touch an enemy, a timer that ends the round, or a shop where coins buy upgrades. Mechanics are exact enough to program, which is why they are the bridge between design and code.

The core loop: The core loop is the short cycle of actions the player repeats most often. For a runner game it might be: see obstacle, dodge, collect coin, repeat, every couple of seconds. For a farming game: plant, wait, harvest, sell, buy seeds, repeat, every few minutes. If the core loop is not fun on its own, nothing built on top will save the game. That is why designers prototype the core loop first, often with plain boxes instead of art.

Secondary and meta loops: Around the core loop sit slower loops. A secondary loop might be: finish a level, earn stars, unlock the next area. A meta loop, spanning days, might be: collect coins over many sessions, upgrade your character, return tomorrow for a daily challenge. Picture nested circles, the fast core loop in the centre, slower loops outside it. Each outer loop gives meaning to the inner one: dodging is fun, but dodging to save coins for a new rickshaw paint job adds purpose.

Pseudo-code view of a loop: You can even write a core loop like code to check it is complete. For a mango-catching game: repeat { spawn mango at random x; player moves basket; if mango touches basket then score = score + 1 and play thud; if mango hits ground then misses = misses + 1; if misses == 3 then game over }. Writing it this way forces you to state every rule, such as what happens at three misses. Missing steps in this pseudo-code are usually missing design decisions.

The MDA framework: In 2004 Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek published the MDA framework: Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics. Mechanics are the rules and data in the code. Dynamics are the behaviour that emerges when players interact with those rules over time. Aesthetics are the emotional responses the player has: the fun. The key insight is about direction. The designer builds mechanics and can only hope the right dynamics and aesthetics follow. The player experiences it the other way round: they feel the aesthetics first and only slowly discover the mechanics.

MDA worked through: Take a simple rule for a cricket batting game: the bowler's speed rises by 2 km per hour every over. That is a mechanic. The dynamic that emerges is that players start safe, then must time shots more precisely as overs pass, and some may start taking risky shots early while the ball is slow. The aesthetic might be rising tension and the satisfaction of surviving. If testers instead report boredom early and frustration late, the designer goes back and adjusts the mechanic, perhaps starting faster and rising more slowly.

Eight kinds of fun: The MDA paper listed several aesthetics as a vocabulary instead of the vague word fun: sensation, the game as sense-pleasure; fantasy, make-believe; narrative, drama; challenge, an obstacle course; fellowship, social play; discovery, uncharted territory; expression, self-discovery and creativity; and submission, the game as a relaxing pastime. A puzzle game aims mostly at challenge and discovery; a dress-up game at expression; a calm fishing game at submission and sensation. Choosing your target aesthetics early keeps the design focused.

Goals, win and lose conditions: Every loop needs clear goals at its own scale. A short-term goal might be clear this gap; a medium-term goal, finish this level with three stars; a long-term goal, rescue the village or reach the top of the leaderboard. Each goal needs a win condition and usually a lose condition, written as exact rules: the round ends when the timer reaches zero; you lose when health is 0 or below. Players also invent their own goals, such as finishing without collecting any coins. Good designs leave room for such self-set challenges instead of punishing them.

Meaningful choices: Many designers say a game is a series of interesting decisions. A choice is meaningful when the options differ in an important way and none is obviously best. Choosing between a fast but fragile character and a slow but tough one is meaningful. Choosing between a sword that does 10 damage and an identical sword that does 12 is not, because everyone picks 12. When reviewing a design, list the choices the player makes and ask of each: would different players pick differently for good reasons?

Rules as systems and feedback loops: Mechanics connect into systems with feedback loops, a term from systems thinking. A positive feedback loop amplifies: the player who is ahead gets stronger, like a snowball. In some strategy games, more territory gives more income, which buys more army, which takes more territory. That makes games end decisively but can make losing players give up early. A negative feedback loop stabilises: the player behind gets help, like racing games where trailing cars get slightly better items. Designers mix both to keep matches exciting to the end.

Paper prototyping: Before code, many designers prototype on paper with cards, dice, coins and graph paper. A turn-based strategy game can be tested on a chessboard with buttons as units. Even real-time games can be partly tested: a designer can act as the computer and move enemies by hand. Paper prototypes take minutes to change, so you can try ten rule versions in an afternoon. The HCI course used paper prototypes for app screens; games use them for rules.

Digital prototypes and vertical slices: The next step is a rough digital prototype: coloured boxes, no menus, only the core loop. Its only question is: is this fun? Later a team may build a vertical slice: one small part of the game, such as a single level, finished to near-final quality in art, sound and code, to show what the full game will feel like. A prototype answers is it fun; a vertical slice answers can we make it look and play like this at scale.

The game design document: A game design document, often shortened to GDD, records the design so the whole team builds the same game. Typical sections: a one-line pitch, target players and platform, core loop and verbs, mechanics with exact numbers, levels or content list, controls, user interface screens, art and audio style, and monetisation if any. Modern teams keep it short and living, often as a wiki, updated as playtests teach them things, rather than a hundred-page book nobody reads.

The one-page design: For student projects, a one-page design is often enough. It answers: what is the game in one sentence; who is it for; what are the verbs; what is the core loop; how does the player win and lose; what is the target aesthetic; what is the smallest version worth testing. If you cannot fill one page, the idea is not yet clear; if you need ten pages, the first version is too big.

Example, a tea-stall game: Suppose you design a game about running a roadside cha stall in Chattogram. Verbs: brew, pour, serve, collect money. Core loop, about ten seconds: a customer arrives with an order, you pour the right tea, serve before they lose patience, earn taka. Secondary loop: end of day, buy better kettle or more cups. Mechanics: each customer has a patience timer; serving wrong tea halves the tip. Target aesthetics: challenge and a cosy sense of sensation. Already you could paper-prototype it with cards for customers and a phone timer.

Example, a school quiz race: A second design: two players race across a board drawn like the map of Bangladesh, answering quiz cards about districts. Verb: answer. Mechanic: correct answer moves you two districts, wrong answer one district back. Dynamic: players start guessing wildly when behind. If testing shows the leading player always wins, add a negative feedback mechanic: the trailing player picks the category. That small change is exactly the MDA cycle at work.

Common mistakes: Confusing mechanics with aesthetics is the most common exam error; a jump is a mechanic, excitement is an aesthetic. Another is designing features instead of loops: a list of fifty features with no clear repeated action. A third is falling in love with the first version; design is iterative, and the prototype's job is to be thrown away. Finally, beginners forget the lose condition: without a way to fail, challenge disappears.

What exams ask: Define mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics with an example each; explain why designer and player see MDA in opposite directions; describe a core loop for a given game; distinguish positive and negative feedback loops; list the main sections of a GDD; explain the purpose of a prototype versus a vertical slice.

Recap: A designer starts from verbs, turns them into exact mechanics, and arranges them in a fast core loop wrapped by slower secondary and meta loops. The MDA framework reminds you that you only control mechanics, while players experience dynamics and aesthetics. Good games offer meaningful choices and balance positive and negative feedback. Prototype on paper, then in rough code, and record decisions in a short living design document. Next lesson covers balance, difficulty and what motivates players.
key_points: Player verbs are the actions a player can take; listing them is the fastest way to see a game.
A mechanic is an exact rule for how the world responds to verbs or changes by itself.
The core loop is the short, most repeated cycle; secondary and meta loops give it longer-term meaning.
MDA: designers build mechanics, which create dynamics in play, which produce aesthetics (emotions).
Designers see M to D to A; players experience A first and discover M slowly.
Meaningful choices have important differences and no obviously best option.
Positive feedback loops snowball; negative feedback loops help the trailing player and stabilise.
Prototype on paper and in rough code first; a vertical slice shows near-final quality; a GDD records decisions.
lessons.tip: Before writing any code for a game idea, write its core loop as five lines of pseudo-code. If you cannot, the design is not ready; if you can, you already know what to build first.
lessons.task: Choose a game you play often. Write its verbs, its core loop, one secondary loop and one meta loop. Then name one mechanic, the dynamic it creates and the aesthetic it aims for, in a three-column table.

quiz.q: In the MDA framework, which part does the designer directly control?
quiz.explain: Designers write the mechanics; dynamics emerge in play and aesthetics are the player's emotional responses.

quiz.q: Which of these is an aesthetic in MDA terms?
options: Gravity of 30 units per second squared
Collect three keys to open the door
Rising tension in the final minute
quiz.explain: Tension is an emotional response, an aesthetic. The others are mechanics.

quiz.q: What is a core loop?
options: The short cycle of actions the player repeats most often
The main while loop in the engine source code
quiz.explain: The core loop is the most repeated cycle of play, such as see obstacle, dodge, collect.

quiz.q: In a strategy game, more land gives more money, which buys more soldiers, which win more land. This is a:
quiz.explain: The leader gets stronger and stronger, which is a positive (amplifying) feedback loop.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a vertical slice?
options: To list every bug in the game
To show a small part of the game at near-final quality
quiz.explain: A vertical slice finishes one small part, such as a level, to near-final quality to show the target experience.

lessons.title: Game Design II: Balance, Difficulty and Player Motivation
lessons.content:
Think of a gully cricket match where one boy bowls far faster than everyone else. For the first few overs it is exciting; after that nobody else gets a chance, the smaller kids stop enjoying it, and someone suggests he bowl with the other hand. Without knowing the word, the children are balancing their game. In this lesson you will learn how designers make games fair, how they shape difficulty over time, and what actually motivates people to keep playing, with a few numbers worked out along the way.

What balance means: A game is balanced when its choices are fair and interesting: no single strategy, character or item is so strong that everyone must use it, and no option is so weak that nobody ever picks it. Balance does not mean every option is identical. It means the differences create trade-offs. A fast character with low health and a slow one with high health can both be good, in different situations and for different players.

Symmetric and asymmetric games: In a symmetric game every player starts with the same options, as in chess apart from who moves first, or a football match. Balance mostly means fixing first-move advantages and map unfairness. In an asymmetric game players have different abilities or goals, such as one side defending a fort and the other attacking it. Asymmetric games are harder to balance because you must compare very different things, so designers rely heavily on numbers and testing.

Dominant strategies: A dominant strategy is one that is always best no matter what others do. Once players find it, the game collapses into repeating it, and choice disappears. Example: if a racing game's shortcut is both shorter and safer, everyone takes it and the rest of the track is wasted. Fix it by adding a cost: the shortcut is shorter but bumpy, so you lose speed if you hit the rocks. The goal is that every strong option has a weakness.

Intransitive balance: Rock, paper, scissors is the classic balanced system: each choice beats one and loses to one, so no choice dominates. Many strategy games use the same idea: archers beat foot soldiers, cavalry beats archers, spearmen beat cavalry. This is called intransitive balance, because the relation beats does not chain: A beats B and B beats C does not mean A beats C. It forces players to read what the opponent is doing instead of always picking one unit.

Balancing with numbers, damage per second: Designers often reduce a weapon to one comparable number. Damage per second, DPS, is damage per hit times hits per second. A sword does 12 damage at 1.5 hits per second: DPS = 12 x 1.5 = 18. A bow does 30 damage at 0.5 shots per second: DPS = 30 x 0.5 = 15. Against an enemy with 90 health, the sword kills in 90 / 18 = 5 seconds, the bow in 90 / 15 = 6 seconds. The bow is slower but safer, because you shoot from range. That trade-off is balance.

Spotting an overpowered option: Now add a spear doing 20 damage at 1 hit per second: DPS = 20, killing the 90-health enemy in 4.5 seconds, and suppose it also has more reach than the sword. It beats the sword in both speed and safety, so it dominates. Fixes include lowering damage to 16, making it cost more coins, or making it slow to swing back after a miss. A spreadsheet with every weapon's DPS, range and cost makes such problems visible before players find them.

Expected value and chance: When chance is involved, compare expected values. A punch does 10 damage, with a 20 percent chance of a critical hit doing double. Expected damage per punch = 0.8 x 10 + 0.2 x 20 = 8 + 4 = 12. A steady punch doing 12 every time has the same average but less excitement and less risk. Designers choose variance on purpose: high variance creates dramatic moments, low variance rewards planning. The Probability course gave you the tools; games apply them constantly.

Risk and reward: Good designs pair risk with reward. A coin placed near a pit is worth more than a coin in the open. A player who attacks without defending finishes faster but may die. If a risky action gives the same reward as a safe one, players will choose safety and the game becomes dull. If risk gives much more reward, brave players feel clever. This principle is one of the easiest to check in a design: list every risk and ask what the player gains for taking it.

Difficulty curves: A difficulty curve shows how hard the game is over time. A straight steady rise sounds logical but feels tiring. Most games use a sawtooth or wave shape: difficulty rises through a level, peaks with a boss or a hard section, then drops at the start of the next level so the player can enjoy their new skill, and rises again from a slightly higher base. This rhythm of tension and release keeps players engaged far longer than constant pressure.

Flow: The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described flow: a state of deep, enjoyable focus when a challenge matches a person's skill. Too hard compared with skill leads to anxiety; too easy leads to boredom. Picture a channel between those two regions on a graph of challenge against skill. As the player's skill grows, the challenge must grow too, keeping them in the channel. Games are unusually good at producing flow because they can measure performance and adjust immediately.

Teaching through levels: Players learn by doing. A classic pattern is to introduce a new mechanic in a safe place, let the player practise it with a small risk, combine it with something already known, and finally test it under pressure. For example, introduce a moving platform over solid ground, then over a shallow pit, then together with a jumping enemy, then in a fast sequence. Each step adds one new idea. Teaching this way replaces long tutorials and wall-of-text instructions.

Dynamic difficulty adjustment: Some games change difficulty based on how the player is doing, called dynamic difficulty adjustment. If a player dies three times in a row at the same spot, the game might slightly reduce enemy speed or give an extra health pack. A simple rule could be: if deaths_here >= 3 then enemy_speed = enemy_speed x 0.9. Done well, players never notice. Done clumsily, skilled players feel patronised or exploit it by losing on purpose. Many games instead let players choose easy, normal or hard, which is more transparent.

Why people play, motivation: Psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory says people are intrinsically motivated when three needs are met: competence, feeling skilled and improving; autonomy, having real choices; and relatedness, connecting with others. Games can satisfy all three: levels that show growing skill, choices about how to play, and friends to play with. Intrinsic motivation, doing something because it is enjoyable in itself, tends to last longer than extrinsic motivation, doing it for an outside reward.

Extrinsic rewards: Points, badges, stars, unlocks and daily login rewards are extrinsic motivators. They can help guide players, but if overused they can crowd out intrinsic enjoyment: players start chasing the badge and stop enjoying the activity. A useful rule is that rewards should celebrate and support play the player already enjoys, not replace it. Lesson 25 returns to rewards designed to manipulate players, such as loot boxes, and why they raise ethical concerns.

Reward schedules: Behavioural psychology describes how the timing of rewards affects behaviour. A fixed schedule gives a reward every set number of actions, such as a bonus every tenth coin. A variable schedule gives rewards unpredictably, such as a random rare drop. Variable rewards are known to produce persistent repeated behaviour, which is why random loot is so compelling, and also why it must be used responsibly. Mixing predictable progress with occasional surprises usually feels best.

Player types: Richard Bartle, studying text-based online worlds in 1996, suggested four kinds of players: achievers, who want points and levels; explorers, who want to discover how the world works; socialisers, who want to interact with others; and killers, who want to compete with or act on other players. It is a rough model, not a scientific law, and real players mix types. Its value is reminding designers that one game can attract different people for different reasons, so a design should offer something to more than one type.

Example, a Ludo app's difficulty: Suppose your Ludo app has a computer player. Easy mode might pick random legal moves; normal mode prefers cutting tokens; hard mode also protects its own tokens and plans safe squares. Watching testers, you notice beginners quit after losing four games straight to normal mode. A fix: start new players on easy, and suggest normal after they win twice. That small change keeps them in the flow channel instead of the anxiety zone.

Example, an exam-practice quiz game: An app for SSC students asks maths questions against a timer. If every question is equally hard, strong students get bored and weak ones give up. Using a sawtooth curve, each set of ten questions starts with two easy ones, climbs to harder ones and ends with a bonus challenge question worth double points, a risk-reward choice the student can skip. Competence grows, autonomy comes from choosing the bonus, and relatedness from comparing scores with classmates.

Common mistakes: Designers often balance for themselves: they know the game deeply and find it too easy, so they make it brutal for new players. Always test with fresh players, ideally people who have never seen the game, and watch silently instead of explaining. Another mistake is balancing only by feel; numbers like DPS, time to kill and expected value catch problems early. A third is fixing every problem with more rewards instead of improving the core loop. Finally, students confuse balance with sameness; balance needs trade-offs, not copies.

What exams ask: Define balance and dominant strategy; compute DPS or time to kill for two weapons and compare; compute an expected value with a critical hit chance; sketch a sawtooth difficulty curve and explain it; explain flow with the challenge-skill graph; name the three needs of self-determination theory and Bartle's four player types; distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic motivation with examples.

Recap: Balance means every strong choice has a weakness and no strategy dominates. Numbers such as DPS, time to kill and expected value make balance measurable; intransitive designs like rock, paper, scissors keep choices alive. Difficulty should rise in waves and match growing skill to keep players in flow. People play for competence, autonomy and relatedness; extrinsic rewards help only when they support that. Different players seek different things, so test with real, fresh players and adjust.
key_points: Balance means trade-offs: no dominant strategy and no useless option, not identical options.
DPS = damage per hit x hits per second; 12 x 1.5 = 18, so a 90-health enemy dies in 5 seconds.
Expected damage with 20 percent double crits on 10 damage = 0.8 x 10 + 0.2 x 20 = 12.
Intransitive balance (rock, paper, scissors) stops any single choice from dominating.
Sawtooth difficulty curves alternate tension and release; flow happens when challenge matches skill.
Self-determination theory: competence, autonomy and relatedness drive intrinsic motivation.
Variable reward schedules are powerful and must be used responsibly; extrinsic rewards should support enjoyment.
Bartle's player types: achievers, explorers, socialisers, killers; a rough model reminding designers players differ.
lessons.tip: Keep a balancing spreadsheet from day one: one row per weapon, enemy or upgrade, with columns for damage, rate, DPS, cost and time to kill. Ten minutes of formulas saves days of guessing.
lessons.task: Invent three weapons for a small game, each with damage per hit, hits per second and range. Compute each one's DPS and time to kill a 120-health enemy. Adjust the numbers until each weapon is best in some situation and none dominates.

quiz.q: A weapon does 25 damage per hit at 0.8 hits per second. What is its DPS?
What is a dominant strategy?
options: A strategy that only works on easy mode
A strategy that is best regardless of what others do, which removes real choice
Any strategy chosen by the winner
quiz.explain: If one strategy is always best, players stop choosing, so designers add costs or counters.

quiz.q: A hit does 10 damage with a 25 percent chance of a triple-damage critical. What is the expected damage per hit?
According to the idea of flow, what happens when the challenge is much higher than the player's skill?
quiz.explain: Too much challenge for the skill level produces anxiety; too little produces boredom.

quiz.q: Which three needs does self-determination theory name?
quiz.explain: Deci and Ryan's theory names competence, autonomy and relatedness as needs behind intrinsic motivation.

lessons.title: Game Genres and Platforms
lessons.content:
Walk into any bookshop at Nilkhet and the books are sorted: novels here, science there, poetry in the corner. Sorting helps buyers find what they like and helps writers know what readers expect. Games are sorted the same way, into genres, and they run on different machines, called platforms. A puzzle game on a phone and a racing game on a console are different not only in content but in how players hold the device, how long they play and what controls they have. This lesson surveys the main genres and platforms and shows how each shapes design and engineering.

What a genre is: In games, a genre is mostly defined by how you play, the core mechanics and loop, not by the setting or story. A game set in space and a game set in a village can both be platformers if you run and jump between platforms. This differs from films, where genre usually means the story type, like comedy or horror. Game genres are fuzzy and constantly mixed, but they give designers and players a shared shorthand.

Action games: Action games test reflexes, timing and hand-eye coordination. Sub-genres include shooters, where you aim and fire; fighting games, where two characters battle with combos of moves; and beat-em-ups, where one hero fights crowds. Technically they demand low input latency, steady frame rates and precise collision detection, because a hit that should have landed but did not feels unfair. Much of lessons 5, 11 and 14 to 16 matters most for action games.

Platformers: In a platformer the player runs and jumps across platforms, avoiding pits and enemies. The feel of the jump is everything: how high, how fast you fall, how much control you have in the air. That is pure physics tuning, which lesson 12 works through with numbers. Platformers are a common first project because the core loop is clear and 2D art can be simple rectangles at first.

Puzzle games: Puzzle games challenge thinking rather than reflexes: matching tiles, sliding blocks, connecting pipes, logic grids. They often have no time pressure and can be played in short bursts, which suits phones. Engineering challenges include level design tools and making sure every level is solvable, sometimes checked with a search algorithm from the AI course. Puzzle design leans heavily on the teaching-through-levels idea from the last lesson.

Role-playing games: In a role-playing game, RPG, the player controls a character who grows stronger through experience points, levels, equipment and choices, often within a long story. RPGs are heavy on data: hundreds of items, quests and dialogue lines, usually stored in spreadsheets or data files rather than code. Balance spreadsheets like the DPS table in lesson 3 are essential. Saving and loading, lesson 21, is critical, because players invest many hours.

Strategy games: Strategy games reward planning. In turn-based strategy, players take turns, like chess, so they can think as long as they like. In real-time strategy, RTS, everyone acts at once, managing resources, building and commanding many units. Strategy games need good AI opponents, pathfinding for many units at once, and careful balance using intransitive designs. Turn-based games are also easier to make multiplayer, because only moves, not continuous positions, travel across the network.

Simulation games: Simulations model some part of the world: running a city, a farm, a shop, a hospital, flying a plane or driving a truck. Some aim for realism, like flight simulators used in training; others are playful management games. They rely on systems of interacting rules and feedback loops, as in lesson 2. A simulation of running a tea stall or managing traffic in Dhaka would fit here.

Sports and racing: Sports games adapt real sports such as cricket or football; racing games focus on driving fast around tracks. Both need believable physics for balls and vehicles, animation that matches real athletes, and AI teammates or opponents. Racing games often use the negative feedback trick called rubber-banding, where trailing computer cars speed up a little to keep races close. Players notice when it is too strong, so it must be tuned gently.

Casual, hyper-casual and idle: Casual games are easy to learn, played in short sessions, and appeal to people who would not call themselves gamers. Hyper-casual games go further: one-tap controls and a loop understandable in seconds. Idle or incremental games keep progressing while the player is away, so the meta loop is checking back later. These designs are common on phones and are usually funded by ads, which lesson 25 discusses.

Roguelikes and other mixes: Roguelikes, named after an old game called Rogue, generate a new level layout every run, and death usually means starting again. Lighter versions, often called roguelites, let some progress carry over between runs. They rely on procedural generation, lesson 19. Many modern games are hybrids: an action game with RPG levelling, a puzzle game with story, a strategy game with card collecting. Genre labels are a starting point for discussion, not a rulebook.

Adventure and narrative games: Adventure games focus on exploring places, talking to characters and solving story-based puzzles, such as finding which object opens which door. Narrative games put the story first, often with branching dialogue where choices change what happens later. Engineering here means dialogue systems, branching story graphs stored as data, and tracking many flags such as talked_to_grandmother = true. A branching story is really a directed graph, so the Data Structures course quietly powers it.

Serious and educational games: Some games have a purpose beyond entertainment: teaching maths, training pilots or doctors, raising awareness about flood safety, or helping patients with physiotherapy exercises. These are called serious games, and educational games are the best-known kind. The design challenge is to make the learning part of the core loop, not a quiz glued onto unrelated play. A game where you must balance a family budget through a monsoon season teaches by making you live the trade-offs.

What a platform is: A platform is the hardware and software environment a game runs on: personal computer, game console, mobile phone or tablet, web browser, or virtual and augmented reality headsets. Each platform has its own processor and graphics power, memory, input devices, screen size, operating system, store and rules. Choosing a platform early shapes almost every later decision, from art style to controls to monetisation.

PC: Personal computers offer keyboard and mouse, which allow precise aiming and many shortcut keys, plus large screens. PCs vary enormously, from old office laptops to powerful gaming machines, so PC games usually provide graphics settings: resolution, texture quality, shadows. Developers must test on a range of hardware. Digital storefronts distribute most PC games, and players expect features like remappable keys and windowed modes.

Consoles: Consoles are dedicated gaming machines connected to a TV and controlled with a gamepad. Because every unit of a given console model has the same hardware, developers can optimise precisely for it. Publishing on consoles usually requires approval from the console maker, special development kits and certification tests that check things like how the game handles a disconnected controller. Gamepads have fewer buttons than keyboards, so interfaces must be simple and readable from a sofa.

Mobile: Phones and tablets are the most widely owned gaming platform. Their constraints, which you met in the Mobile App Development course, shape game design: a small touch screen where fingers cover part of the view, limited battery, heat that can force the processor to slow down, varied screen sizes and aspect ratios, interruptions from calls and notifications, and players who often play in short sessions while waiting or travelling. Good mobile games use simple touch controls, pause automatically when interrupted and save often.

Web: Browser games run using HTML5 canvas, WebGL and JavaScript or WebAssembly. Their big advantage is zero installation: a link is enough to play. They suit game jams, prototypes, educational games and casual games. Limits include varying browser performance and that players can close a tab at any time. Many engines can export a web build alongside other platforms.

VR and AR: Virtual reality headsets put the player inside a 3D world, tracking head and hand movement. Their key engineering demand is high, steady frame rates and low latency, because lag between head movement and the image can cause motion sickness. Augmented reality overlays game objects on the real world through a phone camera or glasses. Both require designs built around the body: movement methods such as teleporting are used to reduce discomfort.

How platform shapes design: Session length: a console player may sit for two hours; a mobile player may have three minutes on a bus. Input: a mouse can aim to a single pixel; a thumb on glass cannot, so mobile shooters often add aim assistance. Screen: a TV is viewed from far away, so text must be large; a phone in portrait mode is narrow and tall. Performance: a budget phone has a fraction of a gaming PC's power. A game moved from one platform to another, called a port, usually needs redesign, not just recompiling.

Example, Bangladesh is mobile-first: Most players in Bangladesh first meet games on a smartphone, and most smartphones in use here are Android phones, many of them budget models with limited memory and storage. A Bangladeshi student designing a game for local players should therefore think mobile first: a small download size, smooth play on modest hardware, support for low-bandwidth or offline play, short sessions that fit a commute, and Bangla text that renders correctly. Testing on a cheap phone, not only on a flagship, matters.

Example, one idea, three platforms: Take a game about steering a boat on a river in Barishal, avoiding logs. On PC, you could steer with arrow keys and show a wide view of the river. On a phone, you might tilt the device or swipe, use portrait mode so the river runs upward, and make sessions two minutes long. On the web, you would keep the download tiny so it starts instantly from a shared link. Same core loop, three different designs.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often define genre by theme, saying a zombie game is a genre; it is a setting. Another mistake is designing for your own powerful laptop and forgetting the target device. Exams ask you to define genre and platform, describe the characteristics of given genres, compare PC, console and mobile constraints, explain why a port needs redesign, and suggest a platform for a given game idea with reasons.

Recap: Genres group games by how they are played: action, platformer, puzzle, RPG, strategy, simulation, sports and racing, casual, roguelike and many hybrids. Platforms are the environments games run on: PC, console, mobile, web and VR or AR, each with its own input, screen, power, store and session length. Choose the platform early, let it shape controls and scope, and in Bangladesh think mobile-first with modest hardware in mind.
key_points: A game genre is defined mainly by how you play (mechanics and loop), not by setting or story.
Main genres: action, platformer, puzzle, RPG, strategy (turn-based and real-time), simulation, sports and racing, casual, roguelike, plus many hybrids.
A platform is the hardware and software a game runs on: PC, console, mobile, web, VR and AR.
PCs vary widely so games offer settings; consoles have fixed hardware and certification.
Mobile constraints: small touch screen, battery, heat, varied screens, interruptions and short sessions.
VR needs high steady frame rates and low latency to avoid motion sickness.
Platform shapes session length, input, readable text and performance; a port usually needs redesign.
In Bangladesh, design mobile-first for modest Android phones, small downloads and Bangla text.
lessons.tip: For every game you analyse, write two labels: genre (how it plays) and platform (where it runs). Then ask how the game would change on a different platform; this one question exercises most of this lesson.
lessons.task: Pick one simple game idea. Write a short table with three columns, PC, mobile and web, and fill rows for controls, screen orientation, session length, download size and one design change each platform needs.

quiz.q: What mainly defines a game's genre?
options: How it is played, its core mechanics and loop
Its setting, such as space or a village
The engine it was made with
quiz.explain: Game genres are mostly about gameplay; a space game and a village game can both be platformers.

quiz.q: Which genre is built around randomly generated runs where death usually means starting again?
quiz.explain: Roguelikes generate new layouts each run and usually restart on death; roguelites keep some progress.

quiz.q: Why can console developers optimise very precisely?
options: Every unit of a given console model has the same hardware
quiz.explain: Fixed hardware lets developers tune exactly for one known machine.

quiz.q: Which is the key technical demand that helps avoid motion sickness in VR?
options: High, steady frame rate and low latency
quiz.explain: Lag between head movement and image can cause sickness, so VR needs fast, steady rendering.

quiz.q: Which design choice best suits a mobile-first game for players in Bangladesh?
options: A very large download that needs a fast connection
Small download, smooth play on modest phones and short sessions
Only supporting the newest flagship phones
quiz.explain: Many players use budget Android phones, so small size, modest requirements and short sessions fit best.

lessons.title: The Game Loop: Input, Update, Render and Delta Time
lessons.content:
Imagine a flip book where, instead of drawing all pages in advance, an artist draws each next page at the moment you are about to see it, and changes the drawing based on what you shouted a moment ago. That is a video game. Every fraction of a second the program asks: what did the player do, how does the world change, and what does it look like now? Then it does it again, and again, sixty or more times every second. This repeating cycle is the game loop, and it is the single most important structure in game programming.

Why games need a loop: An ordinary app, like a calculator, is event-driven: it sits idle until you tap a button, reacts, and goes back to waiting. A game cannot wait. Enemies keep walking, rain keeps falling and the timer keeps counting even if the player touches nothing. So instead of waiting for events, a game runs a loop that continuously advances the world in small steps of time and redraws it. Even engines that hide the loop from you, which most do, are running one underneath.

The three stages: The classic loop has three stages. Process input: read the keyboard, touch screen or gamepad and turn it into intentions, such as move left or jump. Update: advance the game world by one step, moving objects, applying physics, running AI, checking collisions, updating scores and timers. Render: draw the current state of the world to the screen. In pseudo-code: while running { processInput(); update(); render(); }. Each pass through the loop produces one frame, one picture on the screen.

Frames per second and frame time: The number of frames produced each second is the frame rate, measured in frames per second, fps. Its inverse is the frame time: how long each frame takes. At 60 fps each frame gets 1000 / 60 = 16.67 milliseconds. At 30 fps it gets 33.33 ms; at 144 fps only about 6.94 ms. Frame time is more useful for engineers than fps, because time adds up: if input takes 1 ms, update 6 ms and render 8 ms, the total 15 ms fits in a 60 fps budget. Lesson 22 works through these budgets in detail.

The naive loop and its bug: The simplest update moves things a fixed amount per frame: x = x + 3. On a machine running at 60 fps, the object moves 3 x 60 = 180 pixels per second. On a slower phone running at 30 fps, it moves only 90 pixels per second, half as fast. The game literally plays at different speeds on different hardware. Very old games really did this, which is why some of them run impossibly fast on modern computers. The fix is to make movement depend on time, not on frame count.

Delta time: Delta time, usually written dt, is the time that passed since the last frame, in seconds. Movement becomes speed times time: x = x + speed x dt. Suppose speed is 200 pixels per second. At 60 fps, dt is about 0.0167 s, so each frame the object moves 200 x 0.0167, about 3.33 pixels; over 60 frames that is 200 pixels. At 30 fps, dt is about 0.0333, so it moves about 6.67 pixels per frame; over 30 frames that is again 200 pixels. Same speed in the world, regardless of frame rate. This is called a variable timestep loop.

Measuring delta time: The loop reads a high-resolution clock each frame: now = clock(); dt = now - last; last = now. Engines hand you dt directly: Unity exposes it as Time.deltaTime, Godot passes delta to its process functions, and Flame passes dt to each component's update method. Units matter: some clocks return milliseconds, and mixing milliseconds with speeds in pixels per second is a classic bug that makes things move 1000 times too fast.

Problems with variable timesteps: Delta time fixes speed, but not everything. Physics calculations give slightly different answers with different step sizes, so a jump might reach a slightly different height on a fast PC than on a slow phone. Very large steps can cause tunnelling, where a fast object moves from one side of a thin wall to the other in a single frame and never collides, lesson 13. And the game is not exactly repeatable: replaying the same inputs can give a different outcome, which breaks replays and some kinds of multiplayer.

Fixed timestep: The alternative is to always update the simulation with the same dt, say exactly 1/60 of a second, no matter how fast frames are drawn. Physics then behaves identically on every machine, which makes jumps consistent, collisions reliable and simulations deterministic, meaning the same inputs always produce the same result. But real frames do not arrive exactly every 16.67 ms. The solution is an accumulator that stores leftover time.

The accumulator loop: In pseudo-code: acc = 0; while running { frame = now - last; last = now; acc = acc + frame; processInput(); while acc >= STEP { update(STEP); acc = acc - STEP; } render(); }. Each frame adds the real time to the bank, then runs as many fixed updates as the bank can pay for. Slow frames pay for several updates; fast frames may pay for none, in which case the screen is simply redrawn.

Accumulator worked: Let STEP = 16.67 ms. Frame 1 takes 25 ms: acc = 25, one update runs, acc = 25 - 16.67 = 8.33. Frame 2 takes 10 ms: acc = 18.33, one update, acc = 1.67. Frame 3 takes 40 ms: acc = 41.67, two updates, acc = 8.33. Over 75 ms the simulation advanced 4 steps, 66.67 ms, with 8.33 ms still banked for the next frame. Over time the simulation keeps pace with real time exactly, while every individual update uses the same dt.

Interpolation for smooth rendering: With a fixed timestep, the rendered picture can stutter, because the leftover time in the accumulator is not shown. The fix is to draw objects between their previous and current simulated positions. The fraction alpha = acc / STEP says how far into the next step we are. After frame 1 above, alpha = 8.33 / 16.67 = 0.5, so we draw each object halfway between its last two positions: drawX = prevX + (currX - prevX) x alpha. This costs a frame of visual delay but looks smooth. It is the lerp you met in Computer Graphics, applied to time.

The spiral of death: If one update takes longer than STEP of real time, for example a 20 ms update on a slow phone with a 16.67 ms step, each frame adds more debt to the accumulator than the updates can pay off. The loop runs more updates per frame, which makes frames slower, which adds more debt: the game freezes. This is called the spiral of death. Defences: cap the frame time added to the accumulator, for example at 0.25 s, or cap the number of updates per frame and let the game slow down gracefully instead.

Semi-fixed and engine approaches: Many engines combine both ideas. Physics and gameplay that need consistency run in a fixed update at a set rate, while animation, camera smoothing and visual effects run in the variable per-frame update with dt. Unity separates FixedUpdate from Update, and Godot separates physics processing from idle processing in the same spirit. Knowing which code belongs where is a key skill: movement of a physics body in the fixed step, reading a button press every frame.

Vsync and frame pacing: The monitor refreshes at its own rate, often 60 Hz. If the game swaps the finished image while the monitor is halfway through drawing, the top and bottom halves come from different frames: screen tearing, which you met in Computer Graphics with double buffering. Vertical synchronisation, vsync, makes the game wait for the monitor's refresh before swapping. It removes tearing but can add input latency, and if a frame misses the deadline it waits a whole extra refresh, so fps can drop from 60 straight to 30. On phones the operating system usually drives the frame timing.

Sleeping and power: On a PC a loop that runs as fast as possible might render 1000 frames per second, heating the machine for no benefit. On a phone that would drain the battery quickly. Games therefore cap their frame rate, either through vsync or by sleeping until the next frame is due. Many mobile games offer a 30 fps battery-saving mode. Flutter's Flame, for example, runs its loop on the frames the operating system schedules, rather than spinning freely.

Loops and threads: In a simple game everything runs on one thread, in order. Larger engines spread work across processor cores: one thread prepares rendering commands for the previous frame while another updates the current one, and worker threads handle physics, audio mixing or loading assets in the background. The idea of input, update, render stays the same; only the stages overlap in time. For a student project, a single-threaded loop is easier to reason about and almost always fast enough.

Example, cricket ball on two phones: Two friends in Rajshahi play the same cricket game, one on a new phone at 60 fps and one on an old phone at 30 fps. With the naive per-frame movement, the ball would reach the batsman twice as fast on the new phone: unfair and unplayable. With delta time, both balls travel at, say, 25 metres per second in the game world. With a fixed physics step and the accumulator, the ball's bounce is identical on both phones, so the same shot gives the same result. Only the smoothness of the picture differs.

Example, a turn-based board game: A carrom or Ludo app does not need a continuous simulation while waiting for a move, so it can render only when something changes, saving battery. During the short animation of a striker shot, though, it runs a fixed-timestep physics loop so the pieces bounce consistently. Choosing the loop to fit the game, not copying the most complex one, is good engineering.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to multiply by dt, or multiplying by it twice; mixing milliseconds and seconds; putting physics in the variable update so jumps differ on different machines; not capping dt, so a pause in the debugger produces one giant step that teleports the player through walls; and doing heavy work such as loading files inside the loop, causing hitches. Exams ask you to draw the game loop, explain fps versus frame time, compute frame time for a given fps, show how delta time fixes speed differences, and trace an accumulator loop.

Recap: The game loop repeats input, update and render, producing one frame per pass. Frame time is 1000 / fps milliseconds. Variable timesteps multiply movement by delta time so speed is the same on all hardware; fixed timesteps with an accumulator make physics consistent and deterministic, with interpolation for smooth drawing. Guard against the spiral of death, understand vsync, and cap the frame rate to save power. Next lesson looks at the engines that run this loop for you.
key_points: The game loop repeats three stages: process input, update the world, render a frame.
Frame time = 1000 / fps ms: 16.67 ms at 60 fps, 33.33 ms at 30 fps.
Moving a fixed amount per frame makes speed depend on hardware; use x = x + speed x dt instead.
Variable timesteps are simple but make physics slightly different per machine and can cause tunnelling.
A fixed timestep with an accumulator runs updates of identical size, giving consistent, deterministic physics.
Accumulator trace: frames of 25, 10, 40 ms with a 16.67 ms step run 1, 1, 2 updates, leaving 8.33 ms.
Interpolate drawing with alpha = acc / STEP; cap frame time to avoid the spiral of death.
Vsync removes tearing but can add latency; cap frame rate to save battery on phones.
lessons.tip: When learning any engine, find out first where it gives you delta time and where its fixed update lives. Most early bugs in student games come from putting code in the wrong one.
lessons.task: On paper, trace an accumulator loop with STEP = 20 ms for frames of 15, 30, 18 and 50 ms. Write how many updates run each frame, the accumulator after each frame and the interpolation alpha. Then check your answers with a five-line program.

quiz.q: What is the frame time at 50 frames per second?
quiz.explain: Frame time = 1000 / 50 = 20 milliseconds.

quiz.q: A game moves a sprite 4 pixels every frame with no delta time. How fast does it move at 30 fps?
quiz.explain: 4 x 30 = 120 pixels per second; at 60 fps it would be 240, which is the bug delta time fixes.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a fixed timestep for physics?
options: Every update uses the same dt, so physics is consistent and deterministic
It removes the need for collision detection
It makes the game ignore slow hardware
quiz.explain: Identical step sizes give the same physical results on every machine for the same inputs.

quiz.q: With STEP = 16.67 ms and acc = 5 ms, a 30 ms frame arrives. How many fixed updates run?
quiz.explain: acc becomes 35 ms; two steps of 16.67 ms fit (33.33 ms), leaving 1.67 ms.

quiz.q: What is the spiral of death?
options: Updates take longer than the time they simulate, so the accumulator debt keeps growing and the game freezes
The screen tears because vsync is off
Objects pass through walls at high speed
The player loses all lives in one frame
quiz.explain: If each update costs more real time than STEP, more and more updates are needed each frame, a runaway loop; capping prevents it.

lessons.title: Game Engines: What They Do and How to Choose One
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to open a small restaurant in Sylhet. You could make your own bricks, build the walls, forge the cooking pots and weave the tablecloths, but you would never get to cook. Sensibly, you rent a building, buy a stove and pots, and spend your energy on the food. A game engine is the rented building and kitchen equipment of game development: the reusable machinery for drawing, sound, physics, input and loading files, so that you can spend your effort on the game itself. This lesson explains what an engine contains, how it is organised, and how to choose one.

What a game engine is: A game engine is a software framework that provides the common systems most games need, plus usually an editor for building content. The term became popular in the 1990s when studios began licensing the core technology of one game to build others with different art, levels and rules. The key idea is separating reusable technology, the engine, from game-specific content and logic, the game. Code that says how to draw a sprite belongs to the engine; code that says the rickshaw loses a life when it hits a bus belongs to the game.

Before engines: Early games were written from scratch, often in assembly language, for one specific machine. Every team rewrote the same things: drawing routines, sound drivers, input reading. Porting a game to another machine could mean rewriting most of it. As hardware grew more complex, with 3D graphics cards, multi-core processors and many platforms, building everything yourself became too expensive for most teams. Engines spread the cost: one well-tested system used by thousands of games.

The runtime systems: Inside a typical engine you find: a rendering system that draws 2D sprites or 3D meshes using the GPU; a physics system for movement and collisions; an audio system that plays and mixes sounds; an input system for keyboards, touch and gamepads; an animation system; a scene or world manager that holds all the objects; a resource manager that loads and caches assets like images, sounds and models; a scripting layer where game logic is written; a user interface toolkit; often networking; and the game loop from lesson 5 tying them together.

Layered architecture: Engines are usually built in layers, each using only those below it. At the bottom is the platform layer, which talks to the operating system and hardware and hides their differences: opening a window, reading files, getting touch events. Above it, core systems such as memory management, maths libraries, logging and containers. Then resource management. Then the big subsystems: rendering, physics, audio, animation. On top sits the gameplay foundation: game objects, scripting and events, where your game code lives. Because of the platform layer, the same game code can run on Windows, Android and the web.

The editor and tools: Most modern engines come with a visual editor: you drag objects into a scene, set properties in a panel, paint tilemaps, preview animations and press play to test immediately. Designers and artists can work without writing code. Tools also include the asset pipeline, which imports source files, such as a large PNG or a 3D model, and converts them into compact formats suited to each platform, for example compressing textures differently for phones. The editor itself is usually built on the same engine.

Runtime versus editor: It helps to separate two programs. The editor runs on the developer's computer and is heavy, full of tools. The runtime, also called the player or build, is the lean version that ships to players with only what the game needs. When you export a build for Android, the engine compiles your scripts, packs assets into files, includes the runtime libraries for that platform and produces an installable package. Bugs that only appear in builds, not in the editor, are common and worth testing for early.

Scripting: Game logic is written in a scripting or programming language the engine supports. It might be C#, C++, a Python-like language, Lua, JavaScript or Dart, depending on the engine. Some engines also offer visual scripting: you connect boxes with wires to express logic, like a flowchart. Scripts typically attach to objects and have functions the engine calls at the right times: once when the object is created, every frame with delta time, and when a collision happens. This callback style is the engine's game loop calling your code.

Iteration speed: The most valuable thing an engine gives a small team is often not graphics but fast iteration: the time between changing something and seeing the result. If changing a jump height means recompiling for two minutes, you will try five versions a day; if you can tweak a number in the editor while the game runs, you will try fifty. Live property editing, hot reload of scripts and instant play buttons all exist for this reason. Game feel is found by experiment, so iteration speed directly shapes how good the game becomes.

Unity as a concept: Unity is a widely used engine for both 2D and 3D, popular for mobile games. Its scripts are written in C#. A scene contains GameObjects, and each GameObject is a container for components: a Transform for position, a SpriteRenderer to draw, a Rigidbody for physics, and your own script components. Your script has methods like Start, called once, Update, called every frame, and FixedUpdate, called at the fixed physics rate. Unity's licensing terms have changed over time, so always check the current terms yourself.

Unreal Engine as a concept: Unreal Engine is known for high-end 3D graphics and is used for many large console and PC games, as well as film and architecture visualisation. Game logic can be written in C++ or with Blueprints, a visual scripting system where you connect nodes. Its world is built from Actors, objects placed in a level, which own Components. Its strengths in lighting and rendering come at the cost of larger builds and higher hardware demands, which matters for budget phones.

Godot as a concept: Godot is a free and open-source engine under the MIT licence, light enough to run on modest computers and supporting both 2D and 3D. Its main language is GDScript, which looks similar to Python, and it also supports C#. Everything in Godot is a node, arranged in a tree, and a group of nodes saved together is a scene, which can be placed inside other scenes like a reusable building block. Signals let nodes notify each other of events. Its small size and open source code make it popular for learning and indie games.

Flame as a small example: Flame is an open-source game engine built on top of Flutter, written in Dart, so a Flutter developer can make 2D games with tools they already know. A game extends FlameGame; content is built from components arranged in a tree. Each component has an update method that receives dt and a render method that draws onto a canvas. A tiny example: class Ball extends CircleComponent { update(dt) { position.y += 200 * dt; } }. Flame provides the game loop, sprites, animation, input, collision detection and camera, and it can sit inside a normal Flutter app, so menus can be ordinary Flutter widgets.

Other options: Many other engines and frameworks exist. GameMaker is popular for 2D. Phaser is a JavaScript framework for browser games. libGDX is a Java framework; Pygame is a Python library well suited to learning; Bevy is a Rust engine built around the entity-component-system idea of lesson 7. Frameworks give you building blocks without a full editor, while engines give you everything including tools. For learning, a framework teaches more of what happens underneath; for shipping, an engine saves time.

Build versus buy: Should you build your own engine? Writing a small engine is an excellent learning exercise and teaches the material of this whole course. For shipping a commercial game, most teams use an existing engine because it handles platforms, tools and many bugs already. Studios do build their own engines when they need unusual technology, have many games to share it across, or want full control over costs and features. A useful rule: build a game, not an engine, unless the engine is the thing you are trying to learn.

How to choose an engine: Ask practical questions. Which platforms must the game run on? 2D or 3D? What languages does the team know? How heavy is the engine's runtime, and will it run on the target phones? What does the licence cost, now and if the game succeeds? How good are the documentation, tutorials and community, and can you find help in forums when stuck? Is the source code available if you hit a deep bug? For a small 2D mobile game by a Flutter developer, Flame is a reasonable choice; for a large 3D game, a heavier engine fits better.

Example, a student team in Khulna: Three students want to make a 2D puzzle game for an inter-university contest in eight weeks, targeting Android phones. One knows C#, two know Python. They try Godot because GDScript feels familiar, it runs well on their older laptops, and it exports to Android and the web, so judges can play in a browser. They spend week one on tutorials and a core loop prototype instead of reading engine source code. The engine choice saved them from writing rendering and input code they had no time for.

Example, adding a game to a Flutter app: A company already has a Flutter app for teaching children Bangla letters and wants a small game where children catch falling letters. Rewriting the app in another engine would be wasteful. With Flame, the game becomes one screen inside the existing app: the letter components fall using update(dt), taps are detected by Flame's input system, and the score screen and menus remain ordinary Flutter widgets. The same team, same language, same codebase.

Common mistakes: Choosing an engine because a famous game used it, without checking your own platform and team; switching engines halfway through a project; fighting the engine's way of doing things instead of learning its patterns; ignoring build size on mobile; and assuming the editor's preview performance equals the performance on a real budget phone. Exams ask: what is a game engine and why use one; list its subsystems; explain layered engine architecture; compare frameworks and engines; discuss building versus buying; and suggest an engine for a scenario with reasons.

Recap: A game engine packages reusable systems, rendering, physics, audio, input, animation, scenes, resources and scripting, around a game loop, usually with an editor and an asset pipeline. Engines are layered so a platform layer hides hardware differences. Unity, Unreal, Godot and Flame each organise games as objects with components or nodes, with code called by the engine every frame. Choose an engine by platform, 2D or 3D, team skills, performance, licence and community, and build a game rather than an engine unless learning is the goal.
key_points: A game engine separates reusable technology (rendering, physics, audio, input, resources) from game-specific content and logic.
Engines are layered: platform layer, core systems, resource management, subsystems, gameplay foundation.
The editor and asset pipeline let designers and artists build content; the runtime is the lean shipped build.
Scripts attach to objects and are called by the engine: on creation, every frame with dt, and on events.
Unity: C#, GameObjects with components; Unreal: C++ and Blueprints, Actors; Godot: open source, GDScript, nodes and scenes.
Flame: a Flutter game engine in Dart with components that have update(dt) and render(canvas).
Frameworks give building blocks without full tools; engines give everything including the editor.
Choose by platform, 2D or 3D, team skills, runtime weight, licence and community; build a game, not an engine.
lessons.tip: Before committing to an engine, build the same tiny test in it: a box that moves with the arrow keys or a swipe and stops at a wall. Two hours of this tells you more about fit than two days of reading reviews.
