lessons.title: Game Objects, Scene Graphs and Entity-Component-System
lessons.content:
Look at a cycle rickshaw on a Dhaka street. The rickshaw itself moves, the wheels spin relative to the rickshaw, the bell swings on the handlebar, the passenger sits on the seat and the hood folds over the passenger. Move the rickshaw and everything attached moves with it. A game world is full of such things: characters holding swords, cars with wheels, enemies with health bars floating above their heads. How should a program organise thousands of these objects so they are easy to build, easy to change and fast to update? This lesson covers three answers: game object hierarchies, scene graphs and the entity-component-system pattern.

What a game object is: A game object, also called an entity or actor, is anything that exists in the game world: the player, an enemy, a coin, a bullet, a camera, even an invisible trigger zone that starts a cutscene. Each has some data, such as position, speed, health or a picture, and some behaviour, such as moving, shooting or being collected. Most of a game's code is about creating, updating and destroying these objects every frame.

The inheritance approach: Programmers who learned object-oriented programming first often model game objects with class inheritance. A base class GameObject has position and an update method. Character extends GameObject and adds health. Player extends Character and adds input handling; Enemy extends Character and adds AI. Vehicle extends GameObject and adds wheels. At first this feels natural, exactly as the OOP course taught.

Where inheritance breaks: Problems appear as the game grows. Suppose the designer wants a talking tree that is also a shop. Is it a Character, because it talks, or a Building, because it does not move? Suppose an enemy can be ridden like a vehicle. You need both Enemy and Vehicle behaviour, but single inheritance gives you one parent. Programmers then push features upward into the base class until GameObject contains everything, health, wheels, AI and dialogue, and every object carries data it never uses. This is called the deep hierarchy or blob problem.

Composition over inheritance: The common fix is composition: instead of an object being a kind of thing, it has parts. A game object becomes a mostly empty container holding components. A Transform component stores position, rotation and scale. A Sprite component draws a picture. A Health component stores hit points. A Collider component defines a shape for collisions. An AI component makes decisions. The talking shop tree is simply an object with Transform, Sprite, Dialogue and Shop components. The rideable enemy has AI, Health and Rideable. New combinations need no new classes.

Components in engines: This is how Unity and Flame work in practice. In Unity, you add components to a GameObject in the editor. In Flame, a game object is a Component that can have child components, such as a SpriteComponent with a RectangleHitbox child. In Godot, the same idea appears as a tree of specialised nodes: a CharacterBody2D node with child Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D nodes. The vocabulary differs; the principle of building objects from small reusable parts is the same.

Templates and prefabs: Once objects are built from components, you rarely build each one by hand. Engines let you save a configured object as a template, called a prefab in Unity and a packed scene in Godot. A Coin prefab might contain Transform, Sprite, Collider and Collectable components with chosen values. Placing fifty coins in a level means placing fifty instances of the prefab; changing the prefab's sound later updates all fifty. Templates can also be stored as data files, so designers can add a new enemy type by writing a small file rather than asking a programmer.

Scene graphs: A scene graph is a tree that organises objects by parent-child relationships. The root is the world or level. Children hang below parents: the rickshaw is a child of the road scene; the wheels, seat and bell are children of the rickshaw; the passenger is a child of the seat. The crucial rule is that a child's position, rotation and scale are stored relative to its parent, called local transform, and its actual position in the world, its world transform, is computed by combining all the transforms up the tree.

Scene graph worked: Let the rickshaw be at world position (100, 50) with no rotation and scale 1. The passenger's local position is (10, -20), meaning 10 pixels right of and 20 pixels above the rickshaw's origin on a y-down screen. The passenger's world position is (100 + 10, 50 - 20) = (110, 30). Move the rickshaw to (300, 50) and the passenger, without any code touching it, is now at (310, 30). Now give the rickshaw a scale of 2, as if the camera zoomed into it: the local offset doubles to (20, -40), so the passenger is at (120, 10) when the rickshaw is at (100, 50).

Transforms as matrices: In general, each node's local transform is a matrix combining translation, rotation and scale, exactly the homogeneous matrices from Computer Graphics. A node's world matrix is its parent's world matrix multiplied by its own local matrix: world = parentWorld x local. Walking the tree from the root, each node's world matrix is computed once per frame from its parent's. Engines cache these and recompute only when something changes, using a dirty flag that marks a node and its descendants as needing an update.

What scene graphs are good for: Attaching things: a sword to a hand, a health bar above an enemy, a hat on a head. Grouping: hide a parent and all its children disappear; delete a level and everything in it is freed. Organisation in the editor: designers see a clear tree. Rendering order: 2D engines often draw children after parents so they appear on top. One caution: deep trees cost time to update, and not everything needs a parent; a thousand bullets do not need to be children of the gun that fired them.

Entity-component-system: ECS takes composition further and separates data from behaviour completely. An entity is just an ID number, like 42, with no data or code of its own. A component is plain data with no methods: Position {x, y}, Velocity {vx, vy}, Health {hp}. A system is a function that runs every frame over all entities that have a certain set of components. For example, the MovementSystem processes every entity with both Position and Velocity: for each such entity, position.x += velocity.vx x dt; position.y += velocity.vy x dt.

ECS in pseudo-code: A tiny world might store components in arrays indexed by entity: positions[42] = (10, 5); velocities[42] = (200, 0); health[42] = 3. A coin entity 43 has a position but no velocity, so the MovementSystem skips it. A RenderSystem draws every entity with Position and Sprite; a DamageSystem reduces Health for entities that collided with something harmful. Adding a new behaviour, such as slowly regenerating health, means writing one new system, not editing dozens of classes.

Why ECS is fast: The big performance advantage comes from memory layout. Processors read memory in chunks called cache lines, commonly 64 bytes. If all positions are stored side by side in one array, each position being two 4-byte floats, one cache line holds 8 positions, and a loop over 10,000 entities reads memory in a smooth stream that the processor predicts and prefetches. In a classic object design, each object lives somewhere different in memory with lots of unrelated data in between, so the loop jumps around and waits for memory. Storing each component type in its own packed array is called data-oriented design.

ECS trade-offs: ECS shines when there are many similar entities: bullets, particles, units in a strategy game, cars in a traffic simulation. It also makes saving the game and networking easier, since all state is plain data. But it can feel indirect for beginners, because behaviour is spread across systems rather than kept with the object, and simple one-off objects such as a menu can be more awkward. Many games mix approaches: a scene graph or component objects for most things, and ECS-style arrays for the hot paths that handle thousands of items.

Communication and events: Objects must talk: a coin tells the score it was collected; the player's death tells the music to change. Calling each other directly creates tight coupling, where changing one object breaks others. A common alternative is events, also called messages or signals: the coin publishes a CoinCollected event, and any interested system, score, sound or achievements, subscribes to it. The coin does not need to know who is listening. This is the observer pattern from Software Engineering, and Godot's signals are a built-in example.

Creating and destroying objects safely: Removing an object from a list while looping over that list is a classic bug: the loop skips the next item or crashes. Engines usually mark objects for removal during the update and actually delete them at the end of the frame. Creating many short-lived objects, such as bullets, also strains memory; lesson 22 shows object pooling, which reuses old objects instead of creating new ones.

Example, a ferry crossing game: Imagine a game about a launch crossing the Padma. The launch is a scene graph node; passengers, cargo crates and a flag are its children, so when waves rock the launch, everything on it rocks too. Each passenger is built from components: Transform, Sprite, Walker and Patience. A seagull flock of two hundred birds overhead is better handled ECS-style: positions and velocities in packed arrays, one FlockingSystem updating them all. Two organising ideas, each used where it fits best.

Example, adding a feature late: A week before a game jam deadline in Dhaka, the team decides some enemies should glow and drop extra coins when hit by a special attack. With a deep inheritance tree, they would need a new subclass for every glowing enemy type. With components, they create a Glow component and a BonusLoot component and attach them to any enemy in the editor, plus one small system to handle them. The feature lands in an afternoon.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include building deep inheritance trees, putting game logic into components meant to be pure data in an ECS, forgetting that child transforms are relative, and deleting objects mid-loop. Exams ask you to explain the problem with deep hierarchies, compare inheritance and composition, compute a child's world position from a parent's transform, define entity, component and system with examples, and explain why ECS is cache-friendly.

Recap: Game objects are everything that exists in the world. Deep inheritance breaks when features cross categories, so engines favour composition, building objects from reusable components. Scene graphs organise objects in parent-child trees where local transforms combine into world transforms, making attachment and grouping easy. ECS separates entities as IDs, components as plain data and systems as loops, giving flexible design and cache-friendly speed. Events decouple objects, and removal is deferred to the end of the frame.
key_points: A game object is anything in the world: player, enemy, coin, camera, trigger; it has data and behaviour.
Deep inheritance hierarchies break when features cross categories, leading to bloated base classes.
Composition builds objects from reusable components such as Transform, Sprite, Health and Collider.
A scene graph is a parent-child tree; a child's local transform combines with its parent's: world = parentWorld x local.
Worked: parent at (100, 50), child local (10, -20) gives world (110, 30); parent scale 2 gives (120, 10).
ECS: entities are IDs, components are plain data, systems loop over entities with certain components.
Packed component arrays are cache-friendly: a 64-byte cache line holds 8 two-float positions.
Events (observer pattern) decouple objects; delete objects at the end of the frame, not mid-loop.
lessons.tip: When you design a new object, list its components before thinking about classes. If two objects share a component list except one item, you have just found a reusable component.

quiz.explain: Objects like a talking shop tree do not fit a single parent class, so features pile up in the base class.

In ECS, what is an entity?
options: Just an identifier that components are attached to
A class with many virtual methods
A system that runs every frame
quiz.explain: Entities are IDs; data lives in components and behaviour lives in systems.

quiz.q: Why is storing each component type in a packed array fast?
options: Loops read memory contiguously, making good use of cache lines
It removes the need for delta time
quiz.explain: Contiguous data lets the processor stream and prefetch cache lines instead of jumping around memory.

quiz.explain: The coin publishes an event and any interested system subscribes, keeping objects decoupled.

lessons.title: Vectors and Everyday Maths for Games
lessons.content:
A fielder on a cricket ground needs to know two things about a ball coming towards him: which way it is going and how fast. A guard in a game needs to know whether the player is in front of it or behind it, and whether to turn left or right to face them. A camera needs to glide smoothly behind a running character instead of snapping. All of these are answered with a small toolbox of maths: vectors, their length, the dot and cross products, linear interpolation and a little trigonometry. You met vectors in Linear Algebra; this lesson shows exactly how games use them, with worked numbers.

What a vector is in a game: A 2D vector is a pair of numbers (x, y). Games use it in two ways. As a point, it is a position: the player is at (120, 300). As a direction with size, it is a displacement or velocity: the ball moves by (3, 4) each step, or travels at (200, 0) pixels per second. The same type of value holds both, which is convenient, but it pays to keep in mind which meaning you intend, because adding two positions makes no sense while adding a velocity to a position does.

Screen coordinates: Maths textbooks put the origin at the bottom left with y going up. Most 2D game screens put the origin at the top left with y going down, because screens are drawn row by row from the top. So in screen space, moving up means decreasing y. Many engines let you choose, and 3D engines usually use y up. Always check which convention your engine uses; many sign errors in angles and jumps come from mixing them.

Basic operations: Add vectors component by component: (2, 3) + (4, -1) = (6, 2). Subtract to get the vector from one point to another: from A = (1, 2) to B = (7, 10) is B - A = (6, 8). Multiply by a number, a scalar, to scale: 2 x (6, 8) = (12, 16). Movement is just vector arithmetic: position = position + velocity x dt. If velocity is (200, -100) and dt is 0.02, the position changes by (4, -2) this frame.

Length: The length or magnitude of (x, y) is sqrt(x^2 + y^2), from Pythagoras. For (3, 4) it is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. For (6, 8) it is 10. The distance between two points is the length of their difference: the distance from A = (1, 2) to B = (7, 10) is 10. Because square roots are relatively slow and often unnecessary, games frequently compare squared distances: to check whether the enemy is within 10 units, test dx^2 + dy^2 < 100 instead of sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2) < 10.

Normalising: A unit vector has length 1 and represents a pure direction. To normalise a vector, divide it by its length: (3, 4) / 5 = (0.6, 0.8). Normalised directions are used everywhere: to move towards a target at a chosen speed, compute dir = normalise(target - position), then velocity = dir x speed. Careful: normalising a zero vector divides by zero, so check the length is above a tiny threshold first, for example when the enemy is already standing on the target.

The diagonal speed bug: A classic beginner bug: reading keys as input = (right - left, down - up) and moving by input x speed. Pressing right alone gives (1, 0) and speed 200 pixels per second. Pressing right and down together gives (1, 1), whose length is sqrt(2), about 1.414, so the player moves at about 282.8 pixels per second, 41 percent faster diagonally. Players notice and exploit this. The fix is to normalise the input when its length exceeds 1: (1, 1) becomes about (0.707, 0.707), giving about 141.4 in each axis and 200 overall.

The dot product: The dot product of a = (ax, ay) and b = (bx, by) is a . b = ax x bx + ay x by, a single number. Its key property: a . b = |a| |b| cos(angle between them). For unit vectors, the dot product is simply the cosine of the angle. So it equals 1 when they point the same way, 0 when perpendicular, and -1 when opposite. That makes it the perfect tool for asking: is something in front of me or behind me, and how directly?

Dot product worked, front or behind: A guard stands at G = (0, 0) facing f = (1, 0), to the right. The player is at P = (6, 8). The direction to the player is (6, 8) normalised = (0.6, 0.8). The dot product f . d = 1 x 0.6 + 0 x 0.8 = 0.6. Positive means the player is in front of the guard, somewhere within 90 degrees of its facing; negative would mean behind. The angle is arccos(0.6), about 53.13 degrees.

Dot product worked, field of view: Suppose the guard sees only within a 90 degree cone, 45 degrees either side of its facing direction. The test is: the player is visible if f . d >= cos(45 degrees), about 0.7071. For the player at (6, 8), 0.6 < 0.7071, so the guard does not see them. If the player moves to (8, 6), d = (0.8, 0.6), the dot product is 0.8, which is above 0.7071, so the guard sees them, at about 36.87 degrees off centre. No angles or trig functions are computed at run time: precompute cos of the half-angle once, then each check is two multiplications and an addition.

The 2D cross product: In 3D, the cross product of two vectors is a vector perpendicular to both, used for surface normals in Computer Graphics. In 2D games, programmers use a reduced version that gives a single number: cross(a, b) = ax x by - ay x bx. Its sign tells you which side b is on relative to a. With the guard facing f = (1, 0) and the direction to the player d = (0.6, 0.8): cross = 1 x 0.8 - 0 x 0.6 = 0.8, positive. In y-up maths coordinates, positive means b is counter-clockwise from a, so the guard should turn left; negative would mean turn right; zero means straight ahead or directly behind.

Careful with the cross product on screens: On a y-down screen the visual meaning flips: a positive cross product then means clockwise as you see it on screen. Rather than memorising, test once in your engine: put a target clearly on one side, print the sign and note it. Combining both products gives a complete picture: the dot product says front or behind and how close to straight ahead; the cross product says left or right. A turret can use these two numbers to decide whether to turn, which way, and whether to fire.

Linear interpolation: Lerp blends between two values: lerp(a, b, t) = a + (b - a) x t, where t runs from 0 to 1. At t = 0 you get a, at t = 1 you get b, in between you get a proportional mix. Worked: lerp(10, 50, 0.25) = 10 + 40 x 0.25 = 20. Lerp works on vectors component by component, on colours to fade between them, and on angles with care around the wrap from 359 degrees to 0. You met it in Computer Graphics for keyframes; games use it constantly for health bars that slide down, fades and camera motion.

Smoothing with lerp and delta time: A popular trick moves the camera a fraction of the remaining distance each frame: camX = lerp(camX, targetX, 0.08). It produces smooth ease-out motion, but the fixed 0.08 means it behaves differently at different frame rates. A frame-rate-independent version uses t = 1 - e^(-k x dt). With k = 5 and dt = 1/60, t = 1 - e^(-0.0833), about 0.0800 per frame. At 30 fps, dt = 1/30 gives about 0.1535, almost exactly what two 60 fps frames give together, 1 - (1 - 0.08)^2 = 0.1536. Same smoothing on all hardware.

Angles and atan2: To turn a direction into an angle, use atan2(y, x), available in every maths library, which handles all four quadrants correctly, unlike plain arctan(y / x). atan2(8, 6) is about 53.13 degrees, matching the dot product result above. Most libraries work in radians: 180 degrees equals pi radians, so 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees. To rotate a sprite to face its velocity, set rotation = atan2(vy, vx). To go back from an angle to a direction, use (cos(angle), sin(angle)).

Circles, orbits and bobbing: Sine and cosine create circular and wave motion. A coin orbiting a point C with radius r at angle theta sits at (Cx + r cos(theta), Cy + r sin(theta)). With r = 50 and theta = 30 degrees, the offset is (50 x 0.866, 50 x 0.5), about (43.30, 25). Increasing theta each frame by angularSpeed x dt makes it orbit. For a gentle floating effect, a pickup's height can be y = baseY + 4 x sin(2 x pi x f x t): with f = 0.5, it rises and falls 4 pixels once every 2 seconds. These tiny touches make a world feel alive.

Example, a goalkeeper in a football game: A computer goalkeeper must face the ball. Each frame, it computes d = normalise(ball - keeper), then cross(facing, d) to decide which way to turn and the dot product to check whether the ball is within its reaction cone. It moves towards a point between the ball and the goal centre found with lerp(goalCentre, ballPosition, 0.2), so it stays near the goal but leans towards the ball. Four small formulas produce believable behaviour.

Example, a fishing boat on the Meghna: In a fishing game, the boat's velocity points along its heading (cos(angle), sin(angle)) times speed. The net is dropped at a point behind the boat: position - heading x 30. Fish within the squared distance of 40^2 = 1600 are caught, avoiding square roots entirely. The camera follows with frame-rate-independent lerp, and the floating catch counter bobs with a sine wave. Every part of that description is a formula from this lesson.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to normalise before using a direction, so speed depends on distance; normalising zero vectors; mixing degrees and radians; forgetting that screen y points down; using plain arctan instead of atan2 and getting angles wrong in half the quadrants; and using a fixed lerp factor that changes with frame rate. Exams ask you to compute lengths and unit vectors, use the dot product to find an angle or a front/behind test, use the cross product sign for left or right, evaluate a lerp, and explain the diagonal speed bug.

Recap: Vectors store positions and velocities; movement is position plus velocity times dt. Length comes from Pythagoras, and squared distances avoid square roots. Normalising gives directions and fixes diagonal speed. The dot product measures alignment for front, behind and field-of-view tests; the 2D cross product's sign gives left or right. Lerp blends values and, with an exponential factor, smooths motion independently of frame rate. atan2, sine and cosine convert between angles and directions and create orbits and gentle waves.
key_points: A 2D vector (x, y) holds a position or a velocity; movement is position += velocity x dt.
Length = sqrt(x^2 + y^2); (3, 4) has length 5; compare squared distances to skip square roots.
Normalise by dividing by length: (3, 4) becomes (0.6, 0.8); guard against zero vectors.
Diagonal bug: input (1, 1) is 1.414 long, so speed 200 becomes about 282.8 unless normalised.
Dot product of unit vectors = cos(angle): positive in front, negative behind; FOV test d . f >= cos(half-angle).
2D cross ax x by - ay x bx: its sign tells left or right (flips meaning on y-down screens).
lerp(a, b, t) = a + (b - a) x t; lerp(10, 50, 0.25) = 20; use t = 1 - e^(-k dt) for frame-rate-independent smoothing.
atan2(y, x) gives correct angles in all quadrants; (cos, sin) turns an angle back into a direction.
lessons.tip: Keep a one-page cheat sheet of these eight formulas next to your keyboard during your first game project. After a few weeks you will notice you no longer look at it, and that is when they have become tools.

For each player, compute the normalised direction, the dot product and the cross product, then say whether the guard sees them with a 90 degree field of view and which way it should turn.

quiz.q: What is the length of the vector (5, 12)?
Without normalising, a player moving diagonally with input (1, 1) and speed 100 moves at about:
quiz.explain: The input's length is sqrt(2), about 1.414, so the speed becomes about 141.4.

quiz.q: For two unit vectors, a dot product of -1 means they:
quiz.explain: The dot product of unit vectors is the cosine of the angle; cos(180 degrees) = -1.

quiz.q: What is lerp(20, 80, 0.75)?
Why use atan2(y, x) instead of arctan(y / x)?
options: It returns the correct angle in all four quadrants and handles x = 0
quiz.explain: arctan(y / x) loses the signs of x and y and fails when x = 0; atan2 uses both to pick the right quadrant.

lessons.title: 2D Rendering: Sprites, Animation and Tilemaps
lessons.content:
Think of a shadow puppet show at a village fair. The puppeteer has a box of cut-out figures, a horse, a king, a boat, and moves them in front of a painted backdrop, swapping in a figure with raised arms when the king gets angry. Most 2D games work in almost exactly this way. Small pictures called sprites are moved over a background, swapped quickly to create animation, and the background itself is often built from small repeated tiles, like floor tiles in a house. This lesson explains sprites, sprite sheets, frame animation, draw order and tilemaps, with the numbers that make them efficient.

Recap of the pipeline: In Computer Graphics you learned how a GPU draws triangles: vertices are transformed, triangles are rasterised into pixels, and each pixel's colour is computed, often by sampling a texture. A 2D game engine uses exactly this pipeline. Each sprite is drawn as a rectangle made of two triangles, with a texture mapped onto it. So 2D rendering is really 3D hardware drawing flat textured rectangles, which is why modern 2D games can draw thousands of sprites smoothly.

What a sprite is: A sprite is a 2D image drawn at a position in the game world, usually with transparency so that only the shape shows, not a rectangular box. Images with an alpha channel, such as PNG files, store a transparency value for every pixel. A sprite has a position, often a rotation and scale, a size, and a reference to the image or part of an image to draw. The player, enemies, coins, bullets and even buttons are usually sprites.

The pivot or anchor: Every sprite has a pivot, also called the anchor or origin: the point of the image that sits exactly at the sprite's position and around which it rotates and scales. For a character, the pivot is usually at the feet, so placing it at a ground height y puts its feet on the ground. For a spinning coin, it is the centre. A wrong pivot is a common source of bugs: characters floating above floors or wheels rotating around a corner instead of their axle.

Flipping and tinting: To make a character face left instead of right, there is no need for separate art: set its horizontal scale to -1 and it is drawn mirrored. Tinting multiplies the sprite's colours by a colour, so one grey enemy image can appear red when hit or blue when frozen. Fading changes the overall alpha. These cheap tricks multiply the variety you get from a small set of images, which matters for download size on phones.

Sprite sheets: Loading hundreds of separate small image files is slow and wasteful. Instead, many frames are packed into one larger image called a sprite sheet. In a simple grid sheet, every frame has the same size. Worked: a 512 x 512 pixel sheet with 64 x 64 frames holds 512 / 64 = 8 columns and 8 rows, 64 frames. To find frame number i, counting from 0 left to right and top to bottom, use column = i mod 8 and row = i div 8. Frame 13 is at column 5, row 1, so its source rectangle starts at pixel (5 x 64, 1 x 64) = (320, 64).

Texture atlases: A texture atlas is a sprite sheet where images of different sizes are packed tightly, with a small data file listing each image's name and rectangle. Tools pack them automatically to waste little space. The big benefit is performance: the GPU works best when it can draw many sprites in one batch using the same texture. If the player, coins and enemies all live in one atlas, the engine can send them in one draw call instead of switching textures between them. Lesson 22 returns to draw calls and batching.

Frame animation: Animation in 2D is mostly flip-book style: show frame 0, then frame 1, then frame 2, each for a short time. An animation is described by a list of frames and a frame rate or duration per frame. A run cycle might use 8 frames at 12 frames per second, so each frame shows for 1 / 12, about 0.083 seconds, and the full cycle takes 8 / 12, about 0.667 seconds. Note that the animation frame rate, 12 here, is independent of the game's rendering rate of 60 fps: each animation frame simply stays on screen for several rendered frames.

Animation timing in code: Keep a timer that adds dt each frame, and compute the current frame from it: elapsed = elapsed + dt; frame = floor(elapsed x 12) mod 8. After 0.3 seconds, floor(3.6) = 3, so frame 3 shows. After 1.0 second, floor(12) mod 8 = 4. Using elapsed time, not frame counting, keeps animation speed correct on slow and fast devices, exactly like delta time for movement in lesson 5. Non-looping animations, such as a death animation, stop at the last frame and often fire an event when finished.

Animation states: A character has several animations: idle, run, jump, fall, hurt. Which one plays depends on game state: if not on the ground and moving up, play jump; if moving down, play fall; if on ground and moving, play run; otherwise idle. This is a small state machine, the same idea that lesson 17 uses for AI. Engines provide animation state machines in their editors, where transitions are drawn as arrows. Matching animation speed to movement speed, for example faster run frames when running faster, prevents feet from appearing to slide.

Draw order: Sprites drawn later appear on top of sprites drawn earlier, the painter's algorithm from Computer Graphics. 2D engines usually let you assign layers or a z-index: background at 0, game objects at 10, effects at 20, user interface at 100. Within a layer, objects may be sorted. In top-down games, where the camera looks down at an angle, sorting by the y coordinate of the feet makes a character walking in front of a tree appear over it, and behind it when further up the screen.

Tilemaps: Large levels are rarely drawn as one huge picture. Instead they are built from small square tiles, such as 32 x 32 pixels, taken from a tileset image: grass, road, water, wall, corners and edges. A tilemap is a 2D grid of numbers, where each number is the ID of a tile in the tileset. Level designers paint tilemaps in an editor like painting with stamps. The same 50 tiles can build hundreds of different levels.

Tilemap memory worked: Consider a side-scrolling level 200 tiles wide and 15 tiles tall with 32 pixel tiles. As pixels, that is 6400 x 480. Stored as one big image with 4 bytes per pixel, it would take 6400 x 480 x 4 = 12,288,000 bytes, about 12.3 MB. As a tilemap with one byte per tile ID, it needs 200 x 15 = 3000 bytes, plus the small tileset image. That is roughly four thousand times smaller, and the tile data is easy to edit, save and send over a network.

Tile and pixel conversion: Converting between pixels and tiles is simple integer division. A point at pixel (100, 70) lies in tile column 100 div 32 = 3 and row 70 div 32 = 2. Going back, tile (3, 2) has its top-left corner at pixel (3 x 32, 2 x 32) = (96, 64). This conversion is how games answer questions such as what is the player standing on: look up the tile under the feet, check whether that tile ID is solid. Tiles can also carry properties like slippery, damaging or water.

Drawing tilemaps efficiently: The renderer draws only tiles visible on screen. If the screen shows 20 x 12 tiles, it loops over about 240 tiles per frame, not all 3000. Engines often go further and pre-build chunks, for example blocks of 16 x 16 tiles, into single meshes, so a whole chunk is one draw call. Animated tiles, such as flowing water, cycle through a few tile IDs on a timer. Autotiling picks the right edge or corner tile automatically based on neighbouring tiles, saving designers from placing every edge by hand.

Nine-slice for interfaces: Buttons and dialogue boxes must stretch to fit different text without the corners looking squashed. Nine-slice scaling divides an image into a 3 x 3 grid: the four corners never stretch, the four edges stretch in one direction only, and the centre stretches in both. One small panel image can then make boxes of any size. This is the same idea used by Android's nine-patch images, which you may have met in Mobile App Development.

Pixel art and filtering: Pixel art uses deliberately low-resolution images with crisp pixels. When it is scaled up, bilinear filtering, which you met in Computer Graphics, blurs it. For pixel art, use nearest-neighbour filtering and scale by whole numbers, 2x, 3x or 4x, so every art pixel becomes an exact block of screen pixels. Smooth hand-painted art, on the other hand, looks better with bilinear filtering and mipmaps when scaled down.

Example, a rickshaw road scene: A side-scrolling Dhaka road could use a tileset with road, footpath, drain and wall tiles, painted into a tilemap 300 tiles long. The rickshaw is a sprite with a pivot at the bottom centre between the wheels, and its pedalling animation has 6 frames at 10 frames per second, sped up when the rickshaw goes faster. Buses, auto-rickshaws and people are sprites from the same texture atlas, so they draw in one batch. Shop signs are on a background layer, the HUD on the top layer.

Example, a festival poster game for phones: A small game about decorating a Pohela Boishakh fair stall uses nine-slice panels for its menus, tinting to show the same flower sprite in five colours, and mirrored sprites so one dancing figure faces both ways. Total art: a single 1024 x 1024 atlas, about 4 MB in memory uncompressed, small enough for budget phones. Careful sprite reuse makes a colourful game with very little art.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes include wrong pivots, animating by frame count instead of time, forgetting that later-drawn sprites appear on top, loading many separate images instead of an atlas, and blurry pixel art from bilinear filtering. Exams ask you to define sprite, sprite sheet, atlas and tilemap; compute the frame position in a sheet; compute animation timing; compare tilemap memory to a full image; and convert between pixel and tile coordinates.

Recap: 2D games draw textured rectangles called sprites, each with a pivot, scale, rotation and optional flip or tint. Sprite sheets and atlases pack many images into one texture for speed. Frame animation shows frames at their own rate based on elapsed time, chosen by a small state machine. Layers and sorting control draw order. Tilemaps build big levels from small tiles and a grid of IDs, saving huge amounts of memory and making tile lookups simple.
key_points: A sprite is a 2D image drawn as a textured rectangle with a position, pivot, rotation, scale, flip and tint.
The pivot is the point placed at the sprite's position and the centre of rotation; feet for characters.
In a 512 x 512 sheet of 64 x 64 frames: 64 frames; frame i is at column i mod 8, row i div 8; frame 13 at (320, 64).
Atlases pack images of different sizes into one texture so many sprites draw in one batch.
Frame animation by time: frame = floor(elapsed x fps) mod count; 8 frames at 12 fps loop every 0.667 s.
Draw order follows layers (z-index); top-down games often sort by y.
Tilemaps store tile IDs in a grid: 200 x 15 tiles = 3000 bytes vs about 12.3 MB as a full image.
Pixel to tile: column = x div tileSize; pixel (100, 70) with 32 px tiles is tile (3, 2).
lessons.tip: Draw a tiny 4-frame walking stick figure on squared paper, number the frames and time them at 8 frames per second by tapping a pencil. Feeling the timing by hand makes frame-rate numbers intuitive.
lessons.task: A sprite sheet is 768 x 256 pixels with 64 x 64 frames. Work out how many frames it holds, the pixel rectangle of frame 17, and which frame shows after 1.4 seconds of a 10 frames per second animation that loops over frames 0 to 11.

quiz.q: A 256 x 256 sprite sheet has 32 x 32 frames. How many frames does it contain?
quiz.explain: 256 / 32 = 8 columns and 8 rows, so 64 frames.

quiz.q: What is the main performance benefit of a texture atlas?
options: Many sprites can be drawn in one batch without switching textures
It removes the need for transparency
quiz.explain: Sprites sharing one texture can be batched into fewer draw calls.

quiz.q: An animation runs at 10 frames per second over 6 looping frames. Which frame is shown after 0.75 seconds?
quiz.explain: floor(0.75 x 10) = 7, and 7 mod 6 = 1.

quiz.q: With 32 x 32 pixel tiles, which tile contains pixel (130, 40)?
Which filtering suits pixel art when scaling it up?
quiz.explain: Nearest-neighbour keeps pixels crisp; whole-number scales keep every art pixel the same size.

lessons.title: Cameras, Parallax and Screen Space
lessons.content:
Sit by the window of a train from Dhaka to Chattogram. The electric poles next to the track flash past, the paddy fields slide by more slowly, and the distant hills seem to barely move at all. Your eyes are a camera moving through a world, and that difference in speed is how your brain senses depth. A 2D game uses the same trick, and a lot more, through its camera: the object that decides which part of the large game world appears on the small screen. This lesson covers world and screen coordinates, following the player smoothly, keeping the camera inside the level, parallax, zoom and shake, and fitting a game onto screens of many shapes.

Why a camera: A level might be 6400 pixels wide, but a phone screen shows maybe 800 game units across. The camera is a rectangle in the world, the viewport into it, and only what is inside is drawn. Moving the camera instead of moving every object is far simpler: objects keep their true world positions, and the renderer converts them to screen positions each frame. In 2D, a camera is described by a position, a zoom and sometimes a rotation; in 3D it has a full view and projection, which lesson 23 recaps.

World and screen coordinates: World coordinates describe where things are in the game world. Screen coordinates describe where they appear on the display. If the camera's top-left corner is at world (camX, camY) and zoom is 1, then screenX = worldX - camX and screenY = worldY - camY. Worked: camera top-left at (500, 200), a coin at world (650, 380) appears at screen (150, 180). This is the window-to-viewport mapping you met in Computer Graphics, specialised for games.

Centring on the player: Usually we want the player in the middle of the screen. With a view 800 wide and 480 tall, the camera's top-left is the player position minus half the view: if the player is at (1000, 300), the camera's top-left is (1000 - 400, 300 - 240) = (600, 60). An enemy at world (1100, 250) then appears at screen (1100 - 600, 250 - 60) = (500, 190): 100 pixels right of centre and 50 above it, exactly its offset from the player.

Zoom: With zoom, it is cleaner to think about the camera's centre. screen = (world - camCentre) x zoom + screenCentre. With the camera centred on (1000, 300), zoom 2 and a screen centre of (400, 240), the enemy at (1100, 250) appears at ((100) x 2 + 400, (-50) x 2 + 240) = (600, 140). Zooming in doubles every offset from the centre. Zoom is useful for dramatic moments, for showing more of the map in strategy games, and for adapting to screen sizes.

Screen to world: Input arrives in screen coordinates: a tap at screen (600, 140). To know what the player touched in the world, invert the formula: world = (screen - screenCentre) / zoom + camCentre = ((600 - 400) / 2 + 1000, (140 - 240) / 2 + 300) = (1100, 250), the enemy. Forgetting this conversion is the most common reason why taps land in the wrong place once the camera moves. Engines provide helper functions for both directions; know which one to call.

Following the player: Hard-locking the camera to the player works but feels stiff and can be nauseating when the player jitters. A smoother approach lerps the camera towards its target each frame, using the frame-rate-independent factor from lesson 8: cam = lerp(cam, target, 1 - e^(-k x dt)). Higher k follows tightly; lower k lags more. A small lag makes motion feel weighty, but too much makes the player run off screen, so it is tuned by feel.

Dead zones: A dead zone is a rectangle in the centre of the screen inside which the player can move without the camera moving. Only when the player crosses its edge does the camera follow. For example, with a dead zone 100 pixels wide, small steps back and forth do not shake the view. Platformers often use a wide horizontal dead zone and treat vertical movement differently: the camera moves up only when the player lands on a higher platform, so jumps do not bounce the whole screen.

Look-ahead: In fast games the player needs to see what is coming. Look-ahead shifts the camera's target in the direction of motion: target = player + velocity x 0.3, clamped to a maximum offset. A runner moving right then sees more of the road ahead and less behind. Combined with smoothing, the camera glides forward as speed increases. Shooters may shift the camera towards where the player is aiming instead.

Clamping to level bounds: Players should not see beyond the edges of the level, the empty void outside. Clamp the camera so its view stays inside: for a level 6400 wide and a view 800 wide, the camera's left edge must stay between 0 and 6400 - 800 = 5600. In pseudo-code: camLeft = clamp(camLeft, 0, levelWidth - viewWidth). Near the edges the player then moves off-centre, which is expected. If a level is smaller than the view, centre it instead.

Parallax scrolling: Parallax gives a 2D scene depth by moving background layers more slowly than the foreground, like the train window. Each layer has a factor f between 0 and 1: it is drawn at screenX = worldX - camX x f. If the camera moves 1000 pixels right, the ground layer with f = 1 shifts 1000 pixels, a tree layer with f = 0.5 shifts 500, and distant mountains with f = 0.2 shift only 200. A sky with f = 0 never moves. Layers with f above 1, drawn in front, rush past and feel very close.

Repeating backgrounds: Background layers usually repeat horizontally so they never run out. If a cloud layer image is 1024 pixels wide, draw it at offset = -(camX x f) mod 1024, and again 1024 pixels to the right, so the screen is always covered. Two or three images per layer are enough. Combining four or five parallax layers, a sky, far hills, near trees, the road and a foreground fence, produces a rich sense of depth with very little art.

Screen shake: When something big happens, an explosion, a heavy landing, a hit, a brief shake makes it feel powerful. A common method stores a trauma value between 0 and 1 that jumps up on impacts and decays over time; each frame the camera is offset by a random amount scaled by trauma squared, so small shakes are gentle and big ones are strong. Smooth noise gives better results than pure random jumps. Always offer an option to reduce shake, because it can cause discomfort for some players.

Camera cuts and framing: Sometimes the camera should not just follow. When a boss appears, the camera can pan to show it, then return; when two players are on screen, it can centre on their midpoint and zoom out as they move apart. These are scripted camera moves, usually written as a sequence of targets with eased lerps between them. A good rule: never take camera control away from the player for long, and never during tense action, or the game will feel unfair.

Multiple cameras and UI: Games often use more than one camera or layer: the world camera that moves and zooms, and a fixed interface layer for health, score and buttons, which must not move with the world. Split-screen multiplayer uses two world cameras, each drawing to half the screen. A minimap is a second camera with a large zoom out, drawn into a small corner. Keeping HUD elements in screen space and game objects in world space prevents bugs such as the score drifting off when the camera shakes.

Resolutions and aspect ratios: Phones come in many shapes. A game designed for 1280 x 720, a 16:9 aspect ratio, may run on a phone of 2400 x 1080, about 20:9, wider and narrower. If we scale to fit the height, the scale is 1080 / 720 = 1.5, and the design width becomes 1280 x 1.5 = 1920 pixels, leaving 2400 - 1920 = 480 pixels unused: 240 on each side. There are three common responses: letterbox or pillarbox the extra space with bars; stretch, which distorts shapes and is usually wrong; or expand the view, showing more of the world: 2400 / 1.5 = 1600 world units across instead of 1280.

Choosing a scaling strategy: Expanding the view is fair for exploration games but can give wide-screen players an advantage in competitive games, because they see enemies earlier; those games often fix the visible width. Pixel-art games prefer whole-number scaling, accepting borders. Menus and HUDs use anchors: a pause button anchored to the top right corner stays there on any screen. Test on several aspect ratios, including tablets, which are closer to 4:3.

Safe areas: Many phones have notches, punch-hole cameras and rounded corners, and some have gesture bars at the bottom. The operating system reports safe-area insets, regions where content may be hidden. The game world can extend under them, but important HUD elements and buttons should stay inside the safe area. Flutter exposes this through its padding information, and engines have similar settings. A score hidden under a camera notch is a classic review complaint.

Example, a river boat game: In a boat game on the Jamuna, the river level is 9000 units long. The camera follows the boat with smoothing and a look-ahead in the direction of travel, clamped to the river's banks. Three parallax layers, distant char lands at 0.2, village trees at 0.5 and riverside reeds at 1.3 in front, give depth. When the boat hits a log, trauma rises to 0.6 and the camera shakes briefly. On a wide 20:9 phone, the view expands to show more river ahead.

Example, a tap-to-collect game: A game where children tap mangoes in a tree uses a camera that can zoom in on branches. A bug report says taps miss after zooming. The cause: the code compared the screen tap position directly to the mangoes' world positions. The fix converts the tap to world coordinates with world = (screen - screenCentre) / zoom + camCentre before checking. One line, and it works at every zoom level.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing world and screen coordinates; following the player rigidly; forgetting to clamp; putting the HUD in world space; stretching to fit new aspect ratios; ignoring safe areas. Exams ask you to convert between world and screen coordinates with and without zoom, explain dead zones and look-ahead, compute parallax shifts for given factors, and compute scale and borders for a resolution change.

Recap: The camera selects which part of the world is drawn. screen = (world - camCentre) x zoom + screenCentre, and its inverse turns taps into world positions. Smooth following uses lerp with dead zones, look-ahead and clamping to level bounds. Parallax layers move by factor f to create depth, and screen shake adds impact. Different aspect ratios are handled by letterboxing, expanding the view or anchoring UI, always keeping important elements in the safe area.
key_points: The camera is a rectangle in the world; only what is inside is drawn, and objects keep world positions.
World to screen: screen = (world - camCentre) x zoom + screenCentre; the inverse converts taps to world positions.
Worked: camera centre (1000, 300), zoom 2, screen centre (400, 240): world (1100, 250) appears at (600, 140).
Smooth follow with lerp; dead zones ignore small moves; look-ahead shows more in the direction of motion.
Clamp the camera: with level 6400 and view 800, the left edge stays between 0 and 5600.
Parallax: screenX = worldX - camX x f; camera moves 1000, layers with f = 0.5 and 0.2 move 500 and 200.
Screen shake scales random offsets by trauma squared; offer an option to reduce it.
A 1280 x 720 design on a 2400 x 1080 screen scales by 1.5 and leaves 480 pixels: letterbox or expand the view.
lessons.tip: Add a debug overlay to your first game that draws the camera's dead zone and the level bounds as thin lines. Seeing the camera logic makes tuning it ten times faster.
lessons.task: A camera is centred on (500, 400) with zoom 1.5 on a 960 x 540 screen. Compute where a tree at world (620, 340) appears on screen. Then a player taps screen (300, 200): find the world point. Finally, compute how far layers with f = 0.3 and 0.8 shift when the camera moves 600 units.

quiz.q: The camera's top-left is at world (300, 100) with zoom 1. Where does an object at world (450, 260) appear on screen?
The camera moves 800 units right. How far does a parallax layer with factor 0.25 shift?
quiz.explain: Shift = 800 x 0.25 = 200 units, so the layer appears farther away.

quiz.q: What is a camera dead zone?
options: A central region where the player can move without the camera following
The region hidden by a phone's notch
quiz.explain: The camera only moves when the player leaves the dead zone, preventing jittery small movements.

quiz.q: A 1280 x 720 design is scaled to fit the height of a 2400 x 1080 phone. How many unused pixels remain across the width?
After zooming, taps hit the wrong objects. What is the most likely cause?
options: Tap positions were not converted from screen to world coordinates
The parallax factor is too high
The game uses a fixed timestep
The texture atlas is too small
quiz.explain: Taps arrive in screen space and must be converted with the inverse camera transform before comparing to world positions.

lessons.title: Input Handling: From Fingers to Actions
lessons.content:
Ask anyone who has played a game with sticky, laggy controls and they will tell you the game felt broken, even if everything else was beautiful. Input is the player's only voice in the game. Every jump, swipe and button press must be read correctly, turned into the right action at the right moment, and never lost. This lesson covers how games read input devices, polling versus events, mapping raw input to actions, virtual joysticks and dead zones with worked numbers, forgiving tricks like coyote time and jump buffering, input latency, and accessibility.

Input devices: Games read many devices. Keyboards report which keys are down. Mice report movement and button clicks. Touch screens report one or more touch points with positions, each with its own ID, so two fingers can be tracked separately. Gamepads report buttons and analogue sticks and triggers, which give values between -1 and 1 or 0 and 1 rather than just on or off. Phones also have motion sensors, the accelerometer and gyroscope, and microphones and cameras can be used too. The operating system collects these and delivers them to the game.

Polling versus events: There are two ways to read input. Polling asks the device for its current state whenever the game wants: is the left key down right now? Events deliver a message each time something changes: key pressed, key released, finger touched down at (200, 560). Games often use both: the operating system sends events, the engine records them into a state table, and gameplay code polls that table during update. This keeps all input for one frame consistent, so two systems checking the jump button in the same frame see the same answer.

Pressed, held and released: For buttons, games care about three moments. Pressed means it went down this frame; held means it is down now; released means it went up this frame. Jump should trigger on pressed, otherwise holding the button would jump again and again. You can derive pressed from two frames of state: pressed = downNow and not downLastFrame. Engines provide functions for all three. Mixing them up produces bugs such as a menu that skips two screens on one tap.

Why events can be lost: If the game only polls state once per frame, a very quick tap that goes down and up between two frames could be missed entirely, because both checks see the button up. Engines avoid this by recording the press event even if the release arrived in the same frame. Similarly, keyboard events arrive in order with timestamps, which fighting games use to detect precise sequences of moves. Never assume that one frame contains at most one change.

Input and the fixed timestep: Lesson 5 showed that a frame may run zero, one or several fixed updates. That creates a subtle bug: a jump pressed in a frame that runs zero fixed updates is never seen by the physics, and one pressed in a frame that runs two fixed updates may trigger twice. The usual fix is to read input every rendered frame and store intentions, such as jumpRequested = true, then let the next fixed update consume the flag and clear it. Continuous inputs like steering can simply be read as the latest value.

Input mapping and actions: Gameplay code should not ask is the space bar down; it should ask is the jump action pressed. An input map connects physical inputs to named actions: jump may be space, the up arrow, gamepad button A, or a tap on the right half of the screen. Changing controls, or supporting a new device, then means changing the map, not the gameplay code. It also makes rebinding by the player easy, which matters for accessibility. Unity's input system and Godot's input map both follow this action-based idea.

Analogue sticks and dead zones: A gamepad stick at rest rarely reads exactly (0, 0); worn sticks may report (0.1, 0.05) while untouched, making the character drift. A dead zone ignores small values. A radial dead zone checks the vector's length: the length of (0.1, 0.05) is about 0.112, below a dead zone of 0.2, so it is treated as zero. Better still, rescale the remaining range so movement starts smoothly from zero: output = (m - 0.2) / (1 - 0.2) along the same direction. A stick pushed to 0.6 then gives (0.6 - 0.2) / 0.8 = 0.5, and full push still gives 1.

Virtual joysticks on touch screens: Mobile action games often draw an on-screen joystick. Worked: the joystick's centre is at screen (150, 600) with a radius of 80 pixels. A finger at (200, 560) is offset (50, -40) from the centre, with length about 64.03, inside the radius. Dividing by the radius gives input (0.625, -0.5) with a magnitude of about 0.8, so the character moves at 80 percent speed up and to the right on a y-down screen. A finger at (250, 600) is 100 pixels away, beyond the radius, so the input is clamped to length 1: (1, 0).

Floating joysticks and touch zones: A fixed joystick forces players to find its exact spot. A floating joystick appears wherever the thumb first touches within, say, the left half of the screen, and measures offsets from that point. Buttons on the right half handle jump or attack. Each touch ID is assigned to one control when it begins and stays with it until lifted, so dragging a thumb across the middle does not suddenly switch controls. Visual feedback, such as the knob moving under the thumb, tells players the input was received.

Gestures: Touch games also recognise gestures: a tap is a short touch with little movement; a swipe is a movement of more than some distance, say 50 pixels, within a short time, say 0.3 seconds, with its direction found from the larger of the x and y movement; a long press is a touch held still for some time; pinch is two touches moving apart or together, used for zoom. Thresholds need tuning on real phones, because screen sizes and pixel densities vary; measuring in density-independent units helps.

Motion controls: The accelerometer measures acceleration including gravity, so a phone tilted to the left shows gravity partly along its x axis. Games can use tilt to steer a boat or roll a ball. Raw sensor data is noisy, so it is smoothed with a lerp filter, and a calibration step records the player's comfortable neutral angle, because few people hold a phone perfectly flat on a bus. Always offer a touch alternative, since tilt is awkward lying down or in a moving vehicle.

Coyote time: In platformers, a player who presses jump a fraction of a second after running off a ledge expects to jump; strict rules say they are already falling. Coyote time, named after cartoon characters who run off cliffs, allows a jump for a short time after leaving the ground, such as 0.1 seconds. Worked: at 60 fps, a press 4 frames after leaving the ledge is 4 / 60, about 0.067 seconds, inside the window, so the jump happens. In code: if onGround then coyoteTimer = 0.1 else coyoteTimer = coyoteTimer - dt; canJump = coyoteTimer > 0.

Jump buffering: The reverse problem: a player presses jump just before landing, and the press is ignored because they were still in the air. Jump buffering remembers a press for a short window, such as 0.15 seconds. If the character lands within that window, the jump executes immediately on landing. In code: on jump pressed, bufferTimer = 0.15; each frame bufferTimer = bufferTimer - dt; if onGround and bufferTimer > 0 then jump and set bufferTimer = 0. Players rarely notice these tricks consciously; they simply feel that the controls do what they meant.

Input latency: Input latency is the time between a physical action and its visible result. It includes the device and operating system reporting the input, waiting for the next frame to start, the update, rendering, the GPU finishing, waiting for the display's refresh, and the display itself. Each stage can add milliseconds; at 60 fps, waiting for frame boundaries alone can add a frame or more, roughly 17 ms each. Reducing latency means reading input as late as possible before update, avoiding extra buffered frames, and keeping frame rate high and steady.

Feedback confirms input: Players judge responsiveness by how quickly they see or hear a reaction. Starting a jump animation, a sound or a small dust puff on the very frame the button is pressed makes controls feel instant, even if the physics take a few frames to lift the character visibly. On phones, short vibrations can confirm button taps. Lack of immediate feedback makes players press again, causing double actions.

Accessibility in input: Good games let players remap every action, offer hold-or-toggle options for actions that require holding a button, avoid requiring rapid button mashing or provide an alternative, support one-handed play where possible, and allow adjustable sensitivity and dead zones. Many players have motor impairments, injuries, or simply different devices. The HCI course covered accessibility principles; in games they mostly come down to flexible, forgiving input.

Example, a cricket batting game: In a phone batting game, the player swipes to play a shot. The swipe's direction picks the shot, cover drive or pull, and its speed sets power. A tap during the bowler's run-up is buffered for 0.15 seconds so a slightly early touch still counts. Timing windows are generous on easy mode and tighter on hard. On the frame the swipe ends, a bat sound plays immediately, before the physics of the ball are even resolved, so the shot feels crisp.

Example, a ferry-dodging game on keyboard and touch: A game where the player steers a small boat between ferries supports keyboard arrows on PC and a floating joystick on phones. Both map to the same action, steer, with a value between -1 and 1. The keyboard gives -1, 0 or 1; the joystick gives smooth values. Gameplay code reads only steer, so adding gamepad support later is one line in the input map.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes include triggering actions on held instead of pressed, reading device keys directly in gameplay code, no dead zone, forgetting to normalise joystick input, ignoring multi-touch IDs, and adding latency through extra buffering. Exams ask: compare polling and event-driven input; explain input mapping; compute a joystick vector with clamping; apply a dead zone; explain coyote time and jump buffering; list sources of input latency.

Recap: Games read keyboards, mice, touch, gamepads and sensors through events recorded into per-frame state, distinguishing pressed, held and released. An input map turns physical inputs into named actions. Analogue inputs need dead zones and clamping; virtual joysticks compute offsets from a centre divided by the radius. Coyote time and jump buffering make controls forgiving. Keep latency low, give instant feedback, and let players remap and adjust controls.
key_points: Devices: keyboard, mouse, multi-touch with IDs, gamepad sticks and triggers, motion sensors.
Engines record OS events into per-frame state; gameplay polls it so one frame sees consistent input.
Pressed = down now and not down last frame; trigger jumps on pressed, not held.
An input map links physical inputs to named actions, enabling multiple devices and rebinding.
Radial dead zone with rescale: output = (m - 0.2) / 0.8; a 0.6 push becomes 0.5.
Virtual joystick: offset / radius, clamped to length 1; offset (50, -40) with radius 80 gives (0.625, -0.5).
Coyote time (about 0.1 s) allows late jumps after leaving a ledge; jump buffering (about 0.15 s) keeps early presses.
Latency comes from every pipeline stage; give instant feedback and allow remapping for accessibility.
lessons.tip: Add coyote time and jump buffering to any platformer prototype on day one, then ask a friend to play with them switched off and on. The difference in how fair the game feels is the best lesson about input.
lessons.task: A virtual joystick has centre (120, 500) and radius 60. Compute the normalised input for touches at (150, 460), (120, 500) and (200, 500). Then apply a radial dead zone of 0.25 with rescaling to the first result.

quiz.q: How should a game detect that the jump button was pressed this frame?
options: Check whether it is down now only
Check whether it was down last frame only
Count how many frames it has been held
Check that it is down now and was not down last frame
quiz.explain: Pressed is the transition from up to down; checking only down now repeats the jump while held.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of an input map with named actions?
options: Gameplay code is independent of the physical device, and controls can be rebound
It makes the game render faster
It removes the need for dead zones
quiz.explain: Code asks for jump or steer; the map decides which keys, buttons or touches produce them.

quiz.q: A stick reads magnitude 0.6. With a radial dead zone of 0.2 and rescaling, what is the output magnitude?
What does coyote time do?
options: Speeds up the character after a jump
Remembers a jump press before landing
Allows a jump for a short time after leaving the ground
quiz.explain: It gives a small grace window after running off a ledge, so slightly late jumps still work.

quiz.explain: 80 / 50 = 1.6 exceeds 1, so the input is clamped to length 1: (1, 0).

lessons.title: Physics I: Motion, Euler Integration and Jump Arcs
lessons.content:
Throw a ball to a friend across the courtyard. It rises, slows, hangs for a moment, and curves down into their hands. You never calculated anything, yet your brain predicted that curve well enough to throw accurately. A game must calculate it, sixty times a second, using simple rules from school physics. This lesson covers kinematics, the description of motion; how games step motion forward in time with Euler integration, worked with numbers and errors; and how to design jumps that feel good by choosing gravity from a desired height and time. The next lesson covers forces, rigid bodies and physics engines.

Position, velocity and acceleration: Position is where something is. Velocity is how fast position changes, with direction: (200, 0) pixels per second means moving right at 200. Acceleration is how fast velocity changes: gravity accelerates objects downward. In continuous physics, velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration the derivative of velocity. A game cannot do calculus on infinitely small moments; it steps forward in small chunks of time, dt, which is called numerical integration.

Units in games: Real physics uses metres and seconds, with gravity about 9.8 metres per second squared near the Earth's surface. 2D games often work in pixels, so gravity might be 1500 or 2000 pixels per second squared. Many games also use stronger gravity than real life, because realistic jumps feel floaty and slow on screen. The key is consistency: decide units once, write them in comments, and convert carefully if a physics engine expects metres, as many do, with a pixels-per-metre scale.

Explicit Euler: The simplest integration rule, named after the mathematician Leonhard Euler, updates position using the old velocity and then velocity using acceleration: x = x + v x dt; v = v + a x dt. It assumes velocity stayed constant over the step, which is not quite true when accelerating, so it introduces error. It is easy to understand and good for teaching, but it can gain energy over time, making orbits spiral outward or springs oscillate more and more.

Semi-implicit Euler: Swap the two lines: update velocity first, then use the new velocity for position: v = v + a x dt; x = x + v x dt. This tiny change, also called symplectic Euler, is much more stable for games: springs and orbits stay bounded instead of exploding. It is what many game physics engines use at their core. Remember the order: velocity first, then position.

Worked comparison: Drop a stone from rest with g = 10 metres per second squared for 1 second. The exact distance is 0.5 x g x t^2 = 0.5 x 10 x 1 = 5 metres. With dt = 0.1, explicit Euler moves the stone using the old velocities 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 9 metres per second, each multiplied by 0.1 seconds, summing to 4.5 metres. Semi-implicit Euler uses the freshly updated velocities 1 to 10 metres per second, each times 0.1, summing to 5.5 metres. Both have 0.5 metres of error, in opposite directions, and both end with the correct velocity of 10 metres per second.

Error and step size: Halve the step to dt = 0.05 and run 20 steps: explicit Euler gives 4.75 metres, semi-implicit 5.25. The error halves to 0.25. This shows that Euler methods are first-order: error is proportional to dt. Smaller fixed steps are more accurate but cost more updates per second. This is why lesson 5's fixed timestep matters: with the same dt everywhere, the error is at least the same on every machine, so a jump that clears a gap on one phone clears it on all of them.

Better integrators: More accurate methods exist. Velocity Verlet uses the average of old and new acceleration and is popular for particle and cloth simulations. Runge-Kutta 4 samples the acceleration four times per step and is very accurate, used in scientific simulation, but costs more. For constant acceleration such as simple gravity, you can even use the exact formula x = x + v x dt + 0.5 x a x dt^2. Most games simply use semi-implicit Euler with a small fixed step, because it is fast, stable and good enough.

The jump: A jump is an initial upward velocity followed by gravity pulling the character back down. On a y-up axis: when jump is pressed while on the ground, set vy = v0. Each step, vy = vy - g x dt, y = y + vy x dt. The character rises, slows to zero at the apex, and falls. The shape traced is a parabola, the same curve as a thrown ball, which players recognise instinctively.

Jump numbers worked: Take v0 = 600 pixels per second and g = 1800 pixels per second squared. Time to the apex, when velocity reaches zero, is t = v0 / g = 600 / 1800, about 0.333 seconds. Jump height is h = v0^2 / (2g) = 360000 / 3600 = 100 pixels. Total air time on flat ground is twice the apex time, about 0.667 seconds. If the character runs at 300 pixels per second, the jump covers 300 x 0.667, about 200 pixels horizontally, which tells the level designer the widest gap players can clear.

Designing from height and time: Designers think in jump height and how long it takes, not in v0 and g. Rearranging the formulas: g = 2h / t^2 and v0 = 2h / t, where t is the time to the apex. Want a jump 120 pixels high reaching its peak in 0.4 seconds? g = 2 x 120 / 0.16 = 1500 and v0 = 2 x 120 / 0.4 = 600. Check: v0^2 / (2g) = 360000 / 3000 = 120. Now designers can tune feel directly: higher jump, change h; snappier jump, reduce t.

Variable jump height: Many platformers let players jump higher by holding the button longer. A common method: if the jump button is released while the character is still rising, cut the upward velocity, for example vy = vy x 0.5, or apply extra gravity until the apex. A quick tap then gives a small hop and a long press a full jump. This gives players fine control over every jump with one button.

Signs on y-down screens: On most 2D screens y grows downward, so gravity is positive and a jump sets a negative velocity: vy = -600 to go up, then vy = vy + 1800 x dt. The formulas for height and time are unchanged; only the signs flip. Mixing conventions is the most common reason a character falls upward or a jump sinks into the floor. Pick one convention, write it at the top of the physics code, and test with a single dropped object before building anything else on top.

Faster falling: A perfect parabola often feels floaty on the way down. Games commonly increase gravity while falling, for example multiplying g by 2 when vy is negative, so the character drops quickly and lands with weight. They also cap falling speed at a terminal velocity, such as 1000 pixels per second, so long falls stay readable and collisions stay reliable. These deliberate departures from real physics are part of game feel.

Horizontal movement: Instead of instantly snapping to full speed, characters usually accelerate and decelerate. With acceleration 2000 pixels per second squared and maximum speed 300, reaching full speed takes 300 / 2000 = 0.15 seconds. Using a lower acceleration in the air than on the ground gives less air control, which some games want and others avoid. Ice can use a very low deceleration so characters slide. Each number changes how the game feels, so expose them for tuning.

Friction and drag: Drag slows moving objects in proportion to their speed. A frame-rate-independent way is exponential decay: v = v x e^(-k x dt). With k = 3, after 0.5 seconds a speed of 400 falls to 400 x e^(-1.5), about 89. Applying v = v x (1 - k x dt) each frame is close for small dt: at 60 fps for 30 frames it gives about 86, slightly different, which is why the exponential form is preferred when frame rates vary. Ground friction is often simpler: reduce speed toward zero by a fixed deceleration each second.

Projectiles and aiming: A cannonball fired at speed s and angle theta starts with velocity (s cos theta, s sin theta) and then follows the same gravity rule. Game AI often needs the reverse: which angle hits a target? There are formulas for that, but many games simply simulate a few candidate angles quickly and pick the closest, or draw a dotted predicted path for the player by running the same integration ahead of time. Using the same integration for prediction and the real flight keeps the preview honest.

Example, a kite-flying game for Shakrain: In a kite game for Old Dhaka's kite festival, the kite has velocity, gravity pulls it down, wind pushes it sideways, and the string pulls toward the player's hand. Each force adds to acceleration, then semi-implicit Euler steps velocity and position at a fixed 1/60 step. Drag with k = 1.5 keeps the kite from flying away. Designers tweak gravity and drag until the kite swoops nicely. Exactly the tools of this lesson, combined.

Example, tuning a runner's jump: A student runner game's rickshaw must jump over open manholes 150 pixels wide while moving at 360 pixels per second. The designer wants an apex height of 90 pixels in 0.3 seconds: g = 2 x 90 / 0.09 = 2000 and v0 = 2 x 90 / 0.3 = 600. Air time is 0.6 seconds, covering 360 x 0.6 = 216 pixels, enough for the 150-pixel gaps with a comfortable margin. The numbers prove the level is fair before anyone plays it.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include updating position before velocity when you meant semi-implicit Euler, putting physics in the variable timestep, forgetting dt in acceleration, sign errors from y-down screens, and assuming real-world gravity feels right. Exams ask you to write explicit and semi-implicit Euler, compute positions for a few steps, compare to the exact answer, explain first-order error, and compute jump apex time, height and air time, or g and v0 from a desired height and time.

Recap: Motion is position, velocity and acceleration, stepped forward in time with numerical integration. Explicit Euler updates position with old velocity; semi-implicit Euler updates velocity first and is more stable; both have error proportional to dt. A jump is an initial velocity plus gravity: apex time v0 / g, height v0^2 / 2g, and designers choose g = 2h / t^2, v0 = 2h / t. Variable jump height, faster falling, acceleration and frame-rate-independent drag turn physics into good game feel.
key_points: Velocity is the rate of change of position; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
Explicit Euler: x += v dt, then v += a dt; semi-implicit: v += a dt, then x += v dt (more stable).
Drop with g = 10 for 1 s, dt = 0.1: exact 5 m, explicit 4.5 m, semi-implicit 5.5 m.
Euler error is first-order: halving dt halves the error (4.75 and 5.25 m at dt = 0.05).
Jump: apex time = v0 / g, height = v0^2 / (2g); v0 = 600, g = 1800 gives 0.333 s and 100 px.
Design from height h and apex time t: g = 2h / t^2, v0 = 2h / t (h = 120, t = 0.4 gives g = 1500, v0 = 600).
Variable jump height, stronger fall gravity and terminal velocity improve feel.
Frame-rate-independent drag: v = v x e^(-k dt).
lessons.tip: Put every movement number, gravity, jump height, apex time, acceleration and drag, in one tuning panel you can change while the game runs. Game feel is found by adjusting, not by calculating once.
lessons.task: Simulate a ball thrown upward at 20 metres per second with g = 10, using dt = 0.25 for 4 steps with both explicit and semi-implicit Euler, on paper. Compare the heights to the exact formula y = 20t - 5t^2. Then choose g and v0 for a jump 80 pixels high with an apex time of 0.35 seconds.

x = x + v dt, then v = v + a dt
x = x + a dt, then v = v + x dt
quiz.explain: Semi-implicit Euler updates velocity first and uses the new velocity to update position.

quiz.explain: Euler methods are first-order, so error is proportional to dt.

quiz.explain: g = 2h / t^2 = 200 / 0.25 = 800 pixels per second squared (and v0 = 2h / t = 400).

It removes the need for gravity
It gives the same slowdown regardless of frame rate
quiz.explain: A fixed per-frame factor depends on how many frames run per second; the exponential form depends only on elapsed time.

lessons.title: Physics II: Forces, Rigid Bodies and Physics Engines
lessons.content:
Picture a carrom board just after a hard strike. The striker smashes into a cluster of pieces; some fly fast, some barely move, some bounce off the cushions and slow down on the board. Each piece has mass, each collision trades momentum, the board's surface steals speed through friction. Simulating that convincingly needs more than the jump formulas from the last lesson. It needs forces, mass, impulses, restitution and friction, usually handled by a physics engine. This lesson explains those ideas with worked numbers, how physics engines are organised, the tunnelling problem, and when a game should fake physics instead.

Forces and Newton's second law: A force is a push or pull. Newton's second law says the acceleration of a body equals the total force on it divided by its mass: a = F / m. Worked: a 20 newton force on a 4 kilogram crate gives a = 20 / 4 = 5 metres per second squared. Starting from rest, after 2 seconds its velocity is 5 x 2 = 10 metres per second. In code, each step sums all forces, gravity, thrust, wind, springs, divides by mass to get acceleration, and integrates with semi-implicit Euler as in lesson 12.

Mass and why it matters: Gravity's force is m x g, so dividing by mass gives the same acceleration g for everything: a feather and a stone fall together without air. But other forces affect light and heavy objects differently. The same wind gust pushes a paper boat far more than a wooden one. Engines often store inverse mass, 1 / m, because it is used in every calculation and lets you represent immovable objects neatly with inverse mass 0, as if their mass were infinite.

Momentum and impulses: Momentum is mass times velocity, p = m x v. An impulse is a sudden change of momentum, equal to force multiplied by the short time it acts: J = F x dt = m x change in v. Worked: kicking a 0.5 kilogram ball from rest to 20 metres per second needs an impulse of 0.5 x 20 = 10 newton seconds. If the foot touches for 0.01 seconds, the average force is 10 / 0.01 = 1000 newtons. Games apply impulses directly for instant events such as kicks, explosions and jumps: v = v + J / m, skipping the force calculation.

Collisions and restitution: When two bodies collide, momentum is conserved, and the coefficient of restitution e, between 0 and 1, says how bouncy the collision is. For a 1D collision: v1' = ((m1 - e m2) v1 + (1 + e) m2 v2) / (m1 + m2), and v2' similarly with the roles swapped. Worked: a 2 kilogram puck at 3 metres per second hits a 1 kilogram puck at rest. With e = 1, perfectly elastic, the results are v1' = 1 and v2' = 4. Check momentum: 2 x 3 = 6 before, 2 x 1 + 1 x 4 = 6 after. With e = 0, perfectly inelastic, both move together at 2.

Bouncing balls: For a ball bouncing on immovable ground, restitution simply scales the rebound speed: speed after = e x speed before. Since height is proportional to speed squared, each bounce reaches e^2 of the previous height. A ball dropped from 2 metres with e = 0.7 rebounds to 2 x 0.49 = 0.98 metres, then about 0.48, and so on. Rubber balls might use 0.8, a cricket ball on a pitch less, a sandbag almost 0. Lesson 16 shows how to apply this in 2D with the collision normal.

Friction: Friction resists sliding between surfaces. In the common Coulomb model, the friction force is at most mu x N, where mu is the friction coefficient and N is the normal force pressing the surfaces together, on flat ground m x g. Worked: a 10 kilogram box on a floor with mu = 0.3 has friction 0.3 x 10 x 9.8 = 29.4 newtons. Pushing with 50 newtons leaves a net 20.6 newtons, so it accelerates at 2.06 metres per second squared. Engines let you set friction per material: ice near 0.05, rubber on concrete high, and combine the two surfaces' values when they touch.

Rigid bodies: A rigid body is an object that never deforms: a crate, a carrom piece, a car chassis. Besides position and velocity, it has orientation and angular velocity, so it can spin. Rotational versions of the same laws apply: torque, the turning effect of a force applied away from the centre, causes angular acceleration, resisted by the moment of inertia, the rotational version of mass.
