A hit off-centre makes a carrom piece both slide and spin. Engines compute all of this for you from the shape and density.

Body types: Physics engines usually offer three kinds of body. Static bodies never move: floors, walls, the carrom board's edges. They have infinite mass and cost almost nothing to simulate. Dynamic bodies are fully simulated: forces, gravity and collisions move them, such as crates and balls. Kinematic bodies move only as your code tells them, unaffected by forces, but they still push dynamic bodies: moving platforms and doors. Choosing the right type for each object is one of the first decisions in a physics-based game.

Constraints and joints: Many objects are connected: a pendulum to its pivot, a car's wheels to its body, a chain of links. Engines model connections as constraints or joints: a revolute joint lets two bodies rotate around a shared point, like a hinge; a distance joint keeps two points at a fixed distance, like a rope; a prismatic joint allows sliding along an axis, like a piston; a spring joint pulls toward a rest length. The solver adjusts velocities each step so all constraints and contacts are satisfied as well as possible.

Inside a physics engine: Each fixed step, a typical engine applies forces and integrates velocities; detects collisions, first broad phase then narrow phase, as lessons 14 and 15 explain; builds contact constraints; runs a solver that iterates several times, adjusting velocities so objects do not move into each other and friction and restitution are respected; integrates positions; and corrects small remaining overlaps. Bodies that have been still for a while are put to sleep and skipped until something touches them, which saves a lot of time in big scenes.

Well-known engines: Box2D is a widely used open-source 2D physics engine originally written by Erin Catto; many 2D tools use it or ports of it. Flame offers Forge2D, a Dart port of Box2D, for Flutter games. For 3D, well-known engines include PhysX, Havok, Bullet and Jolt, and major game engines either include one of these or their own. As always, details change between versions, so rely on each engine's documentation for specifics. Whichever you use, the concepts in this lesson, mass, impulses, restitution, friction, body types and fixed steps, carry over directly, because every engine is built on the same Newtonian ideas.

Tunnelling: Because physics steps in discrete jumps, a fast object can pass through a thin obstacle without ever overlapping it in any step. Worked: a bullet at 1200 pixels per second with a 60 Hz physics step moves 1200 / 60 = 20 pixels per step. A wall 10 pixels thick can sit entirely between two consecutive positions, so no overlap is ever detected and the bullet tunnels through. The rule of thumb: tunnelling is possible when the distance moved per step exceeds the combined thickness of the object and obstacle.

Fixing tunnelling: Options include making walls thicker; substepping, running several smaller steps for fast objects, for example 4 substeps of 5 pixels each; capping maximum speeds; ray casting along the path from the old to the new position and checking what it crosses; and continuous collision detection, CCD, which computes the time of impact between steps. Engines provide CCD as an option for specific bodies, often called bullet mode, because it costs more than normal detection.

Stability tips: Physics engines are happiest with sizes roughly between 0.1 and 10 units, mass ratios that are not extreme, a fixed timestep, and enough solver iterations. A tiny 1 kilogram ball resting on a 1000 kilogram box may jitter. Objects created overlapping each other explode apart. Huge pixel-based coordinates such as 5000 units confuse tuning, which is why engines like Box2D work in metres and games convert with a scale such as 50 pixels per metre.

When to fake physics: Full rigid-body physics is great for crates, ragdolls, carrom and destructible towers, where emergent chaos is fun. It is often bad for the player character in a platformer, where players expect precise, predictable control: no sliding down slopes, no being knocked away by a tiny box. Most platformers therefore use a kinematic character controller with hand-written movement from lesson 12, and collision checks from lessons 14 to 16, while letting dynamic physics handle the props.

Example, a digital carrom board: A carrom app uses a static body for the board frame with restitution 0.8, dynamic circular bodies for the pieces and striker, with mass ratios similar to real pieces, and linear damping to model board friction so pieces glide and stop. The flick applies an impulse to the striker proportional to the drag distance. CCD is enabled on the striker, which moves fastest. Sleeping bodies make the end of each shot cheap: when everything sleeps, the turn ends.

Example, a falling-crates puzzle: A puzzle game asks players to stack crates on a boat without sinking it during monsoon waves. Crates are dynamic bodies, the boat is kinematic, moved by a wave function, and the water line is a trigger zone. Testing reveals that tiny crates jitter on large ones, so the designer limits the mass ratio and raises solver iterations. Physics provides the puzzle; tuning makes it fair.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include using dynamic bodies for precise player characters, mixing pixel and metre units, spawning objects overlapping, extreme mass ratios, and ignoring tunnelling for fast objects. Exams ask you to apply F = ma, compute impulses and average forces, solve a 1D collision with restitution and check momentum, compute bounce heights, compute friction forces, explain static, kinematic and dynamic bodies, and describe tunnelling with its fixes.

Recap: Forces cause acceleration a = F / m; impulses change momentum instantly, J = m x change in v. Collisions conserve momentum, and restitution sets bounciness: a 2 kg puck at 3 m/s hitting a 1 kg puck gives 1 and 4 m/s when elastic, 2 and 2 when inelastic. Friction is at most mu N. Engines simulate rigid bodies of static, kinematic and dynamic types with joints and an iterative solver at a fixed step. Fast objects tunnel unless you substep, ray cast or use CCD, and precise characters are often better faked than simulated.
key_points: Newton's second law: a = F / m; 20 N on 4 kg gives 5 m/s^2.
Impulse J = F x dt = m x change in v; a 0.5 kg ball to 20 m/s needs 10 N s, about 1000 N over 0.01 s.
1D collision conserves momentum; restitution e sets bounciness (2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg: 1 and 4 m/s if e = 1).
Bounce height scales by e^2: from 2 m with e = 0.7 the ball reaches 0.98 m.
Coulomb friction is at most mu x N; 10 kg with mu = 0.3 gives 29.4 N.
Body types: static (never moves), dynamic (fully simulated), kinematic (moved by code, pushes others).
Tunnelling happens when movement per step exceeds thickness; fix with substeps, ray casts or CCD.
Use physics for props and chaos; use kinematic controllers for precise player movement.
lessons.tip: Open any free 2D physics sandbox or a small engine demo and change one property at a time: restitution, friction, mass, damping. Predict the result before pressing play; physics intuition grows fastest through prediction.
lessons.task: Two carrom pieces move along a line: piece A (15 g) at 2 metres per second hits piece B (15 g) at rest. Compute their velocities after collision for e = 1, e = 0.8 and e = 0, and check momentum each time. Then compute how many 60 Hz substeps a striker at 3 metres per second needs to move no more than 5 millimetres per substep.

quiz.q: A 50 newton force acts on a 10 kilogram body. What is its acceleration?
quiz.explain: a = F / m = 50 / 10 = 5 metres per second squared.

quiz.q: Which body type is moved only by code and is not affected by forces, but still pushes dynamic bodies?
quiz.explain: Kinematic bodies follow scripted motion such as moving platforms and still interact with dynamic bodies.

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 4 metres bounces with restitution 0.5. How high does it rise after the first bounce?
quiz.explain: Height scales by e^2 = 0.25, so 4 x 0.25 = 1 metre.

quiz.q: A bullet moves 30 pixels per physics step and a wall is 8 pixels thick. What problem may occur?
options: Tunnelling: the bullet passes through without a detected overlap
quiz.explain: Moving farther per step than the wall's thickness lets the bullet skip over it; substeps, ray casts or CCD fix this.

quiz.q: Why do most platformers use a kinematic character controller instead of a dynamic rigid body for the player?
options: Players expect precise, predictable control rather than being pushed and sliding like a crate
Kinematic bodies are always faster to draw
quiz.explain: Hand-written movement gives exact control over feel; physics props can still be dynamic.

lessons.title: Collision Detection I: Shapes and Overlap Tests
lessons.content:
In a game of gollachut, everything depends on one question asked again and again: did the chaser touch the runner? Video games ask that question thousands of times per second: did the bullet hit the enemy, is the player standing on the platform, did the rickshaw touch the bus, did the mango land in the basket? Answering it is collision detection. It looks simple, but drawn pictures are complicated shapes, and checking every pixel would be far too slow. This lesson shows how games approximate objects with simple shapes and test them quickly: axis-aligned boxes, circles, circle-versus-box, and the separating axis idea for rotated shapes, all with worked numbers.

Detection versus response: Collision handling has two parts. Detection answers whether, and often where and how deeply, two shapes overlap. Response decides what to do about it: stop the player, bounce the ball, damage the enemy, collect the coin. This lesson and the next cover detection; lesson 16 covers response. Keeping them separate in code is good design, because the same detection can feed very different responses.

Why simple shapes: A character sprite might be 64 x 64 pixels with an irregular outline. Testing two such sprites pixel by pixel would mean comparing up to 4096 pixel pairs for each pair of objects, every frame. Instead, games wrap each object in a simple collision shape, also called a bounding volume or collider: a rectangle, a circle, a capsule or a convex polygon. The shape does not need to match the art exactly; it needs to feel fair. Many games make the player's shape slightly smaller than its sprite, so near misses feel lucky rather than unfair.

Axis-aligned bounding boxes: The most common shape is the axis-aligned bounding box, AABB: a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the x and y axes, stored as minimum and maximum corners, (minX, minY) and (maxX, maxY), or as a centre and half-sizes. Because it never rotates, testing two AABBs takes just four comparisons. AABBs fit tiles, platforms, crates and upright characters well.

The AABB overlap test: Two AABBs overlap only if they overlap on both axes. On the x axis, they overlap when A.minX < B.maxX and A.maxX > B.minX; likewise on y. In code: overlap = A.minX < B.maxX and A.maxX > B.minX and A.minY < B.maxY and A.maxY > B.minY. If any one comparison fails, there is a gap on that axis and the boxes cannot touch. Whether to use less-than or less-than-or-equal decides whether boxes that only touch at an edge count as colliding; pick one and be consistent.

AABB worked: Box A has min (10, 20) and max (50, 60). Box B has min (40, 50) and max (90, 80). On x: 10 < 90 and 50 > 40, true. On y: 20 < 80 and 60 > 50, true. So they overlap. The overlap amounts are, on x, min(50, 90) - max(10, 40) = 50 - 40 = 10, and on y, min(60, 80) - max(20, 50) = 60 - 50 = 10. Box C has min (60, 20) and max (80, 40). Testing A against C: on x, A.maxX = 50 is not greater than C.minX = 60, so there is a gap and no collision, without even checking y.

The centre form: Many engines store an AABB as a centre and half-sizes instead. Then the test becomes: |A.cx - B.cx| < A.hw + B.hw and |A.cy - B.cy| < A.hh + B.hh. Box A above has centre (30, 40) and half-sizes (20, 20); box B has centre (65, 65) and half-sizes (25, 15). On x, |30 - 65| = 35 < 45; on y, |40 - 65| = 25 < 35; so they overlap, matching the first method. Both forms are common, so learn to convert between them.

Circles: Circles are the other cheap shape. Two circles overlap when the distance between their centres is less than the sum of their radii. To avoid the square root, compare squared values: (dx^2 + dy^2) < (r1 + r2)^2. Circles rotate freely without changing, which suits balls, coins, carrom pieces, round enemies and characters seen from above. Their collision normal, the direction to push them apart, is simply the line between the centres.

Circle worked: Circle 1 has centre (0, 0) and radius 5; circle 2 has centre (6, 8) and radius 6. dx^2 + dy^2 = 36 + 64 = 100. (r1 + r2)^2 = 11^2 = 121. Since 100 < 121, they overlap. The actual distance is 10 and the radii sum to 11, so the penetration depth is 1. If circle 2 had radius 4, then (5 + 4)^2 = 81 < 100, and they would be separate. No square root was needed for the yes or no answer, only for the depth.

Circle versus AABB: A ball hitting a brick, or a round character against a wall, needs circle-versus-box. The trick is to find the point on the box closest to the circle's centre by clamping: closestX = clamp(cx, minX, maxX); closestY = clamp(cy, minY, maxY). Then test whether that point is inside the circle: (cx - closestX)^2 + (cy - closestY)^2 < r^2. If the centre is inside the box, the closest point is the centre itself and the distance is 0, which correctly reports a collision.

Circle versus AABB worked: The box has min (0, 0) and max (10, 10). A circle with centre (14, 5) and radius 5: the closest point is (clamp(14, 0, 10), clamp(5, 0, 10)) = (10, 5). The squared distance is 16, less than 25, so they collide. A circle with centre (14, 14) and radius 5: the closest point is (10, 10), the corner; the squared distance is 16 + 16 = 32, more than 25, so no collision, even though a quick box-versus-box check of the circle's bounding square would wrongly say yes. Corners are exactly where the clamping method beats approximations.

Point tests: Many questions are about points. Did a tap land on a button? Point in AABB: minX <= px <= maxX and minY <= py <= maxY. Is a point inside a circle? Squared distance to the centre less than r^2. Is the point under the player's feet a solid tile? Convert to tile coordinates as in lesson 9 and look up the tile. Point tests are the cheapest of all and are used constantly for input, triggers and ground checks.

Capsules: A capsule is a rectangle with semicircular ends, or equivalently all points within radius r of a line segment. Its rounded bottom slides smoothly over small steps and slope changes instead of catching on corners, so 3D and many 2D character controllers use capsules. Testing capsule against circle reduces to finding the closest point on the segment to the circle's centre, then a circle test, the same clamping idea along one line.

Oriented boxes and polygons: When a box rotates, such as a car turning or a crate tumbling, an AABB no longer fits it. An oriented bounding box, OBB, has its own rotated axes. More generally, games use convex polygons: shapes where any line between two inside points stays inside, such as triangles, rectangles and hexagons. Concave shapes, like an L or a crescent, are usually split into several convex pieces, because convex shapes allow a clean, fast test.

The separating axis theorem: The separating axis theorem, SAT, says that two convex shapes do not overlap if and only if there exists some line, an axis, onto which their shadows, called projections, do not overlap. For two convex polygons, you only need to test the axes perpendicular to each edge, the edge normals. Project both shapes onto an axis: each becomes an interval [min, max]. If any axis gives separate intervals, such as [0, 4] and [5, 9], the shapes are apart and you can stop early. If every axis overlaps, they collide.

SAT in practice: Two rectangles need at most four axes, two from each, since opposite edges share normals. The axis with the smallest overlap also gives the minimum translation vector: the shortest push to separate the shapes, which lesson 16 uses for response. The AABB test is actually SAT with only the x and y axes. SAT does not work directly on concave shapes, which is another reason they are split into convex pieces.

Hitboxes and hurtboxes: Action and fighting games often use several shapes per character. Hurtboxes mark where a character can be hit: head, body, legs. Hitboxes appear only during attacks, marking where the attack can hit: a fist's box exists for a few frames of a punch animation. A hit happens when an attacker's hitbox overlaps a defender's hurtbox. Designers tune these boxes frame by frame, and many games show them in debug mode, because fair-feeling combat depends on them.

Ray casts: Sometimes the question is not do two shapes overlap but what does a line hit first. A ray cast shoots a line from a point in a direction and reports the first shape it crosses, with distance and normal. Games use rays for line-of-sight checks for AI guards, ground detection under a character's feet, instant bullets, laser beams, and tunnelling prevention as in lesson 13. Ray-versus-AABB and ray-versus-circle tests are standard building blocks in every engine.

Example, catching mangoes: In the mango-catching game, each mango is a circle of radius 12 and the basket is an AABB 80 wide and 30 tall at its rim. Each frame, the game clamps the mango centre to the basket box and compares the squared distance to 144. A mango that clips the basket's corner is correctly accepted or rejected by the corner case. The basket's box is set a little wider than the art, so catches feel generous to young players.

Example, a cricket fielding game: A fielder is a capsule, the ball a small circle. To decide whether the fielder can catch, the game ray casts from the ball along its velocity to see whether it passes within the fielder's reach this frame, avoiding tunnelling at high ball speeds. The stumps are three thin AABBs; a separate small hitbox on the bat is active only during the swing animation. Each shape is the cheapest that feels right.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include using sprites' full rectangles as colliders, using approximate box tests for circles at corners, forgetting that rotated boxes are not AABBs, computing square roots unnecessarily, and inconsistent edge rules. Exams ask you to write and apply the AABB test, test two circles with squared distances, apply circle-versus-AABB clamping, state the separating axis theorem and explain why it needs convex shapes, and distinguish hitboxes from hurtboxes.

Recap: Collision detection tests simple stand-in shapes rather than pixels. AABBs overlap when they overlap on both axes; circles overlap when the squared centre distance is below the squared radius sum; circle-versus-AABB clamps the centre to the box and tests the closest point. Capsules suit characters. SAT handles rotated convex shapes by searching for a separating axis among edge normals. Hitboxes, hurtboxes and ray casts complete the toolbox, and response comes in lesson 16.
key_points: Detection asks whether shapes overlap; response decides what to do; keep them separate.
Games use simple colliders (AABB, circle, capsule, convex polygon) instead of pixels, often slightly smaller than art.
AABB overlap: A.minX < B.maxX and A.maxX > B.minX and the same for y; one failing test means no collision.
Worked: A (10, 20)-(50, 60) and B (40, 50)-(90, 80) overlap by 10 on each axis.
Circles overlap if dx^2 + dy^2 < (r1 + r2)^2; centres (0, 0) and (6, 8) with radii 5 and 6: 100 < 121.
Circle vs AABB: clamp the centre to the box, then test the squared distance to that closest point.
SAT: convex shapes are apart if some axis (an edge normal) separates their projections.
Hitboxes (attacks) hit hurtboxes (vulnerable areas); ray casts find the first thing along a line.
lessons.tip: Draw your colliders on screen in a debug mode from the first day of every project. Most collision bugs are obvious the moment you can see the shapes instead of the sprites.
lessons.task: Box P is (0, 0)-(30, 20). Test it against box Q (25, 15)-(40, 40), circle R with centre (40, 10) and radius 12, and circle S with centre (36, 28) and radius 8, showing each calculation. Report overlaps on each axis where boxes collide.

quiz.q: Box A is (0, 0)-(10, 10) and box B is (12, 3)-(20, 8). Do they overlap?
options: No, because A.maxX = 10 is not greater than B.minX = 12
Yes, because they overlap on y
It cannot be decided without square roots
quiz.explain: The x test fails (10 is not greater than 12), so there is a gap on x and no collision.

quiz.q: Two circles have centres 13 units apart and radii 6 and 8. Using squared values, what is the result?
quiz.explain: Distance squared is 169 and (6 + 8)^2 is 196; 169 < 196, so they overlap.

quiz.q: For circle-versus-AABB, what is the first step?
options: Rotate the box to match the circle
Clamp the circle's centre to the box to find the closest point
quiz.explain: The clamped point is the box point nearest to the centre; then a squared-distance test decides.

quiz.q: What does the separating axis theorem state for convex shapes?
options: They do not overlap if and only if some axis separates their projections
They always overlap if their centres are close
quiz.explain: If any tested axis gives non-overlapping intervals, the shapes are separate; if none does, they collide.

quiz.q: In a fighting game, what is a hitbox?
options: The box around the whole level
A box marking where a character can be hurt
A box active during an attack marking where the attack can land
quiz.explain: Hitboxes belong to attacks; hurtboxes mark vulnerable areas; a hit is a hitbox overlapping a hurtbox.

lessons.title: Collision Detection II: Broad Phase, Narrow Phase and Spatial Grids
lessons.content:
Imagine the head teacher of a big school in Mymensingh wants to know which students are standing close enough to whisper to each other at the assembly. She could compare every student with every other student, but with a thousand students that is nearly half a million comparisons. Instead she looks row by row: only students in the same or neighbouring rows could possibly be whispering. Games face exactly this problem with collisions, and solve it the same way: first quickly throw away pairs that cannot possibly touch, then test the few remaining pairs carefully. This lesson covers the n squared problem, broad and narrow phase, uniform spatial grids worked with numbers, quadtrees, sweep and prune, and collision layers.

The n squared problem: Checking every object against every other object requires n(n - 1) / 2 tests for n objects. For 10 objects that is 45 tests, trivial. For 100 objects, 4950. For 1000 objects, 499,500. For 10,000 objects, about 50 million. At 60 frames per second, 1000 objects would need about 30 million tests per second just for collisions. The count grows with the square of n, written O(n^2) in the Algorithms course, so doubling the objects quadruples the work. A bullet-heavy game reaches these numbers quickly.

Broad phase and narrow phase: The solution splits detection into two stages. The broad phase uses cheap, approximate reasoning to find candidate pairs: objects that are near each other and might touch. Most pairs are rejected here without any shape test. The narrow phase then runs the exact tests from lesson 14, AABB, circle, SAT, on the candidates only. A good broad phase reduces 499,500 pairs to a few thousand or fewer, while never missing a pair that actually collides.

Bounding boxes in the broad phase: Broad phases usually work with each object's AABB, even if its real shape is a circle or a rotated polygon, because AABBs are cheap to compare and easy to place into data structures. A circle's AABB is its centre plus and minus its radius on each axis; a rotated polygon's AABB is the min and max of its vertices. If two AABBs do not overlap, the shapes inside cannot either, so the broad phase is safe.

The uniform grid: The simplest broad phase divides the world into equal square cells, like graph paper. Each object is inserted into every cell its AABB touches. Only objects sharing a cell can collide, so each cell's objects are tested against each other and nothing else. To find an object's cell, divide by the cell size, exactly like tile coordinates in lesson 9: a point at (250, 130) with 100-unit cells is in cell (2, 1).

Grid insertion worked: An object with AABB from (180, 90) to (220, 140) spans cell columns 180 div 100 = 1 to 220 div 100 = 2, and rows 90 div 100 = 0 to 140 div 100 = 1. So it goes into four cells: (1, 0), (2, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 1). Objects in the middle of a cell occupy one cell; objects across a corner occupy up to four, if no object is larger than a cell. Each frame, the grid is cleared and rebuilt, or objects are moved between cells only when they cross a boundary.

Grid savings worked: Suppose 1000 objects are spread evenly over a 1000 x 1000 world with 100-unit cells, 10 x 10 = 100 cells, so about 10 objects per cell. Each cell needs 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 tests, and 100 cells need 4500 tests, compared to 499,500 for brute force: about 111 times fewer. Objects in several cells add a few more tests, but the saving remains huge. In real games objects cluster, so savings vary, but the grid is often the single biggest performance win in a collision system.

Choosing the cell size: If cells are too small, large objects occupy many cells and insertion costs grow. If cells are too large, many objects share each cell and we drift back toward n squared. A common rule is to make cells around the size of a typical object, or a little larger. When object sizes vary wildly, such as tiny bullets and huge bosses, games may use two grids of different sizes or a hierarchical structure.

Duplicate pairs: If two objects share two cells, both cells will report the same pair, and the game might apply damage twice. Fix this by keeping a set of pairs already tested this frame, using the pair of IDs in a fixed order, smaller first, as the key. Alternatively, report a pair only from the cell containing a chosen reference point of their overlap. Either way, each colliding pair must produce exactly one result.

Spatial hashing: A fixed grid needs memory for every cell, even empty ones, which is wasteful for huge or unbounded worlds such as an endless runner. Spatial hashing stores only non-empty cells in a hash table, the dictionary structure from Data Structures, keyed by the cell coordinates (cx, cy). Lookups stay fast on average, memory grows only with the number of occupied cells, and the world can extend forever in any direction.

Quadtrees: A quadtree adapts to where objects are. Start with one square covering the world. When it holds more than a limit, say 4 objects, split it into four equal quadrants and move objects down into them; repeat recursively. Crowded areas get small, deep cells; empty areas stay as large cells. Searching for an object's neighbours walks down only the branches its AABB overlaps. Objects that straddle a split line stay in the parent node. Quadtrees suit uneven distributions, such as a city map with dense markets and empty fields. In 3D the same idea with eight children is an octree.

Sweep and prune: Another approach sorts objects along one axis. Each AABB is an interval [minX, maxX] on the x axis. After sorting by minX, sweep from left to right, keeping a list of active intervals; a new interval is tested only against active intervals it overlaps on x. Pairs that overlap on x then get a y check. Because objects move only a little each frame, the sorted order changes little, and insertion sort re-sorts a nearly sorted list very quickly. Sweep and prune works well when objects are spread along one direction, like a side-scrolling runner.

Bounding volume hierarchies: 3D engines often use bounding volume hierarchies, BVHs: a tree where each node holds a box enclosing all its children, down to individual objects at the leaves. Two objects can only collide if the boxes at every level of their paths overlap, so whole groups are rejected at once. BVHs are also the standard structure for fast ray casting, including in the ray tracing you met in Computer Graphics.

Collision layers and masks: Not everything should collide with everything. Player bullets should hit enemies but not the player or other bullets; coins should only react to the player. Engines assign each object a layer and a mask using bits. Say player is bit value 1, enemy 2, player bullet 4, enemy bullet 8, coin 16. A player bullet has layer 4 and mask 2, enemies only. The player has layer 1 and a mask of 2 + 8 + 16 = 26: enemies, enemy bullets and coins. Two objects interact when (layerA AND maskB) and (layerB AND maskA) are both non-zero.

Layers worked: A player bullet (layer 4, mask 2) meets an enemy (layer 2, mask 1 + 4 = 5). Check: 4 AND 5 = 4, non-zero; 2 AND 2 = 2, non-zero; they collide. A player bullet meets another player bullet: 4 AND 2 = 0, so the pair is skipped immediately, before any geometry. Layers are checked in the broad phase or right after it, and they remove huge numbers of pairs in bullet-heavy games, besides preventing silly bugs like bullets colliding with the gun that fired them.

Inside the narrow phase: Once a candidate pair arrives, the narrow phase still tries to exit early. It checks the cheapest conditions first: are both objects active, do their layers match, do their AABBs really overlap now? Only then does it run the exact shape test, circle, polygon SAT or capsule, and finally computes the contact details that response needs: the normal, the penetration depth and the contact points, sometimes called a contact manifold. Ordering tests from cheapest to most expensive is a general optimisation habit that pays off far beyond collisions.

Measuring before optimising: Not every game needs a clever broad phase. A puzzle game with 40 objects has only 780 pairs, and brute force takes a tiny fraction of a millisecond. The profiler from lesson 22 tells you whether collisions are actually expensive; add a grid when they are, not before.

Static versus moving objects: Walls and tilemaps never move, so they need not be re-inserted each frame. Many engines keep static objects in a separate structure built once, and test only moving objects against them. Tilemaps need no broad phase at all: to find which tiles a moving AABB might touch, convert its corners to tile coordinates and check only those few tiles, a direct lookup with no searching.

Example, a bullet-hell festival game: A game where the player dodges hundreds of colourful fireworks during a festival has 2000 bullets and 30 enemies. Brute force would mean about 2 million pairs per frame. With layers, enemy bullets ignore each other and only test the player; player bullets only test enemies. With a uniform grid of 64-pixel cells, each test touches only nearby objects. The frame fits in its budget on a mid-range phone.

Example, a crowded Sadarghat ferry terminal: A simulation of passengers boarding launches at a busy terminal has 3000 walking people whose density is very uneven: packed near gangways, sparse on the open quay. A quadtree adapts: deep subdivision near gangways, large cells elsewhere. Each person queries neighbours only in nearby quadtree nodes to avoid bumping into others. Static railings and pillars sit in a separate structure built once at load time.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include brute-force checking everything, choosing cell sizes far from object sizes, double-reporting pairs from multiple cells, rebuilding static structures every frame, and forgetting layers so bullets hit their own shooters. Exams ask: compute n(n - 1) / 2 for given n; explain broad versus narrow phase; place objects into grid cells; estimate grid savings; describe quadtrees and sweep and prune; and evaluate collision layer and mask checks with bitwise AND.

Recap: Testing all pairs costs n(n - 1) / 2, about half a million for 1000 objects. The broad phase uses AABBs and spatial structures, uniform grids, spatial hashes, quadtrees, sweep and prune or BVHs, to find candidate pairs; the narrow phase tests only those exactly. A grid with 100 cells cut 499,500 tests to about 4500 in our example. Layers and masks remove pairs that should never interact, and static geometry and tilemaps get special cheap treatment.
key_points: Brute force needs n(n - 1) / 2 tests: 45 for 10, 4950 for 100, 499,500 for 1000 objects.
Broad phase finds candidate pairs cheaply with AABBs; narrow phase runs exact shape tests on candidates only.
Uniform grid: cell = position div cell size; an AABB (180, 90)-(220, 140) with 100-unit cells covers 4 cells.
1000 evenly spread objects in 100 cells: about 4500 tests instead of 499,500 (about 111 times fewer).
Choose cells about the size of typical objects; avoid duplicate pairs with an ordered-ID set.
Spatial hashing stores only occupied cells; quadtrees subdivide crowded areas; sweep and prune sorts along an axis.
Layers and masks: collide when (layerA AND maskB) and (layerB AND maskA) are both non-zero.
Static objects and tilemaps are handled separately; tiles are looked up directly from coordinates.
lessons.tip: Before optimising collisions, count them: print how many narrow-phase tests run per frame. Watching that number fall from hundreds of thousands to a few thousand when you add a grid is the most convincing lesson in algorithmic complexity you will ever see.
lessons.task: A world 800 x 600 uses a grid with 100-unit cells. List the cells touched by AABBs (90, 40)-(130, 70), (310, 210)-(330, 260) and (450, 450)-(560, 520). Then, with layers player 1, enemy 2, player bullet 4 and coin 8, choose masks so player bullets hit only enemies and coins react only to the player, and verify two pairs with bitwise AND.

quiz.q: How many pairwise tests does brute force need for 200 objects?
What is the job of the broad phase?
options: Quickly find candidate pairs that might collide, rejecting most pairs cheaply
Resolve overlaps by pushing objects apart
quiz.explain: The broad phase filters pairs cheaply; the narrow phase does exact tests on the survivors.

quiz.q: With 50-unit grid cells, which cell contains the point (175, 60)?
Which structure adapts by subdividing only crowded regions into four smaller squares?
quiz.explain: A quadtree splits a node into four quadrants when it holds too many objects.

quiz.q: A player bullet has layer 4 and mask 2. An enemy has layer 2 and mask 5. Do they collide?
options: Yes, because 4 AND 5 and 2 AND 2 are both non-zero
No, because layers must be equal
quiz.explain: 4 AND 5 = 4 and 2 AND 2 = 2; both non-zero, so the pair interacts.

lessons.title: Collision Response: Separating, Sliding and Bouncing
lessons.content:
Knowing that two things touched is only half the story. When you walk into a wall, you stop. When a cricket ball hits the pitch, it bounces up at a slightly lower speed. When a rickshaw scrapes along a footpath kerb, it slides along instead of sticking. When you walk through a shop doorway, a bell rings but nothing stops you. Each is a different response to a detected collision. This lesson covers how games push overlapping objects apart with the minimum translation vector, resolve platformer movement axis by axis, slide along walls, bounce with reflection and restitution, handle triggers and one-way platforms, all with worked numbers.

Detection gives you facts, response makes decisions: From lesson 14 and 15 the narrow phase delivers, for each colliding pair, a collision normal n, the unit direction to push one object out of the other, and a penetration depth d, how far they overlap. Response uses these facts. Since physics advances in discrete steps, objects usually overlap a little by the time we notice, so the first job is often to separate them, and the second is to fix their velocities so they do not move back in.

The minimum translation vector: The minimum translation vector, MTV, is the shortest move that separates two overlapping shapes: direction n, length d. For two AABBs, compute the overlap on each axis and choose the smaller. Worked: the player's box is (100, 100)-(140, 160) and a wall is (130, 0)-(200, 300). Overlap on x is min(140, 200) - max(100, 130) = 10; on y it is min(160, 300) - max(100, 0) = 60. The smaller is x, 10. The player's centre x is 120, left of the wall's centre 165, so push the player left by 10: its box becomes (90, 100)-(130, 160), just touching the wall.

Why the smallest axis: Pushing along the axis of least overlap matches how the objects most likely met. A player who walked sideways into a wall overlaps it slightly on x but a lot on y, since the wall is tall. Pushing up by 60 instead would pop the player onto the top of the wall, an infamous bug. For circles, the MTV points along the line between centres: with centres (0, 0) and (6, 8), radii 5 and 6, the normal is (0.6, 0.8) and depth 1, as in lesson 14. If both objects can move and have equal mass, move each by half the depth, 0.5, in opposite directions.

Axis-by-axis resolution for platformers: For tile-based platformers, a robust and simple method moves and resolves one axis at a time. First apply horizontal movement: x = x + vx x dt; then check collisions and push out along x only, setting vx = 0 if blocked. Then apply vertical movement: y = y + vy x dt; check again and push out along y only. If pushed up out of the floor, set vy = 0 and onGround = true; if pushed down from a ceiling, set vy = 0. Because each push is on a known axis, corner cases that confuse the MTV method disappear.

Landing worked: A character falls with vy = 300 pixels per second on a y-down screen at 60 fps, so this step moves it 300 / 60 = 5 pixels down. Its feet were 2 pixels above the floor, so after moving they are 3 pixels inside the floor. The y-resolution pushes the character up by 3 so the feet sit exactly on the floor, sets vy = 0 and sets onGround = true, which allows the next jump and switches the animation from fall to idle or run. Without setting vy to 0, gravity would keep growing vy and the character would sink deeper every frame.

Sliding along surfaces: When a character moves diagonally into a wall, it should slide along the wall, not stop dead. The trick is to remove only the part of velocity going into the surface. Using y-up maths and a floor with normal n = (0, 1), a velocity v = (3, -4) heading down-right has v . n = -4. The slide velocity is v - (v . n) n = (3, -4) - (-4)(0, 1) = (3, 0). The downward part is cancelled; the sideways part survives. This works for any surface direction, including slopes, as long as n is a unit vector.

Only resolve approaching objects: Before changing velocities, check that the objects are actually moving toward each other: the relative velocity's dot product with the normal must be negative. If they are already separating, for example after the previous frame's push, changing velocity again would make them stick or jitter. In code: if dot(vRel, n) < 0 then apply the response. This one condition removes a whole family of sticky-collision bugs.

Bouncing with reflection: For a bounce, reverse the velocity component along the normal. A perfect mirror reflection is v' = v - 2 (v . n) n. With restitution e from lesson 13, the general rule is v' = v - (1 + e)(v . n) n: e = 1 reflects perfectly, e = 0 slides, values between give a weaker bounce. Worked with the floor n = (0, 1) and v = (3, -4): with e = 1, v' = (3, 4); with e = 0.5, v' = (3, -4) - 1.5 x (-4)(0, 1) = (3, 2), so the vertical speed after the bounce is half of 4; with e = 0, v' = (3, 0), sliding again.

Bounce off an angled wall: Reflection works for any angle. A ball moving with v = (-5, 0) hits a sloped wall whose unit normal is n = (0.6, 0.8). Then v . n = -3. With e = 1, v' = (-5, 0) - 2 x (-3)(0.6, 0.8) = (-5 + 3.6, 0 + 4.8) = (-1.4, 4.8). Its speed is sqrt(1.96 + 23.04) = 5, unchanged, as a perfect bounce should be, but its direction has turned up and slightly left. Brick-breaker and pinball games depend on exactly this formula.

Friction during contact: When objects slide against each other, friction reduces the tangent part of velocity, the part along the surface. A simple game approach splits velocity into a normal part, handled by restitution, and a tangent part, scaled down by a friction factor each contact: vt = vt x (1 - mu). Physics engines do this more carefully using the Coulomb limit from lesson 13. For a character controller, ground friction is usually handled by the movement code instead.

Triggers: Some colliders should detect overlap but never push anything: coins, checkpoints, damage zones, the finish line, a doorway that starts a cutscene. These are triggers or sensors. Engines report trigger events, usually enter, stay and exit, so code can respond once when the player arrives, continuously while inside, and once when leaving. A coin uses enter: add score, play a sound, remove the coin. A healing spring might use stay, adding health per second times dt.

One-way platforms: Many platformers have platforms you can jump up through from below and then land on. The rule: the platform only collides when the character is moving downward and its feet were above the platform's top in the previous step. In pseudo-code: if vy > 0 on a y-down screen and previousBottom <= platformTop then resolve, else ignore. Dropping down through the platform is added by ignoring it briefly when the player presses down plus jump.

Moving platforms: When a character stands on a moving platform, it should move with it. The usual method is to add the platform's displacement for this frame to the character's position while onGround on that platform, before applying the character's own movement. Forgetting this makes characters slide off moving platforms or jitter on them. Physics engines handle it through friction with kinematic bodies.

Damage response and invulnerability: For gameplay hits, response is not physical. An enemy touching the player triggers damage, a knock-back impulse away from the enemy along the collision normal, a flash and a sound. To avoid losing all health in one long overlap, the player becomes invulnerable for a short time, often around one second, shown by blinking; these are often called invincibility frames, or i-frames. Without them, an overlap lasting 30 frames could deal damage 30 times.

Order of operations: A typical frame's movement and response order: read input; apply forces and update velocities; move along x and resolve; move along y and resolve, setting ground state; process triggers; apply gameplay responses such as damage and pickups; then animation. Physics engines run their own internal order, and gameplay code reacts to the contact and trigger events they report, usually after the physics step. Writing this order down as a comment at the top of the update function saves hours of confusion when two systems disagree about where an object is.

Example, a brick-breaker with Nakshi Kantha patterns: A brick-breaker game uses colourful bricks patterned like Nakshi Kantha embroidery. The ball is a circle with e = 1. Against a brick, circle-versus-AABB gives the closest point; the normal points from that point to the ball's centre. The ball is pushed out by the penetration depth and reflected with v - 2 (v . n) n. Hitting the paddle off-centre tilts the normal slightly, giving players control over the angle. The brick itself is removed as a gameplay response.

Example, a platformer in a jute mill: In a platformer set among stacked jute bales, the character uses axis-by-axis resolution against a tilemap. Bales on conveyor belts are moving platforms, so the character inherits their motion. Wooden shelves are one-way platforms. Steam vents are trigger zones that push the character upward while inside. Sharp machinery has a damage response with knock-back and one second of i-frames. Each object type gets the response that makes the game fair and readable.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include pushing along the wrong axis so characters pop onto walls, not zeroing velocity after landing, resolving objects that are already separating, forgetting to normalise the normal, and applying damage every frame of overlap. Exams ask you to compute the MTV for two boxes, explain axis-by-axis resolution, compute slide and bounce velocities with v - (1 + e)(v . n) n, verify that perfect reflection preserves speed, explain triggers and one-way platforms, and describe invulnerability frames.

Recap: Response turns detection facts, normal and depth, into actions. Separate overlapping shapes along the minimum translation vector, the axis of least overlap; platformers resolve x and y separately for robustness. Remove the normal part of velocity to slide, reverse it with restitution to bounce: v' = v - (1 + e)(v . n) n, applied only when objects approach. Triggers report enter, stay and exit without pushing; one-way and moving platforms and damage with i-frames are special responses built on the same facts.
key_points: Narrow phase gives a unit normal n and penetration depth d; response separates and fixes velocity.
MTV for AABBs: push along the axis of smaller overlap; (100, 100)-(140, 160) vs (130, 0)-(200, 300) overlaps 10 on x, so push 10 left.
Platformers resolve x and y separately; after landing set vy = 0 and onGround = true.
Slide: v - (v . n) n; v = (3, -4) on a floor n = (0, 1) slides as (3, 0).
Bounce: v' = v - (1 + e)(v . n) n; e = 1 gives (3, 4), e = 0.5 gives (3, 2).
Angled wall n = (0.6, 0.8), v = (-5, 0) reflects to (-1.4, 4.8), speed still 5.
Respond only if dot(vRel, n) < 0 (approaching); triggers report enter, stay and exit without pushing.
One-way platforms collide only when falling from above; damage uses knock-back and brief invulnerability.
lessons.tip: When a collision bug appears, pause the game and draw the normal as a short arrow and the penetration depth as text at the contact point. Nine times out of ten the arrow points the wrong way or has the wrong length.
lessons.task: Using y-up maths, a ball with velocity (2, -6) hits a floor with normal (0, 1). Compute the velocity after the bounce for e = 1, e = 0.5 and e = 0. Then a ball with velocity (0, -10) hits a wall with normal (0.8, 0.6); compute the perfect reflection and check that the speed stays 10.

quiz.q: A player box overlaps a wall by 6 on x and 40 on y. Along which axis should it be pushed?
options: x, by 6, because it is the smaller overlap
y, by 40, because it is the larger overlap
quiz.explain: The minimum translation vector uses the axis of least overlap, which matches how the objects met.

quiz.q: Using y-up maths, a ball with velocity (4, -2) hits a floor with normal (0, 1) and e = 1. What is its new velocity?
What does v - (v . n) n compute?
options: The velocity with the part going into the surface removed, so the object slides
quiz.explain: Subtracting the normal component leaves only the tangent part, which produces sliding.

quiz.q: Why check that dot(vRel, n) < 0 before applying a bounce?
options: To respond only when the objects are approaching; separating objects should not be bounced again
quiz.explain: Responding to already-separating objects causes sticking and jitter.

quiz.q: Why do games give the player brief invulnerability after being hit?
options: So one long overlap does not cause damage every frame
quiz.explain: Without i-frames, an overlap lasting many frames would drain health many times.

lessons.title: Game AI I: State Machines and Behaviour Trees
lessons.content:
Think of the night guard, the darwan, at the gate of a housing society. Most of the night he walks his round. If he hears something, he goes to check. If he sees a stranger climbing the wall, he shouts and runs over. If the stranger escapes, he grumbles and goes back to his post. His behaviour is a handful of modes with clear reasons to switch between them. Game characters are built the same way. This lesson covers what game AI is really for, finite state machines with a transition table, hierarchical state machines, behaviour trees traced tick by tick, and utility AI with worked scores.

Game AI is not academic AI: In the Artificial Intelligence course you studied agents that search for optimal solutions: A*, minimax, logic and probability. Game AI borrows those tools but has a different goal: to create an entertaining experience. A perfect enemy that always aims exactly and predicts every move is not fun; players want opponents that are challenging, readable and beatable. Game AI is therefore part design and part engineering, and it often deliberately makes mistakes, hesitates or telegraphs its moves.

The agent loop recap: A game AI character is an agent in the sense of the AI course: it senses the world, decides what to do, and acts. Sensing might be a field-of-view test with the dot product from lesson 8 and a ray cast for line of sight from lesson 14. Acting means setting a velocity, playing an animation or firing. This lesson is about deciding; the next lesson covers moving, with steering and pathfinding.

Perception that feels fair: Sensing should usually be limited on purpose. A guard that knows the player's position through walls feels like cheating. A typical perception system checks, a few times per second rather than every frame, whether the player is within a view distance, inside the view cone and not blocked by walls; whether a noise event happened within hearing range; and whether an ally has raised an alarm. Results go into the AI's memory with a timestamp. Updating perception at a lower rate also saves processing time when many agents share a level, and players rarely notice a delay of a tenth of a second.

Finite state machines: A finite state machine, FSM, has a fixed set of states, exactly one of which is active, and transitions that switch states when conditions are met. Each state has behaviour: what to do when entering, every frame while active, and when exiting. For the guard: Patrol, Chase, Attack, Return, Flee. FSMs are the most common game AI technique because they are simple, fast, easy to debug, and match how designers describe behaviour.

The guard as a transition table: From Patrol, if the player is seen, go to Chase. From Chase, if the player is within 1.5 metres, go to Attack; if the player has not been seen for 3 seconds, go to Return. From Attack, if the player is farther than 1.5 metres, go back to Chase. From Return, when at the post, go to Patrol. From any state, if health falls below 20 percent, go to Flee. Writing transitions as a table, current state, condition, next state, makes missing cases visible: what should happen if the guard is fleeing and its health regenerates?

FSM in code: A simple implementation uses a variable and a switch: switch state { case Patrol: followWaypoints(); if canSeePlayer() then changeState(Chase); case Chase: moveTowards(player); if distance < 1.5 then changeState(Attack) ... }. The changeState function calls the old state's exit behaviour and the new state's enter behaviour, such as playing an alert sound when entering Chase. Larger games make each state its own object with enter, update and exit methods, the State design pattern from Software Engineering.

Timers and memory: Real behaviour needs memory: the last place the player was seen, how long since then, how many times the alarm rang. These live in the AI's blackboard or memory variables, updated by sensing. The Chase-to-Return transition uses a timer: each frame the player is not visible, lostTimer = lostTimer + dt; when it exceeds 3 seconds, give up. Instead of returning straight to patrol, many games first go to Search, moving to the last known position and looking around, which feels far more intelligent for little extra code.

The trouble with big FSMs: As behaviours grow, the number of transitions explodes. Add a Stunned state that can interrupt any other state and must return to whichever state was active before, and you need transitions from every state into Stunned and back. Add Sleep, Talk and Alarm and the diagram becomes a tangle nobody can read. This is called state explosion, and it motivates two improvements: hierarchical state machines and behaviour trees.

Hierarchical state machines: A hierarchical FSM nests machines inside states. The guard's top level has two states, Calm and Alert. Inside Calm is a small machine of Patrol, Idle and Chat; inside Alert is Search, Chase and Attack. A single transition from Calm to Alert, triggered by seeing the player, works from any substate, replacing many separate transitions. A history feature can remember which substate was active, so when the alert ends the guard resumes chatting rather than starting over.

Behaviour trees: A behaviour tree, BT, organises decisions as a tree that is evaluated, or ticked, from the root regularly, often every frame or a few times per second. Leaves are conditions, like CanSeePlayer?, and actions, like Chase or Patrol. Each node returns one of three results: Success, Failure or Running, the last meaning the action is still in progress. Inner nodes, called composites, combine their children's results. Behaviour trees became widely popular in game studios because they are modular: subtrees can be reused, rearranged and edited visually by designers.

Selector and sequence: The two key composites are simple. A sequence runs its children in order and fails as soon as one fails; it succeeds only if all succeed, like an AND: Sequence(CanSeePlayer?, InRange?, Attack). A selector, also called fallback, tries its children in order and succeeds as soon as one succeeds; it fails only if all fail, like an OR with priorities: Selector(Fight, Flee, Hide). Decorators wrap a single child and modify it: Invert flips success and failure; Repeat runs a child several times; Cooldown blocks a child for a few seconds after it runs.

A behaviour tree worked: The guard's root is Selector[ Sequence(CanSeePlayer?, Chase), Sequence(HeardNoise?, Investigate), Patrol ]. Tick 1: the selector tries the first sequence; CanSeePlayer? returns Failure, so the sequence fails. It tries the second; HeardNoise? returns Success, then Investigate starts walking and returns Running, so the sequence returns Running and the selector returns Running. Tick 2: the player steps into view. The selector checks the first child again, CanSeePlayer? succeeds, Chase starts and returns Running. Higher-priority branches win automatically because they come first.

Why behaviour trees scale: Priorities are just the order of children, so adding a new behaviour means inserting a subtree in the right place, not rewiring transitions. A Flee subtree with a LowHealth? condition placed first in the root selector instantly overrides everything else. Subtrees such as TakeCover can be shared between soldiers, guards and animals. The cost is that trees re-evaluate from the root, which is usually cheap but must be tuned for hundreds of agents, for example by ticking far-away agents less often.

Utility AI: Sometimes there is no clear priority order; a character must weigh needs. Utility AI scores every possible action with a number, often between 0 and 1, from the current situation, and picks the highest. Worked: a village character has hunger 0.7 and danger 0.4. Scores: Eat = hunger = 0.7; Flee = danger x 1.5 = 0.6; Work = a constant 0.5. Eat wins. If a dog appears and danger rises to 0.6, Flee = 0.9 and wins. Curves shape how scores respond: hunger might matter little until it is high, then dominate.

Choosing a technique: FSMs suit simple characters with few clear modes: enemies in a platformer, a traffic light, a door. Hierarchical FSMs suit medium complexity. Behaviour trees suit characters with many prioritised behaviours, especially when designers need to edit them. Utility AI suits characters juggling competing needs, such as life simulations. Many games mix them: a behaviour tree whose actions are small state machines, or a utility selector that picks which behaviour tree to run. The guiding question is always what is simplest that produces the behaviour players should see.

Making AI fun: Good game AI shows its thinking: a question mark above the guard's head when it hears a noise, an exclamation mark when it spots you, a shout before attacking. These tells let players understand and outwit it. Add reaction delays, such as 0.3 seconds before a guard notices you, and occasional inaccuracy. Difficulty levels often change these parameters rather than the logic. An enemy that the player can read and beat feels smart; one that seems to cheat feels unfair, even if it is simpler.

Example, a cricket fielding captain: A cricket game's AI captain sets fields with a small utility system. Each option, attacking field, defensive field, spin-friendly field, is scored from the match state: required run rate, wickets left, overs left. If the opposition needs 40 from 18 balls with 2 wickets left, the attacking field scores highest. Individual fielders use a tiny FSM: Ready, Chase ball, Throw, Return. The two techniques work at different levels of decision.

Example, a market seller in an RPG: In a role-playing game set in a busy haat, a seller character uses a behaviour tree: Selector[ Sequence(ThiefNearby?, ShoutForHelp), Sequence(CustomerAtStall?, Haggle), Sequence(StockLow?, Restock), CallOutToPassersby ]. Each tick, the most important applicable behaviour runs. Designers add a new Sequence(RainStarting?, CoverGoods) near the top for monsoon days without touching the rest. The tree reads almost like the description a designer would write in plain words.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include giant FSMs with tangled transitions, forgetting enter and exit actions, behaviour trees whose Running actions are never interrupted, perfect AI that is no fun, and no visible tells. Exams ask you to draw an FSM for a described character, write its transition table, explain state explosion and hierarchical FSMs, define selector, sequence and decorator nodes, trace a behaviour tree tick, compute utility scores to choose an action, and compare the techniques.

Recap: Game AI aims for fun, readable opponents rather than optimal play. FSMs give a fixed set of states with conditions to switch, best written as a transition table; hierarchical FSMs tame state explosion. Behaviour trees tick from the root, using sequences, selectors and decorators returning Success, Failure or Running, with priority set by child order. Utility AI scores actions and picks the best. Choose the simplest technique that works, and show the AI's thinking to the player so they can learn it and outsmart it.
key_points: Game AI aims for fun, challenging and readable behaviour, not optimal play; it may deliberately hesitate or miss.
An FSM has states with enter, update and exit behaviour, and transitions triggered by conditions.
Write FSMs as transition tables (state, condition, next state) to spot missing cases.
State explosion makes big FSMs tangled; hierarchical FSMs nest machines (Calm, Alert) to share transitions.
Behaviour tree nodes return Success, Failure or Running; sequence = AND in order, selector = OR by priority.
Decorators modify one child: Invert, Repeat, Cooldown; priority comes from the order of children.
Utility AI scores actions: hunger 0.7 vs danger 0.4 x 1.5 = 0.6 vs work 0.5 picks Eat.
Show the AI's thinking with tells and reaction delays so players can understand and outwit it.
lessons.tip: Before coding any enemy, write its behaviour in five plain sentences, then circle the nouns that are states and underline the phrases that are conditions. You will have your FSM or behaviour tree drawn before you open the editor.
lessons.task: Design the AI of a stray dog in a Dhaka lane game: it sleeps, wanders, barks at strangers, chases cyclists and runs away from people holding sticks. Draw it first as an FSM with a transition table, then as a behaviour tree with one root selector, and trace one tick for a cyclist passing while the dog is asleep.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of game AI, as distinct from academic AI?
options: Using as much memory as possible
Creating fun, challenging and readable behaviour for players
quiz.explain: Game AI serves the player's experience; perfect play is often not fun.

quiz.q: In a behaviour tree, how does a sequence node behave?
options: Succeeds as soon as any child succeeds
Runs children in order and fails as soon as one fails
quiz.explain: A sequence is like AND: every child must succeed in order.

quiz.q: A selector has children [Flee, Fight, Idle]. Flee returns Failure and Fight returns Running. What does the selector return?
quiz.explain: The selector moves past the failed child and returns the first non-failure result, Running from Fight.

quiz.q: What problem do hierarchical state machines mainly address?
options: State explosion, the tangle of transitions in large FSMs
quiz.explain: Nesting states lets one transition cover many substates, reducing the number of transitions.

quiz.q: Using utility AI, Eat = 0.5, Flee = danger x 2 with danger 0.3, and Sleep = 0.55. Which action is chosen?
quiz.explain: Flee = 0.3 x 2 = 0.6, the highest score.

lessons.title: Game AI II: Steering, Flocking and Pathfinding
lessons.content:
Watch a flock of birds over the Padma at sunset, or a crowd leaving a stadium after a match in Mirpur. Nobody gives orders, yet everyone moves smoothly, avoids bumping into neighbours and heads roughly the same way. Now watch a rickshaw-puller navigate from Shahbag to Old Dhaka: he plans a route through the streets, then weaves around buses and potholes moment by moment. Game characters need both skills: long-range planning to find a route through the level, and short-range steering to move smoothly and avoid obstacles. This lesson covers steering behaviours with worked vectors, flocking, A* on grids recapped with a worked example, navigation meshes and making movement look natural.

Two levels of movement: Pathfinding answers which way to go: given a map, it finds a sequence of waypoints from start to goal, avoiding walls. Steering answers how to move right now: given the next waypoint and nearby obstacles, it produces a velocity change for this frame. Separating them keeps both simple. The path is computed occasionally, when the goal changes or the map changes; steering runs every frame.

Steering behaviours: In the late 1980s and 1990s Craig Reynolds described steering behaviours: simple rules that each produce a steering force from the character's position and velocity, which can be combined. The character has a maximum speed and a maximum steering force, so it cannot turn instantly; this gives motion a natural, vehicle-like quality. Each frame: steering = desiredVelocity - currentVelocity, limited to maxForce; velocity = velocity + steering x dt, limited to maxSpeed; position = position + velocity x dt.

Seek worked: A character at (0, 0) moving with velocity (100, 0) wants to reach a target at (30, 40), with maximum speed 100. The desired velocity points straight at the target at full speed: normalise (30, 40) to (0.6, 0.8), times 100 gives (60, 80). The steering force is desired minus current: (60, 80) - (100, 0) = (-40, 80). Its length is about 89.44; if maxForce is 50, scale it down to length 50: about (-22.36, 44.72). Over the next frames the character curves smoothly toward the target instead of snapping round.

Flee and arrive: Flee is seek reversed: the desired velocity points directly away from the threat, here (-60, -80). Seek has a flaw: it reaches the target at full speed and overshoots, circling back and forth. Arrive fixes this by slowing down inside a slowing radius: desiredSpeed = maxSpeed x (distance / slowRadius) when distance is less than slowRadius. With maxSpeed 100 and slowRadius 100, at distance 50 the desired speed is 50; at distance 10 it is 10, so the character glides to a gentle stop.

Pursue, evade and wander: Pursue predicts where a moving target will be: futurePosition = target.position + target.velocity x T, with T roughly distance divided by speed, then seeks that point; a guard pursuing a running thief cuts corners to intercept. Evade is the opposite. Wander gives natural aimless motion: imagine a small circle ahead of the character and a point on it that jitters randomly a little each frame; seek that point. The result is a smooth meandering path, ideal for grazing goats or idle villagers.

Obstacle and wall avoidance: To avoid obstacles, cast a short feeler ray ahead of the character, length proportional to speed. If it hits an obstacle, steer away along the obstacle's surface normal, with force stronger when the hit is closer. For walls, two or three feelers angled to the sides help in corridors. Avoidance only handles nearby, local problems; it cannot find a way around a long wall, which is why we also need pathfinding.

Combining behaviours: Real characters combine several behaviours with weights: steering = 1.0 x seek(waypoint) + 2.0 x avoid(obstacles) + 0.5 x separation(neighbours). Weighted sums are simple but can cancel out, leaving a character stuck between two pulls. A common improvement is priority: compute the most important behaviour first, such as avoidance, and only add lower-priority ones while there is steering force left. Tuning the weights is part design, part trial and error.

Flocking: Reynolds also showed in 1987 that bird-like flocking emerges from three local rules applied by every member, the agents he called boids. Separation: steer away from neighbours that are too close. Alignment: steer toward the average heading of nearby neighbours. Cohesion: steer toward the average position of nearby neighbours. No leader and no global plan, yet realistic flocks, schools of fish and crowds appear. It is the emergence idea from lesson 1 in action, and finding neighbours quickly uses the spatial grid from lesson 15.

Pathfinding recap: The AI course taught graph search: breadth-first search, uniform-cost search and A*. Games model the level as a graph, most simply a grid where each walkable cell is a node connected to its neighbours. A* finds the cheapest path by always expanding the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g is the cost so far and h is a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. If h never overestimates, it is admissible, and A* returns an optimal path.

Heuristics on grids: With four-way movement and cost 1 per step, the Manhattan distance |dx| + |dy| is admissible and works well. With eight-way movement where diagonals cost about 1.414, use the octile distance: max(|dx|, |dy|) + 0.414 x min(|dx|, |dy|). Using Euclidean distance on a 4-way grid is admissible but weaker, so A* explores more cells. Using a heuristic that overestimates, such as multiplying Manhattan by 2, makes A* faster but no longer guarantees the shortest path, a trade some games accept.

A* worked on a grid: Take a 5 x 5 grid with coordinates (x, y), start at (0, 0), goal at (4, 0), and a wall in column 2 covering rows 0 to 3, so the only gap is at (2, 4). Moves are four-way with cost 1. At the start, g = 0 and h = |4 - 0| + |0 - 0| = 4, so f = 4. A* first tries cells near the wall, where f stays low, discovers the wall blocks the direct route, and then expands cells toward row 4 as their f values become the lowest. It finds a shortest path of 12 moves: down column 1 to row 4, across through the gap at (2, 4) to (3, 4), up column 3 to row 0, then right to the goal. The heuristic's estimate of 4 was admissible: the true cost, 12, is never less than it.

Terrain costs: Not every step costs the same. A grid cell can carry a cost: road 1, grass 2, mud 5, shallow water 8, deep water impassable. A* then prefers longer but cheaper routes, such as walking around a muddy field rather than through it, simply because g adds the cell costs. Designers use costs to shape behaviour too: making cells near the player's base expensive keeps enemy scouts away from it. The heuristic must still not overestimate, so it should assume the cheapest possible cost per step.

Making grid paths look natural: Grid paths zigzag in steps. Path smoothing removes unnecessary waypoints: from the current point, skip ahead to the farthest later waypoint that is directly visible, using a ray cast or line-of-sight check; this is often called string pulling. The character then steers with arrive toward each smoothed waypoint, producing gentle curves. Re-plan only when needed, for example when the goal moves more than a cell or a door closes, because running A* every frame for many agents is wasteful.

Navigation meshes: Large or 3D levels rarely use fine grids. A navigation mesh, navmesh, covers the walkable floor with convex polygons. Within one polygon, a character can walk in a straight line anywhere, so A* runs on the much smaller graph of polygons and the path is then smoothed through the shared edges. Navmeshes represent open spaces with few nodes and handle slopes and multiple floors. Major engines can generate navmeshes automatically from level geometry, and include agents that combine pathfinding with avoidance.

Scaling to many agents: Hundreds of units requesting paths at once can stall a frame. Techniques include spreading path requests across frames, caching paths between common places, hierarchical pathfinding that plans first between regions and then within them, and flow fields: one search from the goal fills every cell with the direction toward it, and all units simply follow the arrows of the cell they stand in. Flow fields suit strategy games where many units share a destination.

Making movement believable: Perfect paths can look robotic. Add slight randomness to waypoints, vary speeds between characters, let them pause to look around, and align their facing with movement using atan2 from lesson 8. Avoid characters vibrating at a target by using arrive with a small stopping distance. Pathfinding also serves design: a guard should take a route the player can predict and exploit, not a strange shortcut through a closed shop.

Example, rickshaws in a city simulation: In a Dhaka traffic simulation, each rickshaw plans a route with A* on a road graph where edge costs include distance and expected congestion. Locally, it uses seek toward the next intersection, arrive at stops, separation from nearby rickshaws, and avoidance feelers for buses and potholes. Thousands of rickshaws find neighbours through a spatial hash. The result looks like real, slightly chaotic but flowing traffic, built from simple rules.

Example, ducks in a village pond game: A calm game about raising ducks in a village pond uses flocking: separation, alignment and cohesion make ducklings follow each other in natural lines, and a seek toward the mother duck with a high weight keeps the group together. When a child runs past, a flee behaviour with a large weight scatters them, and they regroup through cohesion once the danger passes. No pathfinding is needed in the open pond; it appears only when ducks must walk around the bank to reach the field.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include seeking without arrive so characters orbit targets, unlimited steering forces that make turns instant, running A* every frame for every agent, inadmissible heuristics used unknowingly, and unsmoothed grid paths. Exams ask you to compute seek, flee or arrive vectors, explain the three flocking rules, compute f = g + h values, choose a heuristic for 4-way or 8-way grids, run A* on a small grid, and explain navmeshes and path smoothing.

Recap: Pathfinding plans a route; steering moves along it every frame. Steering is desired velocity minus current velocity, limited by maximum force; seek, flee, arrive, pursue, wander and avoidance combine with weights or priorities. Flocking emerges from separation, alignment and cohesion. A* expands nodes by f = g + h; Manhattan suits 4-way grids, octile 8-way grids; our 5 x 5 example found a 12-move path around a wall. Smooth paths, use navmeshes for big levels, and keep movement believable and predictable.
key_points: Pathfinding chooses the route; steering produces a velocity change every frame.
Steering = desired velocity - current velocity, limited to maxForce; speed limited to maxSpeed.
Seek worked: from (0, 0) with v = (100, 0) toward (30, 40) at speed 100: desired (60, 80), steering (-40, 80).
Arrive slows inside a radius: desiredSpeed = maxSpeed x distance / slowRadius (50 at half the radius).
Flocking (Reynolds' boids): separation, alignment, cohesion; neighbours found with a spatial grid.
A*: f = g + h; Manhattan for 4-way grids, octile for 8-way; admissible h gives optimal paths.
5 x 5 grid, wall in column 2 rows 0-3: start (0, 0) to goal (4, 0) takes 12 moves through (2, 4).
Smooth paths with line-of-sight skipping; navmeshes, hierarchical search and flow fields scale to big worlds.
lessons.tip: Implement seek and arrive in any small framework and draw the desired velocity, current velocity and steering force as three coloured arrows on each character. Ten minutes of watching those arrows teaches steering better than any formula.
lessons.task: On a 6 x 6 grid, put the start at (0, 2), the goal at (5, 2) and walls at (2, 0), (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3) and (4, 2), (4, 3), (4, 4), (4, 5). Find a shortest four-way path by hand using A* with Manhattan distance, writing g, h and f for each cell you expand, and give its length.

quiz.q: What is the steering force in Reynolds' steering behaviours?
options: Desired velocity minus current velocity, limited to a maximum force
quiz.explain: Steering pushes the current velocity toward the desired velocity, limited so turns are smooth.

quiz.q: With maxSpeed 80 and slowing radius 40, what is the arrive behaviour's desired speed at distance 10?
quiz.explain: desiredSpeed = 80 x 10 / 40 = 20.

quiz.q: Which three rules produce flocking?
quiz.explain: Each boid avoids crowding, matches neighbours' heading and moves toward their centre.

quiz.q: On a four-way grid with cost 1 per step, which heuristic is admissible and well suited?
options: The number of walls on the map
quiz.explain: Manhattan distance never overestimates on a 4-way grid and guides A* well.

quiz.q: Why do games often smooth grid paths before following them?
options: Grid paths zigzag; skipping visible waypoints gives natural, direct movement
quiz.explain: String pulling with line-of-sight checks removes unnecessary steps so characters move naturally.

lessons.title: Procedural Generation: Seeds, Noise and Controlled Randomness
lessons.content:
Every nakshi kantha quilt is different, yet you can recognise one instantly. The embroiderer follows traditional rules, borders, central lotus, flowing vines, but chooses the details freshly each time. Procedural generation in games works the same way: instead of designers building every level, tree and treasure by hand, the computer creates content from rules plus controlled randomness. Done well, it gives endless variety from a small amount of work. This lesson covers why games generate content, how pseudo-random numbers and seeds work with a worked generator, random walks and cellular automata for caves, noise for terrain, weighted loot tables and shuffle bags with worked probabilities, and how to keep randomness fair and fun.

Why generate content: Hand-made content is expensive: a skilled designer may spend days on one level. Procedural generation offers replayability, since every run of a roguelike is different; scale, since a game can have huge worlds without huge downloads; and surprise, even for the developers. It is also used quietly in hand-made games: scattering grass, placing rocks, varying trees, generating textures. The cost is control: generated content can be boring, broken or unfair, so generation needs rules, constraints and testing.

Pseudo-random numbers: Computers are deterministic machines, so they usually produce pseudo-random numbers: sequences computed by a formula that look random but are completely determined by a starting value called the seed. Same seed, same sequence, every time. For games this is a feature, not a flaw: it lets a whole level be described by one number, lets players share seeds, makes bugs reproducible, and keeps multiplayer clients in sync without sending the whole level.

A linear congruential generator worked: One of the oldest generators is the LCG: x_next = (a x x + c) mod m. Take a toy version with a = 5, c = 3, m = 16 and seed 7. The sequence is: (5 x 7 + 3) mod 16 = 38 mod 16 = 6; then (5 x 6 + 3) mod 16 = 33 mod 16 = 1; then 8, then 11, then 10, then 5. It looks scattered, and with well-chosen constants, as here, it visits all 16 values before repeating, its period. Real LCGs use huge m, such as 2^32 or 2^64, but simple LCGs have statistical weaknesses, so modern libraries use better generators, such as the xorshift and PCG families.

Using random numbers: A generator usually gives a value in [0, 1) or a large integer. To get an integer in a range, such as a dice roll from 1 to 6, use 1 + floor(r x 6) with r in [0, 1). To pick a random element from a list, use list[floor(r x length)]. To choose with probability p, test r < p. For game logic, keep separate generators for separate purposes, one for level layout, one for combat, one for cosmetic effects, so that adding a sparkle effect does not change the level a seed produces.

Seeds in practice: A daily challenge can use the date as the seed, for example 20261105, so every player in the world gets the same level that day and can compare scores fairly. A level editor can show the seed so testers report exactly which level broke. Replays can store only the seed and the player's inputs instead of every object's position. Never seed from the current time inside the game loop each frame; seed once, then draw numbers from the same generator.

Cryptographic versus game randomness: Game PRNGs are fast but predictable if someone knows the algorithm and seed. That is fine for level layouts, but for anything involving money or fairness against cheaters, such as loot box results on a server or a card shuffle in an online card game, developers use cryptographically secure generators provided by the operating system, and run them on the server where players cannot inspect or manipulate them.

Random walk generation: A simple way to carve caves or dungeon corridors is the random walk, also called the drunkard's walk. Start with a grid full of walls. Place a walker in the middle. Each step, move it one cell in a random direction and turn that cell into floor. Stop when a target percentage of the map, say 40 percent, is floor. The result is a connected, organic-looking cave, guaranteed connected because the walker carved every floor cell from one continuous path.

Cellular automata caves: Another classic method uses a cellular automaton, a grid where each cell updates based on its neighbours, like Conway's Game of Life. Start by filling each cell randomly with wall at about 45 percent probability. Then repeat a smoothing rule four or five times: a cell becomes wall if 5 or more of its 8 neighbours are walls, otherwise floor. Noise clumps into smooth cave shapes. Because some regions may be disconnected, a final pass uses flood fill from the Computer Graphics course to keep the largest connected area or to dig tunnels between regions.

Rooms and corridors: Dungeon generators often place rooms and then connect them.
