One method splits the map recursively into rectangles, a binary space partition: split the area in two at a random position, split each half again, and so on, then place a room inside each leaf rectangle and connect sibling rooms with corridors. Because the splitting forms a tree, every room is connected. Designers then place the entrance and exit far apart, compute distances with breadth-first search from the AI course, and put keys and locked doors so that the key is always reachable before its door.

Noise for terrain: Pure random values per cell look like television static, useless for landscapes. Coherent noise produces smoothly varying values: nearby points get similar values. Value noise picks random values at grid points and interpolates between them with smooth curves. Perlin noise, developed by Ken Perlin in the 1980s, uses random gradients at grid points and gives more natural results; related variants exist. Sampling noise at each map position gives a height: low values become water, middle values grass, high values hills.

Octaves: One layer of noise gives smooth, boring hills. Layering several octaves gives realistic detail: each octave doubles the frequency, making features smaller, and halves the amplitude, making them weaker. With four octaves of amplitudes 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125, the total possible range is 1.875, so values are divided by 1.875 to normalise. Big shapes come from the first octave, rivers and valleys from the middle ones, small bumps from the last. Adjusting the number of octaves and their ratio changes the landscape's character.

Weighted loot tables: Rewards are often chosen from weighted tables. Example: common item weight 70, rare 25, epic 5, total 100. Draw r uniformly in [0, 100): if r < 70 give common, else if r < 95 give rare, else epic. A roll of 82 gives rare; 97 gives epic. Over many drops, about 5 in 100 are epic. The chance of at least one epic in 20 drops is 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.64, so roughly a third of players will get none in 20 tries, which can feel unfair.

Pity timers and shuffle bags: Pure randomness creates streaks that players experience as unfair, both droughts and floods. A pity timer guarantees a rare reward after a set number of misses, for example an epic is certain on the 30th drop if none has appeared. A shuffle bag puts a fixed mix of outcomes in a bag, shuffles it with the Fisher-Yates shuffle, and deals them out in order until empty, then refills. A bag of 7 coins and 3 obstacles guarantees exactly 3 obstacles in every 10 spawns, varying only the order. Randomness feels fair when its extremes are limited.

The Fisher-Yates shuffle: Shuffling correctly matters, because a naive shuffle that swaps each item with any random position gives some orders more often than others. The Fisher-Yates shuffle is simple and unbiased: for i from the last index down to 1, pick j uniformly from 0 to i, and swap items i and j. Every possible order is equally likely, and it runs in a single pass over the list. It is the standard way to shuffle bags, decks of cards and playlists.

Beyond levels: Procedural techniques reach far beyond maps. Names for characters can be built from syllable tables; quests from templates such as bring X to Y in Z; textures such as wood grain, marble and clouds from noise; animation from rules, such as grass swaying with a sine wave; and music that rearranges short loops based on what is happening. Each uses the same ingredients: rules, a seeded generator and constraints that keep results sensible.

Designing with randomness: Good procedural systems mix hand-made and generated pieces. Many games use hand-designed chunks, small level sections built by designers, and let the generator choose and connect them. Constraints keep results playable: every gap must be jumpable using the jump numbers from lesson 12, every room reachable, difficulty rising over time. Automated tests can generate thousands of levels from different seeds and check them with pathfinding, flagging any seed that produces an impossible level.

Example, an endless river boat game: An endless game on the Meghna generates the river ahead of the boat in chunks. Each chunk's width comes from one-dimensional noise, so banks curve smoothly. Logs, fishing nets and other boats are spawned from a shuffle bag so their mix stays fair, with the bag growing harsher as distance increases. The daily challenge seeds the generator with the date, so friends race the same river. Testing runs 10,000 seeds overnight and checks that a gap of at least the boat's width plus margin always exists.

Example, a village farming game: A farming game generates each new player's village map from a seed: noise decides where ponds, paddy fields and bamboo groves go; a random walk carves footpaths between houses; a weighted table chooses which fruit trees grow, mango common, jackfruit rare, lychee epic. A small hand-made chunk always places the player's home, the market and the school, so every village is unique yet every map contains what the story needs.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include seeding from the clock every frame, sharing one generator between layout and cosmetics, using predictable game PRNGs for money-related outcomes, generating unreachable areas, and pure randomness that creates unfair streaks. Exams ask you to explain pseudo-random generators and seeds, run a few steps of an LCG, describe random walk and cellular automaton cave generation, explain noise and octaves, compute loot probabilities from weights, and explain shuffle bags and pity timers.

Recap: Procedural generation creates content from rules plus controlled randomness. Pseudo-random generators produce repeatable sequences from a seed; an LCG with a = 5, c = 3, m = 16 from seed 7 gives 6, 1, 8, 11, 10, 5. Random walks and cellular automata carve caves; space partitioning builds rooms and corridors; coherent noise with octaves shapes terrain. Weighted tables pick loot, and shuffle bags and pity timers keep randomness fair. Always constrain and test generated content.
key_points: Procedural generation = rules plus controlled randomness, for replayability, scale and surprise.
Pseudo-random generators are deterministic: the same seed always gives the same sequence.
LCG: x_next = (a x + c) mod m; a = 5, c = 3, m = 16, seed 7 gives 6, 1, 8, 11, 10, 5.
Use separate generators per purpose; use secure server-side randomness for money or fairness.
Random walks and cellular automata (wall if 5 or more of 8 neighbours are walls) make caves; BSP makes rooms.
Coherent noise with octaves (frequency doubles, amplitude halves) shapes terrain; 4 octaves sum to 1.875.
Weights 70/25/5: P(at least one epic in 20 drops) = 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.64.
Shuffle bags and pity timers limit unfair streaks; test thousands of seeds automatically.
lessons.tip: Whenever your game uses randomness, print the seed on screen in debug builds. The first time a tester says the level was impossible, you will be able to reproduce it exactly instead of guessing.
lessons.task: Run the LCG x_next = (5x + 3) mod 16 from seed 2 for eight steps on paper and check whether any value repeats. Then design a loot table with weights 60, 30 and 10 and compute the chance of getting no top-tier item in 15 drops.

quiz.q: What does using the same seed with the same pseudo-random generator give?
options: A sequence that is cryptographically secure
Exactly the same sequence every time
quiz.explain: PRNGs are deterministic: the seed fully determines the sequence, which makes levels shareable and bugs reproducible.

quiz.q: For the LCG x_next = (5x + 3) mod 16, what follows x = 6?
In octave noise, each successive octave typically:
options: Halves the frequency and doubles the amplitude
Doubles the frequency and halves the amplitude
quiz.explain: Higher octaves add finer detail (higher frequency) with smaller influence (lower amplitude).

quiz.q: Loot weights are common 70, rare 25, epic 5. A uniform roll in [0, 100) gives 93. What drops?
quiz.explain: 93 is not below 70 but is below 95, so the item is rare.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a shuffle bag?
options: To guarantee a fixed mix of outcomes over a cycle while varying their order
quiz.explain: A shuffle bag deals a fixed set of outcomes in random order, preventing long unfair streaks.

lessons.title: Audio, HUD, Menus and Game Feel
lessons.content:
Try playing a favourite phone game with the sound off and the screen dimmed. It still works, but something important is missing: the satisfying clink of a coin, the rising music before a boss, the clear health bar that tells you how close you are to losing. Sound, interface and small visual touches carry information and emotion at the same time. This lesson covers how games use audio, with a few worked numbers for volume and panning, how heads-up displays and menus are designed and organised, and the craft of game feel, sometimes called juice, that makes actions satisfying. Audio and video formats and compression belong to the Multimedia Systems course; here we only use them.

Kinds of game audio: Games mix several kinds of sound. Sound effects, SFX, are short sounds tied to events: footsteps, jumps, hits, coins, button clicks. Music sets mood and pace. Ambience is the continuous background of a place: rain, birds, traffic, a bazaar's murmur. Voice includes dialogue and short barks like a guard's shout. Each kind has different needs: effects must start instantly, music must loop or transition smoothly, ambience must not become irritating.

Audio as feedback: Sound is often faster to notice than visuals; you hear a hit even when your eyes are elsewhere. Every important action should have an audio response: success sounds bright and rising, failure low and falling. Distinct sounds let players act without looking: a different tone when health is low, a warning before an attack lands. This is the feedback principle from lesson 1 and from HCI, delivered through a second sense, which also helps players with low vision.

Playing sounds efficiently: Short effects are usually loaded into memory once, decoded, and played many times. Long music is streamed from storage while playing, to save memory. As a sense of scale, one minute of uncompressed stereo audio at 44,100 samples per second with 16-bit samples needs 44,100 x 2 channels x 2 bytes x 60 seconds = 10,584,000 bytes, about 10.6 MB, which is why music is stored compressed and streamed. The audio engine mixes all currently playing sounds into one output many times per second on its own thread.

Channels, buses and limits: Too many simultaneous sounds become noise, and hardware has limits. Engines limit the number of voices, often a few dozen, and drop the least important when full. Sounds are routed into groups, called buses or mixer groups: music, effects, voice, interface. Each has its own volume, which is how a settings menu offers separate sliders. Ducking temporarily lowers music when dialogue plays so words stay clear.

Decibels worked: Loudness is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale: the change in decibels is 20 x log10(new amplitude / old amplitude). Doubling the amplitude adds about 6 dB; halving it subtracts about 6 dB. Because hearing is roughly logarithmic, volume sliders should map to decibels, not to raw amplitude; a slider that changes amplitude linearly seems to do almost nothing over most of its range and then everything at the end.

Variation and repetition: A sound heard a hundred times gets annoying. Simple fixes: keep 3 to 5 variations of each common effect and pick randomly without repeating the last one, the shuffle-bag idea from lesson 19; vary pitch slightly, for example by plus or minus 5 percent; and vary volume a little. Footsteps on different surfaces, grass, wood, mud, use different sets chosen by the tile under the character's feet.

Positional audio and panning: Sounds can come from places in the world. In 2D, stereo panning sets left and right volumes from the source's horizontal position. A common constant-power pan uses angle a = (pan + 1) x pi / 4, where pan runs from -1 (left) to 1 (right): left = cos(a), right = sin(a). At pan 0 both are about 0.707, keeping perceived loudness constant as a sound moves across. At pan 0.5, left is about 0.38 and right about 0.92.

Distance attenuation: Sounds also get quieter with distance. A simple linear falloff uses a minimum distance, inside which volume is full, and a maximum distance, beyond which it is silent: volume = (maxD - d) / (maxD - minD). With minD = 2 and maxD = 20, a sound 11 units away plays at (20 - 11) / 18 = 0.5. Real sound follows an inverse-distance law, so engines offer logarithmic curves too, but linear curves are easier to tune for gameplay. 3D engines add direction relative to the listener's head and effects like echo in caves.

Adaptive music: Music can respond to the game. Horizontal re-sequencing switches between sections, calm exploration music, then a tense section when enemies notice you, aligned to beats so transitions sound natural. Vertical layering keeps several stems playing in sync, drums, strings, melody, and fades layers in or out with intensity: drums join when combat starts. Even a simple game benefits from switching music on state changes and fading rather than cutting abruptly.

The HUD: The heads-up display shows essential information during play: health, score, timer, ammunition, minimap, objectives. Good HUDs show only what players need now, place it at the screen edges away from the action, use icons and bars that can be read in a glance, and stay inside the safe area from lesson 10. Information that changes, such as score, should animate briefly when it changes, so the eye notices it without searching.

Diegetic and non-diegetic UI: Interface elements can live outside or inside the game world. Non-diegetic UI is overlaid on the screen, like a classic health bar. Diegetic UI exists in the world itself: a character's injured walk, a fuel gauge on a rickshaw-van's dashboard, a sign on a shop. In between, spatial UI floats in the world, like a name above a character, and meta UI affects the screen, like red edges when hurt. Diegetic designs improve immersion but must remain readable.

Menus and screen flow: Beyond play, games need a title screen, main menu, settings, level select, pause menu, game over, results and sometimes a shop. Draw this flow as a diagram of screens and transitions, an FSM again, so no screen becomes a dead end. Engines often manage screens as a stack: opening the pause menu pushes it on top of the game; closing pops it, returning to exactly where you were. Lesson 21 adds saving to this flow.

Pausing correctly: Pausing must stop the simulation, timers and physics, but keep the pause menu animated and responsive. A common method sets a time scale of 0 for gameplay while the UI uses unscaled time. On phones, the game must pause automatically when it loses focus, such as when a call arrives, following the app lifecycle from Mobile App Development, and must never resume a tense moment without the player's choice.

Game feel and juice: Game feel is how controls and responses feel in the hands: responsive, weighty, crisp. Juice is extra feedback that makes simple actions satisfying: a coin pops and sparkles with a pleasant sound, the score number bounces, particles burst, the camera shakes slightly on a heavy landing, as in lesson 10. Squash and stretch, from animation principles, makes a jumping character compress when landing. Each touch costs little, but together they turn a working prototype into something that feels alive.

Hit-stop and timing: In action games, freezing the game for a few frames at the moment of a strong hit, called hit-stop, makes impacts feel powerful: 3 frames at 60 fps is 50 milliseconds, barely noticed consciously but clearly felt. Brief white flashes on the hit enemy, a short controller or phone vibration and a punchy sound at the same moment reinforce each other. Timing all feedback to the same frame matters more than the quality of any single effect. Like seasoning in cooking, juice works best in moderation: too much shake and too many particles hide the action and tire the eyes, so tune each effect down until you only just notice it is missing when it is turned off.

Onboarding and loading: The first minute decides whether a new player stays. Instead of a wall of instructions, teach one mechanic at a time inside play: a safe first jump, then a gap, then a gap with an enemy. Show a control prompt only until the player has used it a few times, then hide it. Loading screens should show progress and a useful tip, and loading should happen in the background where possible so the player waits less. Test onboarding with people who have never seen the game, because developers cannot forget what they already know.

Accessibility in audio and UI: Offer subtitles with speaker names and adjustable size, separate volume sliders, visual cues for important sounds, colour-blind-friendly palettes that never rely on colour alone, options to reduce screen shake and flashing, scalable text, and full Bangla text rendering where the game is in Bangla. These follow HCI guidance and widen your audience; many are cheap if planned early.

Example, a cricket game's audio and HUD: A cricket game uses a crowd ambience whose intensity rises with the match situation, a crisp bat sound with slight pitch variation per shot, and a commentator voice line ducking the crowd. The HUD shows score, overs and required rate at the top edge; a small diegetic touch shows the scoreboard in the stadium updating too. When a six is hit, the camera follows, confetti bursts, the score animates and the crowd roars: four kinds of feedback on one event.

Example, a calm learning game for children: A Bangla alphabet game for young children uses soft music in a single loop with a gentle fade, a cheerful chime for correct answers and a soft, non-scary tone for mistakes. The HUD is minimal: large star icons for progress. All buttons are big, labelled with icons and Bangla text, and every spoken letter is also shown on screen. Juice is gentle: letters wobble when touched and sparkle when matched, without flashing.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include no sound for important events, the same sound repeated identically, linear volume sliders, cluttered HUDs, menus that trap the player, pausing that stops the menu too, and screen shake with no way to turn it off. Exams ask you to classify game audio, compute decibel changes, compute stereo pan or distance attenuation, explain diegetic versus non-diegetic UI, draw a screen flow, and explain game feel techniques such as hit-stop.

Recap: Game audio includes effects, music, ambience and voice, mixed through buses with voice limits and ducking; volume is logarithmic, about 6 dB per doubling. Constant-power panning and distance falloff place sounds in space; adaptive music follows game state. The HUD shows only essential information at the edges; UI can be diegetic or not; menus form a screen flow often managed as a stack, and pausing freezes gameplay but not the UI. Juice and hit-stop make actions satisfying, and accessibility options widen the audience.
key_points: Game audio: sound effects, music, ambience and voice, each with different needs.
Effects load into memory; music streams; 1 minute of uncompressed 44.1 kHz 16-bit stereo is about 10.6 MB.
Buses group sounds for separate volume sliders; ducking lowers music under dialogue.
Decibels are logarithmic: doubling amplitude adds about 6 dB; volume sliders should be logarithmic.
Constant-power pan: left = cos(a), right = sin(a), a = (pan + 1) pi / 4; centre gives 0.707 each.
Linear falloff: volume = (maxD - d) / (maxD - minD); minD 2, maxD 20, d 11 gives 0.5.
HUDs show only essentials at the edges; UI can be diegetic, non-diegetic, spatial or meta.
Juice and hit-stop (3 frames at 60 fps = 50 ms) make actions satisfying; always offer accessibility options.
lessons.tip: Record your own sound effects with a phone: a spoon on a glass, a door, a footstep on gravel. Trim and vary them slightly. Original homemade sounds give student games a personality that stock libraries cannot.
lessons.task: Pick a simple game you know and list every event that should have a sound, every HUD element and every screen in its menu flow. Draw the screen flow as boxes and arrows, then compute the stereo volumes for a sound at pan -0.5 and the linear falloff volume at distance 8 with minD 2 and maxD 14.

quiz.q: Which kind of game audio is a continuous background such as rain or a busy bazaar?
quiz.explain: Ambience is the ongoing sound of a place, as opposed to event-based effects.

quiz.q: Halving a sound's amplitude changes its level by about:
quiz.explain: 20 x log10(0.5) is about -6 dB.

quiz.q: With linear falloff, minD = 5 and maxD = 25, what is the volume at distance 20?
A fuel gauge drawn on the dashboard of a vehicle inside the game world is an example of:
quiz.explain: Diegetic UI exists inside the game world rather than overlaid on the screen.

quiz.q: What is hit-stop?
options: Briefly freezing the game for a few frames at a strong impact to make it feel powerful
Stopping music when the player is hit
Pausing the game when a call arrives
quiz.explain: A pause of a few frames, such as 50 ms, at the moment of impact makes hits feel weighty.

lessons.title: Saving, Loading and Game State
lessons.content:
A student plays a long role-playing game on a bus from Dhaka to Sylhet. Halfway there, the phone battery dies. When the phone comes back to life, will the last hour of progress still be there? Few things make players angrier than lost progress, and few bugs are harder to fix after release than a corrupted save file. This lesson treats saving as a real engineering problem: deciding what to save, turning game objects into data with a worked JSON example, save slots, autosave and checkpoints, versioning saves across updates, writing files safely, protecting against tampering, syncing with the cloud, and organising game state so saving stays simple.

What is game state: At any moment, a game's state is everything needed to continue: the current level, player position and health, inventory, quest progress, enemies alive, doors opened, the time of day, settings. Some state is permanent progress, such as unlocked levels and achievements; some is temporary, such as the exact position of a flying arrow. A key design decision is how much of the temporary state to save. Saving everything is complex and fragile; saving only checkpoints is simple but can lose minutes of play.

What to save and what to rebuild: Save the minimum from which the rest can be rebuilt. You do not save the level geometry, because it comes from the game's files; you save the level's identifier. You do not save textures or sounds, only references to them. For a procedurally generated world, save the seed from lesson 19 and the changes the player made, not every tile. Derived values, such as maximum health computed from level and equipment, should be recomputed on loading rather than saved, so they cannot disagree.

Serialisation: Serialisation turns in-memory objects into a sequence of bytes or text that can be stored or sent; deserialisation turns them back. Objects contain references to other objects, so a serialiser saves identifiers instead of memory addresses: an enemy's target is saved as the player's id, not a pointer. The ECS design from lesson 7 helps here: components are plain data, so saving an entity means writing its id and its components.

JSON worked: JSON, from the Web Engineering course, is a common human-readable format. A tiny save might be: {"version":2,"level":7,"coins":350}. Written without spaces it is 35 characters, so 35 bytes in UTF-8. A fuller save adds the player's position as {"x":12.5,"y":3.0}, an inventory list such as [{"id":"mango","n":3},{"id":"key_red","n":1}], and flags for completed quests. Human-readable saves are easy to debug, but larger and slower than binary formats; many games use JSON during development and switch to a compact binary format, or compress the JSON, for release.

Size estimation worked: Suppose an inventory holds up to 200 items and each item record takes about 40 bytes in JSON. The inventory alone is 200 x 40 = 8,000 bytes, about 8 KB. If the world records 5,000 changed tiles at about 20 bytes each, that is 100,000 bytes, about 100 KB. These sizes are small for storage but matter for cloud sync over mobile data and for save time on slow phones, which is why changed tiles are better stored as compact lists than as full maps.

Save slots and profiles: Many games offer several save slots so that siblings can share a device or a player can keep a save before a big choice. Each slot is usually a separate file, plus a small index file listing slot names, play time, level and a thumbnail for the load screen. Settings, such as volume and controls, belong in a separate settings file shared by all slots, because they describe the person and device, not one playthrough.

Autosave and checkpoints: Players forget to save, so modern games autosave. Common triggers are reaching a checkpoint, finishing a level, closing a menu after changes, and a timer such as every 5 minutes. On phones, also save when the app goes to the background, because the operating system may close it at any time without warning, as you learned in Mobile App Development. Show a small saving icon so players do not quit during a save. Design checkpoints so that dying never repeats more than a minute or two of play.

Saving without stutter: Collecting the state must happen at a consistent moment, usually between frames, so the save does not mix data from two frames. Serialising a large world can take longer than a frame's budget, so games copy the needed data quickly into a snapshot, then serialise and write the snapshot on a background thread while the game continues. Writing directly from live objects on another thread risks saving half-updated data.

Atomic writes: The most dangerous moment is while the file is being written. If the battery dies halfway, the file may be half old and half new, unreadable. The safe pattern is: write the new save to a temporary file, flush it so the data actually reaches storage, then rename the temporary file over the old one. On common file systems a rename within the same folder is atomic, so after a crash you have either the complete old save or the complete new one. Keeping one previous save as a backup adds another safety net.

Pseudo-code for a safe save: function saveGame(state): data = serialise(state); write(slotPath + ".tmp", data); flush(); rename(slotPath + ".tmp", slotPath). And for loading: try to read and parse slotPath; if that fails, try the backup; if that fails, tell the player clearly and offer to start fresh, never crash silently. Validate loaded values, such as health between 0 and its maximum, because corrupted or edited files can contain anything.

Versioning and migration: Games are updated after release, and update 1.3 may add a stamina stat that version 2 saves did not have. Always store a version number in the save. On loading, run migration functions step by step: if version is 1, convert it to 2, for example renaming gold to coins; if version is 2, convert it to 3 by adding stamina with a default of 100. Each migration is small and tested with real old saves kept from earlier releases. Never break players' saves with an update. Chaining small steps means a version 1 save loaded by version 5 of the game simply passes through every migration in order, so you never write one giant converter for every possible old version.

Tampering and cheating: In a single-player game, a player editing their own save hurts nobody, and some developers even welcome it. When saves affect leaderboards, multiplayer or purchases, protect them: store a hash or a message authentication code of the data, computed with a key, and reject saves whose code does not match. A determined cheater can still extract a key from the app, so anything valuable, such as purchased coins, must be stored and checked on a server, the authoritative idea you will meet in lesson 24.

Cloud saves: Cloud saving lets a player continue on a new phone or another device. The platform services on mobile stores and consoles, or the game's own server, store the save. The hard part is conflicts: the player played offline on two devices. Simple strategies are to keep the save with the most progress or the latest time, or to ask the player with a clear comparison showing level and play time of each. Upload small saves often, and never overwrite cloud data with an empty new install's save.

Where save files live: Each platform has a proper place for application data. On phones, every app has a private storage area that other apps cannot read, and the operating system removes it when the app is uninstalled. On desktops, use the user's application data folder, never the game's installation folder, which may be read-only. Small key-value settings can use the platform's preferences store, such as the shared preferences you used in Mobile App Development, while larger saves belong in files. Respect storage limits: never let autosaves pile up without deleting old ones.

Game state organisation: Saving is easy when state is organised; it is a nightmare when values hide in hundreds of objects. Keep a clear model: a GameState object or a set of ECS components that hold all saveable data, separate from presentation such as particles and animation. This is the model and view separation from Software Engineering. The screen stack from lesson 20 sits on top: title, menu, game and pause screens push and pop, and only the game screen owns the GameState.

Determinism and replays: Some games save not the state but the inputs. If the simulation is deterministic, the same seed and the same inputs always produce the same result, so a replay file needs only the seed and a list of inputs with their frame numbers, tiny compared with recording every position. Determinism requires the fixed timestep from lesson 5, seeded randomness, and care with floating-point differences between devices. Fighting and strategy games often use it for replays and for multiplayer, as lesson 24 will show.

Example, a Ludo game with family profiles: A Ludo game for a family tablet keeps four profiles. Each profile's file stores name, avatar, wins and settings. An unfinished match is autosaved as JSON after every move: whose turn, the dice seed, and each token's square. If the app is closed when a cousin calls, the match resumes exactly. A version field lets a later update add a new team colour without breaking older saved matches.

Example, an open-world village game: A large village exploration game saves the world seed plus a list of changes: trees cut, houses repaired, items picked. Autosave runs every 5 minutes and when entering a house, writing a snapshot on a background thread with the temporary-file-and-rename pattern. A backup of the previous save is kept. Cloud sync uploads the compressed save when on Wi-Fi, and on conflict shows both saves with play time and village name so the player chooses.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include saving derived data that later disagrees, saving pointers instead of identifiers, writing directly over the only save file, forgetting a version number, crashing on corrupted saves, trusting client-side saves for purchases, and blocking the game while saving. Exams ask you to decide what to save for a described game, write a JSON save structure, explain serialisation, autosave triggers, atomic writes and versioning with migration, estimate save sizes, and discuss tampering protection and cloud conflicts.

Recap: Game state is everything needed to continue; save the minimum and rebuild the rest, using ids rather than pointers. Serialise to JSON for clarity or binary for size; estimate sizes, such as 200 items x 40 bytes = 8 KB. Offer slots and separate settings; autosave at checkpoints, on a timer and when the app goes to the background. Write to a temporary file, flush and rename for atomic saves; keep a backup; store a version and migrate step by step. Protect valuable data on servers and handle cloud conflicts clearly.
key_points: Game state = everything needed to continue; save the minimum and rebuild derived values on load.
Serialisation turns objects into bytes or text; save ids instead of memory pointers.
JSON is readable for debugging; {"version":2,"level":7,"coins":350} is 35 bytes; binary or compression is smaller.
Size estimate: 200 items x 40 bytes = 8 KB; keep settings separate from save slots.
Autosave at checkpoints, on timers and when a phone app goes to the background; show a saving icon.
Atomic save: write a temporary file, flush, then rename over the old file; keep a backup.
Store a version number and migrate old saves step by step after updates.
Protect valuable state with hashes or server checks; resolve cloud conflicts clearly with the player.
lessons.tip: Keep a folder of real save files from every release of your game and load all of them in an automated test before each update. It is the cheapest insurance against angry reviews about lost progress.
lessons.task: Design the save file for a simple farming game: list what you would save and what you would rebuild, write an example JSON save with a version field, estimate its size for 50 crops and 100 inventory items, and write the step-by-step migration from version 1 (no weather) to version 2 (a weather field).

quiz.q: Why should a save file store an object's id rather than a memory pointer?
options: Memory addresses change between runs, so pointers are meaningless when loading
quiz.explain: Each run places objects at different addresses; stable ids let references be rebuilt on load.

quiz.q: What is the safe way to overwrite a save file?
options: Write to a temporary file, flush it, then rename it over the old save
Delete the old save first, then write the new one
Write directly into the old file as fast as possible
Save only when the game closes
quiz.explain: Renaming a complete temporary file is atomic, so a crash leaves either the full old or full new save.

quiz.q: An inventory holds 300 items at about 40 bytes each. Roughly how large is it?
quiz.explain: 300 x 40 = 12,000 bytes, about 12 KB.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a version number in a save file?
options: To let the game detect old saves and migrate them after updates
quiz.explain: The version tells the loader which migration steps to apply to an older save.

quiz.q: Where should purchased coins in an online game ultimately be stored and checked?
options: In the local save file only
quiz.explain: Client-side data can be edited; valuable data must be authoritative on the server.

lessons.title: Performance and Optimisation
lessons.content:
A game that runs smoothly on the developer's new laptop can stutter on a budget Android phone, the kind many players in Bangladesh actually use. Players rarely describe the problem in technical words; they just say the game feels laggy and uninstall it. Performance is not a final polish step; it is a design constraint from day one. This lesson covers the frame budget with worked numbers, the difference between CPU-bound and GPU-bound games, how to profile before optimising, draw calls and batching, overdraw, object pooling with pseudo-code, garbage collection spikes, level of detail and culling, memory and loading, and the special limits of mobile devices: heat and battery.

The frame budget worked: At 60 frames per second, each frame has 1000 / 60, about 16.7 milliseconds, for everything: input, game logic, physics, AI, audio updates, and preparing and drawing the image. At 30 fps the budget is about 33.3 ms; at 120 fps only about 8.3 ms. If a frame on a 60 fps target spends 9 ms on game logic and 5 ms on rendering, the total is 14 ms with about 2.7 ms to spare. Add a 4 ms AI spike and that frame takes 18 ms, misses its deadline and the player sees a stutter.

Average versus worst case: A game that averages 14 ms per frame but has one 50 ms frame every few seconds feels worse than a game that steadily takes 16 ms. Players notice hitches, not averages. Measure frame times, not just frames per second, and look at the slowest frames, for example the 99th percentile. A frame time graph that is flat is the goal; spikes point to work that happens occasionally, such as loading, saving, garbage collection or path planning.

CPU-bound and GPU-bound: The CPU runs game code and prepares rendering commands; the GPU draws pixels, as you learned in Computer Graphics. They work in parallel, so the frame rate is limited by whichever is slower. If the CPU takes 20 ms and the GPU 8 ms, the game is CPU-bound: simpler shaders will not help. If the GPU takes 20 ms and the CPU 8 ms, the game is GPU-bound: faster game code will not help. A quick test is to lower the resolution sharply; if the frame rate rises a lot, you were probably GPU-bound.

Profile first: The first rule of optimisation is to measure before changing anything. A profiler records how long each function or system takes per frame. Engines include profilers, and phone platforms provide tools that show CPU, GPU and memory use. Without measuring, developers routinely guess wrong and spend days speeding up code that took 1 percent of the frame. Profile on the weakest target device, not the development machine, and with a realistic scene, not an empty test level.

Algorithmic wins first: The biggest gains come from doing less work, not doing work faster. Replacing all-pairs collision checks with a spatial grid, from lesson 15, turned about 500,000 checks into a few thousand. Running AI perception a few times per second instead of every frame, from lesson 17, divides its cost. Caching paths, from lesson 18, avoids repeated searches. Only after the algorithm is right is it worth tuning individual lines of code. Design can also remove work: a level that limits how many enemies are active at once, or a camera that never shows the whole map, is often cheaper and better for play than a clever optimisation of an unlimited scene.

Draw calls and batching: Each time the CPU asks the GPU to draw something with a particular texture and settings, that is a draw call, and each call has CPU overhead. Drawing 500 sprites that use 20 different separate textures can need hundreds of draw calls. Putting all sprites into one texture atlas, from lesson 9, lets the engine batch them into a handful of calls, sometimes one. Sorting objects by material, combining static objects, and avoiding needless material changes all reduce draw calls.

Overdraw and fill rate: The GPU must colour every pixel of every drawn layer. A 1920 x 1080 screen has about 2.07 million pixels. Three full-screen layers, such as a sky, a semi-transparent fog and a background image, mean about 6.2 million pixel writes per frame, about 373 million per second at 60 fps. Transparent particles are especially costly because they overlap heavily. Reduce overdraw by trimming transparent sprite edges, limiting particle counts and sizes, and not drawing layers that are completely hidden.

Object pooling: Creating and destroying many objects, such as bullets, coins or particles, costs time and memory. A pool creates a fixed number of objects at loading time and reuses them. Pseudo-code: pool = list of 100 inactive bullets; function spawn(): for b in pool: if not b.active then b.active = true; reset(b); return b; return null or grow the pool. function despawn(b): b.active = false. Nothing is allocated during play, so creation is fast and the memory stays steady.

Garbage collection spikes: Languages with automatic memory management, such as C#, Java, JavaScript and Dart, periodically run a garbage collector that finds and frees unused objects. A collection can pause the game for several milliseconds, causing visible hitches. Reduce garbage by pooling objects, reusing lists instead of creating new ones each frame, avoiding building strings in the update loop, and preallocating at load time. A profiler's allocation view shows which functions allocate every frame.

Culling: The fastest object to draw is one you do not draw. Frustum culling skips objects outside the camera's view; in 2D this is a simple rectangle overlap test with the camera from lesson 10. Occlusion culling skips objects hidden behind others, useful in 3D cities and buildings. Logic can be culled too: enemies far from the player can update less often or sleep until the player comes near, the same idea physics engines use when they let resting bodies sleep, from lesson 13.

Level of detail: Distant objects cover few pixels, so they do not need full detail. Level of detail, LOD, swaps in simpler meshes or smaller textures with distance: a tree near the camera may have thousands of triangles, the same tree far away a few hundred, and very far away a flat image called an impostor. Mipmaps, from Computer Graphics, are LOD for textures. LOD applies to logic and animation too: distant characters animate at lower rates.

Memory and loading: Phones have limited memory, and the operating system may close a game that uses too much. Textures are usually the biggest consumers: one uncompressed 2048 x 2048 texture with 4 bytes per pixel is about 16.8 MB. Use compressed texture formats supported by the GPU, choose texture sizes by how large objects appear on screen, and unload assets that a level no longer needs. Loading in the background with a progress screen, from lesson 20, keeps the game responsive.

Mobile heat and battery: A phone running flat out heats up, and to protect itself it slows the processor, called thermal throttling, so a game that starts at 60 fps may drop to 40 fps after ten minutes. Running faster than needed also drains the battery. Good mobile games cap the frame rate, often offering 30 or 60 fps options, pause rendering when nothing changes such as on menus, reduce effects on low-end devices, and test for long sessions, not just the first minute.

Quality settings and scaling: Because players' devices differ widely, games offer quality levels: low, medium, high, each adjusting resolution, shadow quality, particle counts, draw distance and effects. Some detect the device's capability at first launch and choose defaults. Dynamic resolution lowers the rendering resolution briefly when frames get slow and restores it when there is headroom. Always make the lowest setting look acceptable on the weakest supported phone.

Optimising code itself: Once the hot spots are known, typical improvements include avoiding repeated work inside loops, comparing squared distances instead of computing square roots, as in lesson 8, storing data contiguously so the CPU cache helps, as the ECS data layout from lesson 7 does, and moving heavy independent tasks such as pathfinding or saving to background threads, as lesson 21 did for saves. Measure after each change; an optimisation that does not show in the profiler was not worth its complexity.

Performance budgets per system: Teams often split the frame budget among systems and treat it like money: for a 60 fps phone game, perhaps 4 ms for game logic, 2 ms for physics, 1.5 ms for AI, 1 ms for audio and UI, 4 ms for preparing rendering, leaving a safety margin of over 4 ms for spikes and slower devices. When a feature needs more, it must take time from somewhere else. Automated performance tests run a fixed scene every night and warn when any system goes over budget, so slowdowns are caught the day they are introduced rather than weeks later.

Example, a cricket game on budget phones: A cricket game targets 30 fps on low-end Android phones and 60 on better ones. Profiling on a cheap test phone shows the crowd is the GPU problem: thousands of spectators drawn individually. The fix is crowd impostors, a few animated cards repeated with colour variation, batched into a few draw calls. A CPU spike every few seconds turns out to be garbage collection from creating new ball trail particles, fixed with a pool. Frame times become flat.

Example, a bullet-heavy shooter: A top-down shooter with hundreds of bullets uses a pool of 500 bullets, a spatial grid for collisions, and one texture atlas for all bullets and effects, so all bullets are drawn in a single batch. Enemies off-screen update their AI only twice per second. A low-quality setting halves particle counts. The game keeps a steady frame rate even in the busiest wave, and the phone stays cooler during long sessions.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include optimising without profiling, testing only on powerful machines, focusing on average frame rate instead of spikes, creating objects every frame, using a separate texture for every sprite, ignoring overdraw from particles, and ignoring heat over long sessions. Exams ask you to compute frame budgets, decide whether a described game is CPU- or GPU-bound, explain draw calls and batching, compute overdraw, write object pooling pseudo-code, and explain garbage collection spikes, culling and level of detail.

Recap: The frame budget is 16.7 ms at 60 fps, 33.3 at 30 and 8.3 at 120; players feel spikes more than averages, so watch the slowest frames. Find whether you are CPU- or GPU-bound, and always profile on the weakest target device. Do less work first with better algorithms, then reduce draw calls with atlases and batching, limit overdraw, pool objects to avoid garbage collection spikes, cull and use level of detail, manage memory, and respect heat and battery on phones.
key_points: Frame budget: 16.7 ms at 60 fps, 33.3 ms at 30, 8.3 ms at 120; one long frame is a visible stutter.
Players feel spikes, not averages; watch frame times and the slowest frames.
CPU-bound vs GPU-bound: the slower one limits the frame rate; lowering resolution helps only if GPU-bound.
Profile first, on the weakest target device; algorithmic wins beat micro-optimisation.
Texture atlases and batching cut draw calls; trimming transparency and particles cuts overdraw.
Object pools reuse objects and avoid garbage collection spikes in C#, Java, JavaScript and Dart.
Culling, level of detail and sleeping distant logic skip work that the player cannot see.
Mobile: cap frame rate, offer quality levels, watch memory (2048 x 2048 x 4 bytes is about 16.8 MB) and heat.
lessons.tip: Keep one cheap, old Android phone on your desk as your performance reference. If the game runs well there for twenty minutes without getting hot, it will run well for nearly everyone.
lessons.task: A game targets 60 fps. Its profile shows game logic 7 ms, physics 3 ms, AI 2 ms and rendering commands 4 ms on the CPU, and 12 ms on the GPU. Compute the CPU total, state whether it fits the budget and which side limits the frame rate, then propose three changes that would let it reach 90 fps.

quiz.q: What is the approximate frame budget at 120 frames per second?
quiz.explain: 1000 / 120 is about 8.3 milliseconds.

quiz.q: The CPU takes 9 ms and the GPU 22 ms per frame. What is true?
options: Faster game code will greatly raise the frame rate
The game is GPU-bound, so reducing rendering work will help most
Both are within a 60 fps budget
quiz.explain: The slower side, the GPU at 22 ms, limits the frame rate.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of object pooling?
options: Reusing objects to avoid allocation cost and garbage collection spikes
quiz.explain: Pooling creates objects once and recycles them, keeping memory steady during play.

quiz.q: Why should you profile before optimising?
options: Because developers often guess wrong about where the time actually goes
Because profilers make code faster automatically
Because optimisation is forbidden without a profiler licence
quiz.explain: Measuring shows the real hot spots so effort goes where it matters.

quiz.q: How do texture atlases improve performance?
options: They let many sprites share one texture so they can be batched into fewer draw calls
They remove the need for culling
quiz.explain: Sprites from the same texture can be drawn together, cutting draw call overhead.

lessons.title: 3D Game Basics: Transforms, Cameras, Animation and Worlds
lessons.content:
Step from a 2D side-scroller into a 3D game and suddenly the player can walk around the back of the Lalbagh Fort, look up at the dome, and climb the steps. The ideas you already know, the game loop, entities, collision, AI, still apply, but space gains a third axis and everything from cameras to animation needs more care. The Computer Graphics course taught how 3D images are rendered; this lesson looks at what game developers do with that: transforms and hierarchies, meshes and materials, first- and third-person cameras with worked numbers, lighting choices for games, skeletal animation and blending, 3D physics and navigation, and how a 3D level is put together.

Coordinates and units: A 3D game world uses three axes. Engines disagree on which axis points up, Y in many engines and Z in others, and on whether the system is left- or right-handed, so always check the engine's convention before importing models or writing maths. Pick a unit and stick with it; most engines treat 1 unit as 1 metre, which makes physics values like gravity, 9.81, work without conversion. Models made at the wrong scale are a classic source of floating characters and strange physics.

Transforms in 3D: Every object has a transform: position, rotation and scale. Internally the engine combines them into a 4 x 4 matrix, as in Computer Graphics, and multiplies parent and child matrices for hierarchies: a sword is a child of the hand, the hand of the arm, so moving the arm moves the sword. Rotation is the tricky part. Euler angles, three rotations around the axes, are easy to understand but suffer from gimbal lock, where two axes line up and one degree of freedom is lost. Engines store rotations as quaternions, which interpolate smoothly and avoid gimbal lock, and show Euler angles in the editor for convenience.

Meshes and materials: A 3D object's shape is a mesh: vertices, triangles connecting them, and per-vertex data such as normals and texture coordinates. Its appearance is a material: a shader plus settings such as a colour texture, a normal map adding fine bumps without extra triangles, and values for roughness and metalness in physically based rendering. Game artists keep triangle counts within a budget and reuse materials so objects can be batched, as lesson 22 explained.

Field of view worked: A 3D camera has a field of view. Many engines specify the vertical angle; the horizontal angle then depends on the aspect ratio: horizontal = 2 x atan(tan(vertical / 2) x aspect). With a vertical field of view of 60 degrees on a 16:9 screen, the horizontal view is 2 x atan(tan(30 degrees) x 16/9), about 91.5 degrees. Wider views show more but distort the edges; very narrow views feel zoomed. Some players feel motion sickness with narrow views in first-person games, so a field of view slider is a valued accessibility option.

First-person cameras: A first-person camera sits at the character's eye height, about 1.6 to 1.7 metres for an adult. Mouse or right-stick movement changes yaw, turning left and right, and pitch, looking up and down: yaw = yaw + dx x sensitivity; pitch = clamp(pitch - dy x sensitivity, -89, 89) degrees. Clamping pitch stops the view from flipping over the top. Movement is then relative to yaw: pressing forward moves along the direction the player faces, flattened onto the ground so looking up does not make the player fly.

Third-person cameras worked: A third-person camera follows behind and above the character. Suppose a character stands at (10, 0, 4) facing the +z direction, and the camera should sit 6 metres behind and 3 metres above. Behind means minus the facing direction, so the camera is at (10, 0 + 3, 4 - 6) = (10, 3, -2), looking at a point near the character's head, perhaps (10, 1.5, 4). The camera then follows with smoothing, using the lerp idea from lesson 10, so it trails gently instead of snapping. Players can usually orbit the camera with the right stick or a drag gesture, which rotates the offset around the character while keeping it pointed at the head.

Camera collision: Third-person cameras have a special problem: walls get between the camera and the character. The fix is to cast a ray or sphere from the character toward the desired camera position; if it hits a wall, place the camera just in front of the hit point. The camera then slides closer in tight corridors and back out in open spaces. Also fade out objects that block the view, such as a tree trunk, so the player never loses sight of their character.

Lighting in games: Lighting is expensive, so games mix techniques. Real-time lights are computed every frame and can move, but only a few can cast shadows cheaply. Baked lighting is computed in advance and stored in lightmap textures, giving soft, beautiful light and shadows for static scenes at almost no runtime cost, but it cannot change. Many games bake the static world and use a few real-time lights for moving objects and a day-night sun. Light probes store baked light at points in space so moving characters can pick it up.

Skeletal animation: Characters are animated with a skeleton: a hierarchy of bones such as hips, spine, arm and hand. Each vertex of the mesh is attached to one or more bones with weights, a technique called skinning, so when the arm bone rotates, the skin of the arm follows smoothly. Animators create clips, walk, run, jump, attack, as keyframes of bone rotations; the engine interpolates between keyframes every frame. One skeleton can share many clips, and clips can be reused across characters with similar skeletons.

Animation blending worked: Switching instantly from walk to run looks like a jump cut. Engines blend clips by mixing their bone poses with weights. A blend space chooses weights from parameters such as speed. If the walk clip matches a speed of 2 m/s and the run clip 6 m/s, a character moving at 3 m/s uses run weight (3 - 2) / (6 - 2) = 0.25 and walk weight 0.75. Transitions between states, such as idle to jump, crossfade over a short time, often 0.1 to 0.3 seconds.

Animation state machines: Animation controllers are FSMs again, from lesson 17: states such as Idle, Locomotion, Jump, Fall and Land, with transitions on conditions like isGrounded or speed greater than 0.1. Layers let the upper body play an attack while the legs keep running. Animation events fire game logic at the right frame, such as a footstep sound when the foot touches the ground or damage when the sword swing reaches its target.

Root motion and inverse kinematics: With root motion, the animation itself moves the character, so feet do not slide; the trade-off is less direct control. Inverse kinematics, IK, solves bone angles to reach a target: feet adjust to stand on uneven steps, hands reach a door handle, heads turn to look at a speaker. These small touches greatly increase believability and are common in modern engines.

3D physics and characters: 3D physics engines work like the 2D ones from lesson 13, with spheres, boxes, capsules and convex meshes. Characters usually use a capsule collider, which slides smoothly over steps and edges, and a character controller that handles slopes, stairs and ground checks rather than a fully simulated rigid body, which would tumble over. Complex level geometry uses a mesh collider for static scenery only, because moving mesh colliders are expensive.

Navigation in 3D: Navigation meshes from lesson 18 are the standard for 3D characters. The engine bakes a navmesh from level geometry, considering the agent's radius, height, maximum slope and step height. Off-mesh links connect places the mesh cannot, such as a jump across a gap or a ladder. Agents follow navmesh paths and use local avoidance to stay apart, and the navmesh can be updated when doors open or obstacles move.

Large worlds and precision: Floating-point numbers lose precision far from the origin. A position 100,000 units away can no longer represent small movements accurately, causing jittering characters and shaking cameras in very large worlds. Open-world games handle this by streaming the world in chunks around the player, loading nearby areas in the background and unloading distant ones, and some shift the whole world back toward the origin when the player travels far, called origin rebasing. Streaming also keeps memory within the limits discussed in lesson 22.

Building 3D levels: Levels are often blocked out first with simple grey boxes, called a greybox or blockout, to test distances, sight lines and timing before art is made. Then modular kits, walls, floors, stairs and windows built to a grid, let artists assemble large spaces efficiently. Landscapes use heightmap terrains, often shaped with the noise from lesson 19 and painted with texture layers. Lighting, sound zones and navmesh are added, then performance is checked with culling and LOD from lesson 22.

Example, a third-person game in Old Dhaka: A third-person adventure through Old Dhaka's narrow lanes uses a camera 4 metres behind the hero with collision so it slides close in the alleys, a capsule character controller climbing steps, a blend space mixing walk and run by speed, and foot IK on uneven brick roads. Static buildings use baked lighting with a few real-time lanterns at night. Shopkeepers walk on a navmesh with off-mesh links for steps into shops.

Example, a first-person science lab game: A first-person educational game lets students walk around a 3D chemistry lab. The camera sits at 1.6 metres with clamped pitch, a field of view slider helps players prone to motion sickness, and hands use IK to reach the bottles they pick up. The room is lit with baked light for performance on school computers, and a small greybox was tested with students first to make sure benches were not too close together.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include wrong model scale, mixing up the engine's up axis, rotating with Euler angles and hitting gimbal lock, unclamped camera pitch, third-person cameras that clip through walls, rigid bodies used for player characters, and instant animation switches. Exams ask you to explain transforms and hierarchies, quaternions versus Euler angles, compute field of view or a camera position, explain skinning and blending, compute blend weights, compare baked and real-time lighting, and describe navmeshes for 3D agents.

Recap: 3D games keep the same loop and systems but add a third axis; check the engine's axis conventions and keep 1 unit = 1 metre. Transforms form hierarchies, and quaternions avoid gimbal lock. Meshes give shape and materials give appearance. First-person cameras clamp pitch; third-person cameras follow behind with smoothing and collision, such as (10, 3, -2) for our example. Bake static lighting, blend skeletal animation by weights, use capsule controllers and navmeshes, and build levels from greybox to finished art.
key_points: Check the engine's up axis and handedness; keep 1 unit = 1 metre so physics values work.
Transforms form parent-child hierarchies; quaternions avoid gimbal lock in rotations.
Horizontal FOV = 2 atan(tan(vertical / 2) x aspect); 60 degrees vertical at 16:9 is about 91.5 degrees.
First-person: yaw and clamped pitch (-89 to 89 degrees); movement relative to yaw on the ground.
Third-person worked: character (10, 0, 4) facing +z, camera 6 behind and 3 up = (10, 3, -2); add collision.
Baked lighting is cheap but static; real-time lights move but cost more; probes light moving objects.
Skeletal animation with skinning; blend weight (3 - 2) / (6 - 2) = 0.25 run at 3 m/s.
Capsule character controllers, navmeshes with off-mesh links, and greybox-first level building.
lessons.tip: Before importing any model, place a 1 x 1 x 1 cube and a 1.8-metre capsule in your scene. Every new model should look right beside them; if a chair is taller than the capsule, fix the scale now, not after the physics breaks.
lessons.task: Design the camera for a third-person game set in a village market. Compute the camera position for a character at (4, 0, 7) facing +x, with the camera 5 metres behind and 2 metres above, describe how the camera handles stalls blocking the view, and compute the walk and run blend weights for a speed of 4.5 m/s if walk matches 1.5 and run 6.

quiz.q: Why do engines store rotations as quaternions?
options: They use less memory than a single number
They interpolate smoothly and avoid gimbal lock
quiz.explain: Quaternions avoid the gimbal lock of Euler angles and blend rotations smoothly.

quiz.q: A character at (2, 0, 5) faces +z. The camera should be 4 m behind and 2 m above. Where is it?
quiz.explain: Behind means minus the facing direction: z = 5 - 4 = 1, and y = 0 + 2 = 2.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of baked lighting?
options: It can change in real time with moving lights
It gives high-quality static lighting at very low runtime cost
It removes the need for shadows
quiz.explain: Light is computed in advance and stored in lightmaps, so it is cheap at runtime but cannot change.

quiz.q: In a blend space, walk matches 2 m/s and run 6 m/s. What is the run weight at 5 m/s?
Why do player characters usually use a capsule collider with a character controller?
options: Capsules are required for navmesh baking
It slides smoothly over steps and slopes without tumbling like a free rigid body
It lets the camera pass through walls
quiz.explain: A capsule controller handles slopes, steps and ground checks with stable, controllable movement.

lessons.title: Multiplayer and Networked Games
lessons.content:
Four friends play an online Ludo match: one in Chattogram, one in Rajshahi, one in Dhaka and a cousin abroad. Each sees the same board, the same dice and the same moves, even though their messages travel thousands of kilometres through different networks. When they switch to a fast action game, the problem becomes much harder: everyone moves at once, every few milliseconds, over connections that are slow and unreliable. This lesson covers multiplayer architectures, why games often prefer UDP, tick rates and bandwidth with worked numbers, latency and jitter, client-side prediction, server reconciliation, entity interpolation, lag compensation, cheating and security, and matchmaking.

Kinds of multiplayer: Local multiplayer shares one device or screen, needing no network. Turn-based online games, Ludo, chess, card games, exchange a move every few seconds, so delays of a second are acceptable. Real-time online games, shooters, racing, sports, exchange updates many times per second, so every millisecond matters. Asynchronous games let players act at different times, such as building a village that a friend visits later. The networking design depends heavily on which kind you are building.

Peer-to-peer versus client-server: In peer-to-peer, P2P, each player's device talks directly to the others; there is no central server cost, but every peer must trust the others, connections through home routers are tricky, and one slow peer can hold everyone back. In client-server, every player connects to a server that runs the official game. It costs money to host, but it is the dominant design for competitive online games because the server can enforce the rules. A hybrid is a listen server, where one player's device acts as the server.

The authoritative server: In an authoritative design, clients send only their inputs, such as move left or fire, and the server simulates the game and decides what really happened. Clients display what the server tells them. A client that claims to have 9,999 coins or to have hit a player through a wall is simply ignored, because the server never trusted it in the first place. This is the main defence against cheating, as lesson 21 said for purchases: never trust the client.

TCP versus UDP: From Computer Networks you know that TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery: lost packets are resent, and later packets wait for earlier ones. That waiting, called head-of-line blocking, is harmful in fast games: if a position update from 100 ms ago is lost, you do not want to wait for it, because a newer one is already on its way. UDP sends independent packets with no guarantees, so fast games use UDP and build only the reliability they need on top, such as resending important events like a goal scored, while letting stale position updates go. Turn-based games and lobbies can happily use TCP or WebSockets.

Tick rate worked: The server simulates and sends updates at a fixed tick rate, the fixed timestep from lesson 5 applied to the network. At 20 ticks per second, each tick is 1000 / 20 = 50 ms; at 64 ticks per second, about 15.6 ms. Higher rates feel more responsive but cost more server processing and bandwidth. As a bandwidth estimate, if a server sends the state of 10 players at about 30 bytes each, 20 times per second, each client receives 10 x 30 x 20 = 6,000 bytes per second, about 6 KB/s, before packet headers.

Reducing bandwidth: Send only what changed since the last update the client confirmed, called delta compression. Quantise values: a position on a 1000-metre map needs only centimetre precision, not a full 32-bit float per axis. Send nearby objects more often than distant ones, and do not send objects the player cannot possibly see, which also prevents wall-hack cheats from learning hidden positions. These techniques matter on mobile data plans, which are a real cost for many players.

Latency and jitter worked: Latency is the delay for a packet to travel; round-trip time, RTT, measures there and back. With an RTT of 120 ms, a one-way trip is about 60 ms. A player's input travels 60 ms to the server, waits on average half a tick, 25 ms at 20 Hz, to be processed, and the result travels 60 ms back: about 145 ms before the player sees the server's response. Jitter is variation in latency: packets arriving after 48, 52, 70 and 45 ms average 53.75 ms but spread over 25 ms, so games buffer slightly to smooth it. Packet loss adds gaps.

Client-side prediction: Waiting 145 ms for your own character to move would feel terrible. With client-side prediction, the client applies the player's input immediately to its own character, running the same movement code as the server, while also sending the input. Each input carries a sequence number. Most of the time the server agrees, and the player feels zero delay for their own movement. This requires deterministic, shared movement code, which is one reason engines separate simulation from presentation.

Server reconciliation: Sometimes the prediction is wrong: the server saw a collision the client did not know about. When a server update arrives saying the player was at position P after input number 41, the client resets its character to P and replays its stored inputs 42, 43 and onward that the server has not processed yet. If the difference is small, the client smooths the correction over a few frames so the player does not see a snap. This is called reconciliation, and together with prediction it makes movement feel instant yet stay authoritative.

Entity interpolation: Other players' characters cannot be predicted because you do not know their inputs. Instead the client shows them slightly in the past, interpolating between the two most recent server snapshots, the lerp from lesson 10 again. With a 20 Hz server, rendering others about 100 ms behind, two ticks, means there are almost always two snapshots to interpolate between, even if one packet is late. Movement looks smooth, at the cost of showing others a little late. Extrapolating ahead instead looks responsive but overshoots when players turn.

Lag compensation: In a shooter, you aim at where you see an enemy, but you see them about 100 ms in the past plus your latency. Without help, you would have to lead every target. With lag compensation, the server stores a short history of positions and, when your shot arrives, rewinds the other players to where you saw them at that moment, checks the hit, then returns to the present. Shots feel fair to the shooter; the occasional cost is that a victim may be hit just after reaching cover on their own screen.

Lockstep and determinism: Strategy games with hundreds of units cannot send every unit's position. Instead, they use deterministic lockstep: all players exchange only their inputs per turn, and every machine runs the same deterministic simulation, as in lesson 21's replays. Bandwidth is tiny, but the game waits for the slowest player's inputs, and any difference in floating-point results between devices causes desynchronisation, so these games use fixed-point maths or careful determinism. Fighting games use a related idea, rollback, which predicts the opponent's input and re-simulates when the real input arrives.

Cheating and security: Common cheats include aimbots, wall-hacks that reveal hidden players, speed hacks that send inputs too fast, and modified clients. Defences: an authoritative server that validates every input, such as checking that movement speed is possible; not sending hidden information; rate limits; encrypted and authenticated connections; server-side checks of purchases; and detecting impossible statistics. No defence is perfect, but the server should never be the weak point.

Servers and scaling: Hosting real-time games means running many game server processes, each hosting one or a few matches, on cloud machines in several regions, so that players connect to a nearby one. A separate backend handles accounts, friends, inventories and leaderboards, usually through ordinary web APIs from the Web Engineering course. Servers are started when demand rises in the evening and stopped late at night to save money. Because a match server holds live state in memory, a crash ends the match, so logging and quick restarts matter.

Designing for latency: Good network games are designed to hide delay. Animations that start instantly on input, such as a wind-up before a punch lands, give the network time to confirm the hit. Slower projectiles are easier to make fair than instant shots. Turn-based and cooperative designs tolerate latency far better than twitchy duels, which is why many successful mobile games favour them on unpredictable mobile networks.

Matchmaking and sessions: Matchmaking groups players into games. It balances skill, often with rating systems that estimate skill from wins and losses, latency, putting players near the same server region, and waiting time. Waiting longer gives better matches; the system relaxes its requirements as time passes. Lobbies, parties, reconnection after a dropped connection, and handling a player who leaves mid-match all need design, especially on mobile networks where switching between Wi-Fi and data drops connections.

Example, an online Ludo game: An online Ludo game uses a client-server design over WebSockets, because turns happen every few seconds and reliability matters more than speed. The server rolls the dice with a secure random generator, from lesson 19, so no client can choose its roll. Each move is validated on the server. If a player's phone loses connection, the server waits 30 seconds, then lets a simple AI play for them until they reconnect, and the game state is never lost.

Example, a real-time football game: A five-a-side football game on mobile runs an authoritative server at 30 ticks per second over UDP. Your own player uses prediction and reconciliation; other players and the ball are interpolated about two ticks behind. The ball is the hardest object because everyone interacts with it, so the server owns it fully and clients predict only short, simple kicks. Matchmaking groups players by region to keep RTT below about 100 ms.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include trusting the client, using TCP for fast position updates, sending the whole world every tick, showing other players without interpolation, no prediction for the local player, ignoring packet loss and reconnection, and floating-point desync in lockstep games. Exams ask you to compare P2P and client-server, explain why UDP suits fast games, compute tick intervals, bandwidth and response delays, and explain prediction, reconciliation, interpolation, lag compensation and lockstep.

Recap: Choose the architecture by game type; competitive games use an authoritative client-server design that trusts only inputs. Fast games use UDP with selective reliability. Tick rate sets update intervals, 50 ms at 20 Hz, and bandwidth grows with players, bytes and rate, 6 KB/s in our example. Latency and jitter are unavoidable; prediction and reconciliation hide them for the local player, interpolation smooths others, and lag compensation makes hits fair. Lockstep and rollback suit special genres, and the server is the defence against cheating.
key_points: Multiplayer kinds: local, turn-based, real-time and asynchronous, each with different network needs.
Authoritative client-server: clients send inputs, the server decides; never trust the client.
Fast games use UDP to avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking, adding reliability only for key events.
Tick 20 Hz = 50 ms; bandwidth 10 players x 30 bytes x 20 Hz = 6 KB/s; use delta compression.
RTT 120 ms: about 60 + 25 + 60 = 145 ms from input to seeing the server's result.
Client-side prediction plus reconciliation (replay unacknowledged inputs) makes own movement instant.
Interpolate other players about two ticks in the past; lag compensation rewinds to check hits.
Lockstep sends only inputs but needs determinism; matchmaking balances skill, latency and wait time.
lessons.tip: Test your multiplayer game with an artificial network delay and packet loss tool from day one, for example 150 ms latency and 5 percent loss. Games that only ever ran on a local network almost always break when they meet the real internet.
lessons.task: Design the networking for a two-player online carrom game. Choose P2P or client-server and TCP or UDP with reasons, compute the bandwidth if the server sends 20 coin positions of 8 bytes each 30 times per second, and explain how you would keep the striker shot fair if one player's RTT is 180 ms.

quiz.q: In an authoritative server design, what do clients normally send to the server?
options: Their inputs, such as move or fire commands
The final positions of every object
Their score, which the server accepts
quiz.explain: The server simulates the game from inputs and decides the outcome, so clients cannot simply claim results.

quiz.q: Why do fast real-time games usually prefer UDP?
options: UDP is required by phone stores
It avoids waiting for lost old packets, since newer updates make them obsolete
quiz.explain: TCP's head-of-line blocking delays fresh data while resending stale data.

quiz.q: A server runs at 25 ticks per second. How long is each tick?
quiz.explain: 1000 / 25 = 40 milliseconds.

quiz.q: What does server reconciliation do?
options: Resets the local character to the server's state and replays unacknowledged inputs
Shows other players in the past
quiz.explain: When a server update arrives, the client corrects to it and re-applies inputs the server has not yet processed.

quiz.q: How are other players' characters usually shown smoothly on a client?
options: By interpolating between recent server snapshots, slightly in the past
quiz.explain: Interpolating between two known snapshots gives smooth movement at the cost of a small delay.

lessons.title: Playtesting, Monetisation, Ethics and Publishing
lessons.content:
A group of students in a university club builds a charming little puzzle game about a boatman crossing the rivers of Barishal. Friends love it. Then come the hard questions: will strangers understand it without the developers sitting beside them? Should it cost money, show ads or sell hints? Which store, which age rating, which screenshots? How do you know whether players come back on day two? This lesson covers playtesting and the metrics that guide improvements, with a worked retention and revenue example, the main business models and their ethics, age ratings and legal care, and the practical steps of publishing on stores and the web, including notes for developers in Bangladesh.

Why playtest: Developers cannot see their own game with fresh eyes; they know every rule, every secret and every control. Playtesting means watching real target players use the game and learning where they get confused, bored, frustrated or delighted. It is the usability testing of the HCI course applied to play. Test early with paper or greybox prototypes, then repeatedly as features arrive. A small test with five fresh players often reveals most of the big problems.

Running a playtest: Give the player the game with no explanation beyond what a real player would get. Ask them to think aloud. Watch, take notes, and do not help or defend the design; if you must explain something, that is a finding. Record time to finish each level, where they fail, what they say, and their face. Afterwards ask open questions: what was the goal, what was most fun, what was most frustrating, would you play again. Separate observations, what happened, from opinions, what they suggest; observations are more reliable.

Analytics and metrics: After release, analytics record events: game started, level completed, level failed, purchase made, session length. Key metrics include retention, the percentage of players who return after 1, 7 and 30 days; session length and sessions per day; funnel completion, the percentage who pass each level; and for paid features, conversion, the percentage who pay. A level that half the players fail many times, while other levels have high completion, shows a difficulty spike to fix, the balancing idea from lesson 3.

Retention and revenue worked: Suppose 10,000 players install a game. If day-1 retention is 40 percent, 4,000 return the next day; day-7 retention of 15 percent means 1,500; day-30 retention of 5 percent means 500. If 2 percent of players ever pay, that is 200 payers. If total revenue is 60,000 taka, the average revenue per user, ARPU, is 60,000 / 10,000 = 6 taka, while the average revenue per paying user, ARPPU, is 60,000 / 200 = 300 taka. These numbers are illustrative, not benchmarks; real values vary widely by genre and market.

A/B testing: When a team is unsure which of two versions is better, such as a tutorial with three steps or with five, it can show version A to half of new players and version B to the other half, chosen at random, and compare a metric such as day-1 retention. The difference must be large enough relative to the sample size to be more than chance, a question for the statistics you studied earlier. Decide the metric before the test starts, run one change at a time, and never test things that would be unfair or harmful to the players who receive the worse version.

Privacy and data: Analytics must respect players. Collect only what you need, explain it in a clear privacy policy, ask for consent where the law or the store requires it, never collect sensitive data without strong reason, and take special care with children, whose data is protected by stricter rules in many countries. Use the anonymised aggregate view for design decisions; you rarely need to know who a player is to learn that level 7 is too hard.

Business models: Premium games are paid once up front; simple and honest, but many players hesitate to pay before trying. Free-to-play, F2P, games are free to download and earn from in-app purchases, IAP, such as cosmetic items, extra levels, convenience or currency.
