Ad-supported games show advertisements: banners, interstitials between levels, and rewarded ads that players choose to watch for a bonus. Subscriptions and game services bundle access to many games. Many games mix models, such as free with ads and a one-time purchase to remove them.

Designing fair monetisation: Monetisation that respects players sells things that add enjoyment, such as new levels, costumes for the boatman, or removing ads, and keeps the core game fair for non-payers. Rewarded ads work best when entirely optional and the reward is modest. Interstitial ads should appear only at natural breaks, never in the middle of play. A useful test is whether players feel the game is generous, or feel squeezed: games that feel generous are recommended to friends.

Loot boxes and dark patterns: Loot boxes sell random rewards for money; because they resemble gambling, some countries have regulated them, and rules differ by country and change over time, so developers must check current laws for each market. Dark patterns are designs that push players against their own interest: fake countdown timers, confusing currencies that hide real prices, energy systems that stop play until you pay, guilt messages when you leave, and pressuring children to buy. They may raise short-term revenue but damage trust, invite regulation and are simply unethical. Show real prices, set spending limits for children and make refunds easy.

Ethics beyond money: Games also shape attitudes. Consider representation: who appears as heroes and villains, whether cultures, including our own, are shown with respect rather than stereotypes. Consider time: avoid designs that exploit compulsion, such as endless streak rewards that punish a missed day. Consider accessibility from lesson 20 as an ethical duty, not a bonus. Consider community safety in multiplayer: reporting, blocking and moderation of chat. Ethical design is good business over the long run.

Age ratings and legal care: Stores require age ratings. Google Play uses the International Age Rating Coalition, IARC, questionnaire, which produces ratings for different regions; Apple's App Store uses its own questionnaire. Answer honestly about violence, language, gambling-like features and user interaction. Respect copyright: use only music, fonts, art and code you have rights to, and read every asset's licence, as in the open-source discussion of Software Engineering. Check trademark conflicts before choosing a name.

Preparing for release: A store listing needs an icon that reads at small size, a short and long description, screenshots that show real gameplay, ideally a short video, the age rating, a privacy policy link and category tags. Build signed release versions, test on several real devices, especially low-end ones from lesson 22, and run a closed test with a small group through the store's testing tracks before opening to everyone. Prepare to fix crashes quickly: crash reporting tools show stack traces from players' devices.

Stores and the web: Mobile games publish on Google Play and the App Store, each with developer accounts, fees, review processes and a commission on sales, so check their current terms. PC games publish on digital stores and on itch.io, which is popular with independent and student developers. Web games run in the browser, built with HTML5 engines or engines that export to WebAssembly, and need no installation, which makes them great for game jams and portfolios. Flutter developers can use the Flame engine from lesson 6 to target mobile and web from one codebase.

Notes for Bangladesh: Many players in Bangladesh play on budget Android phones and mobile data, so small download sizes, offline play and modest performance needs, from lesson 22, widen your audience. Bangla language support is a real advantage: test Bangla text rendering carefully, including conjunct letters, and offer both Bangla and English. Many players do not hold international payment cards, so check which local payment options each store supports in Bangladesh before planning in-app purchases, and consider ads or a premium web version as alternatives. Game jams and university clubs are good places to start and to build a portfolio.

Marketing on a small budget: A great game nobody hears about earns nothing. Small teams share development progress early on social media with short gameplay clips, build a simple page where interested players can follow the project, take part in game jams and local events, send the game to reviewers and streamers who cover similar games, and make a short trailer that shows real play in the first few seconds. Good store screenshots and a clear one-sentence pitch do more than an expensive advertisement.

After launch: live operations: Publishing is the start of a new phase. Watch crash reports and reviews daily in the first weeks, reply politely, and fix the top problems first. Use analytics to find funnel drop-offs. Plan regular updates, new levels, seasonal events like Pohela Boishakh or Eid themes, and balance tweaks, but test each update, including save migration from lesson 21. Talk with your community through social media and a simple website, and keep a changelog so players see their feedback matter.

Example, the boatman puzzle game: The student team runs five playtests and finds most players do not notice that tides change the river paths, so they add a short animated hint and an obvious tide icon. Analytics after a closed test show level 12 has a 30 percent completion rate while its neighbours have over 80, so they split it into two levels. They publish free with an optional rewarded ad for a hint and a small one-time purchase that removes ads and adds a bonus chapter, with Bangla and English text, honest pricing and no timers.

Example, a children's learning game: A team building a Bangla alphabet game for children chooses a premium web version for schools and a free mobile version with no ads, no purchases and no data collection, because child safety rules are strict and parents value trust. Playtests with children and teachers at a local school shape button sizes, voice speed and reward sounds. The game earns through school licences and a donation link instead of manipulating young players.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include testing only with friends, explaining the game during tests, ignoring analytics, predatory monetisation, ads interrupting play, collecting unnecessary personal data, using assets without licences, dishonest age rating answers, and publishing without testing on low-end devices. Exams ask you to plan a playtest, define and compute retention, ARPU and ARPPU, compare business models, identify dark patterns, explain age ratings and licensing, and describe the steps of publishing a game.

Recap: Playtest early and often with fresh players, observe rather than explain, and measure retention, funnels and conversion after release, while respecting privacy. In our example 10,000 installs with 40, 15 and 5 percent retention and 60,000 taka revenue give an ARPU of 6 taka and an ARPPU of 300. Choose a fair business model, avoid dark patterns and check loot box laws per market. Rate honestly, license every asset, prepare a strong store listing, publish on stores or the web, design for local players, and keep improving after launch.
key_points: Playtest with fresh target players; ask them to think aloud; observe, do not explain or defend.
Metrics: retention (day 1, 7, 30), funnels, session length and conversion; respect privacy, especially for children.
Worked: 10,000 installs, 40% day-1 retention = 4,000; 2% payers = 200; ARPU 6 taka, ARPPU 300 taka.
Business models: premium, free-to-play with IAP, ads (banner, interstitial, rewarded), subscriptions, mixes.
Fair monetisation sells enjoyment and keeps the core fair; avoid dark patterns like fake timers and hidden prices.
Loot box laws vary by country and change; age ratings via IARC on Google Play and Apple's own questionnaire.
Release: icon, screenshots, privacy policy, signed builds, closed testing, crash reporting; stores, itch.io and web.
Bangladesh: small downloads, offline play, Bangla text support and checking local payment options widen reach.
lessons.tip: Before every playtest, write down three things you expect players to struggle with. Afterwards compare: the problems you did not predict are the most valuable things you will learn that week.

options: Take the controller and show them
Observe and note it, because the confusion itself is a finding
quiz.explain: Helping hides the problem; real players will not have the developer beside them.

quiz.q: 8,000 players install a game and day-1 retention is 35 percent. How many return on day 1?
Revenue is 40,000 taka from 10,000 players, of whom 100 paid. What is the ARPPU?
quiz.explain: ARPPU = revenue / paying users = 40,000 / 100 = 400 taka.

quiz.q: Which of these is a dark pattern?
options: A clear one-time price to remove ads
An optional rewarded ad for a small bonus
A fake countdown timer pressuring players to buy now
quiz.explain: Fake urgency pushes players to act against their interest, a classic dark pattern.

quiz.q: Which statement about loot boxes is most accurate?
options: They are legal and unregulated everywhere
They are banned in every country
They must be offered in every free game
Some countries regulate them, rules differ and change, so developers must check each market
quiz.explain: Laws on paid random rewards vary by country and over time.

lessons.title: Capstone: Designing and Building Rickshaw Rush
lessons.content:
This final lesson pulls the whole course into one project: Rickshaw Rush, an endless runner where the player steers a colourful rickshaw down a busy Dhaka road, switching lanes to dodge buses, potholes and puddles while collecting coins, as the road gets faster and busier. It is small enough for a student team to finish in a few weeks, yet it touches nearly every topic: design and loops, the game loop, entities, maths, rendering and cameras, input, physics-lite motion, collision, procedural spawning, audio and juice, saving, performance, testing and publishing. We will design it step by step with worked numbers, then recap the course.

The concept and core loop: The one-sentence pitch is: steer a rickshaw through ever faster Dhaka traffic and see how far you can go. The core loop, from lesson 2, takes seconds: see an obstacle, choose a lane, swipe, survive, grab coins. The secondary loop spans a run: survive longer, beat your best distance. The meta loop spans days: spend coins on rickshaw paint designs and bells that are purely cosmetic, so the challenge stays fair. In MDA terms, the mechanics of lanes and speed create dynamics of quick decisions under pressure, aiming for aesthetics of challenge and a little humour.

Lanes and movement: The road has three lanes at x = -2, 0 and 2 metres. A swipe left or right sets a target lane; the rickshaw slides there over 0.15 seconds using smoothed interpolation from lesson 10 rather than teleporting, and tilts slightly for juice. Forward motion is not simulated with forces; the world scrolls toward the player at the current speed, a common runner trick that keeps the player near the camera and avoids floating-point drift from lesson 23. A jump over puddles can use the jump design from lesson 12: choose height and time to apex, then derive gravity and initial velocity.

The difficulty curve worked: Speed grows with time t in seconds: speed = min(6 + 0.1 x t, 14) metres per second. At the start the speed is 6; after 30 seconds it is 9; it reaches the cap of 14 at t = 80 seconds. Obstacle rows spawn at an interval of max(0.6, 1.5 - 0.01 x t) seconds: 1.5 at the start, 0.9 at 60 seconds, reaching the minimum 0.6 at 90 seconds. At top speed and minimum interval, rows are 14 x 0.6 = 8.4 metres apart, and a lane switch covers 14 x 0.15 = 2.1 metres of road, so a skilled player always has room to react.

Fairness checks: An obstacle row spawned 30 metres ahead at 14 metres per second arrives in 30 / 14, about 2.1 seconds, well above a human reaction time of a few hundred milliseconds. Each row blocks at most two of the three lanes, so at least one lane is always free, and the generator never blocks the only lane reachable within the switching time from the previous free lane. These rules are constraints on the procedural generator, exactly the kind lesson 19 recommended, and they are tested automatically.

Screens and states: The screen flow from lesson 20 is a small FSM: Title, Play, Pause, GameOver and Shop, with Settings reachable from Title and Pause. Screens live on a stack: Pause is pushed over Play and popped on resume, with gameplay time scale set to 0 while the pause menu animates. When the phone receives a call or the app goes to the background, the game pauses itself, following the app lifecycle, and the run state is saved so the player can continue.

Entities and systems: Following lesson 7, entities are simple: the rickshaw, obstacles, coins, road tiles and particles. Components hold data: Transform, Sprite, Collider with an AABB, Lane, Mover with velocity, Coin with value, Obstacle with kind. Systems run in a fixed order each step: InputSystem, LaneSystem, ScrollSystem, SpawnSystem, CollisionSystem, ScoreSystem, CleanupSystem, then rendering. The game loop uses a fixed timestep with an accumulator from lesson 5, so the difficulty formulas behave the same on fast and slow phones.

Input details: Swipes are detected as a touch that moves more than a small threshold, such as 30 logical pixels, within a quarter of a second; shorter movements are ignored so a resting thumb does not change lanes. Following lesson 11, an input that arrives during a lane switch is buffered and applied when the switch ends, so fast double swipes from the left lane to the right lane work as the player intends. On keyboards for the web version, arrow keys map to the same commands, so all game logic sees only abstract actions such as MoveLeft and MoveRight.

Rendering and camera: The road, rickshaw and obstacles use sprites packed into one texture atlas, from lesson 9, so the whole scene draws in a few batches. A slightly top-down camera follows the rickshaw's lane position with gentle smoothing, and shakes for a short moment on a crash, from lesson 10. Background layers of buildings and billboards scroll at slower speeds for parallax, giving depth with no 3D cost. The HUD shows distance and coins at the top edge inside the safe area.

Collision: Each object has an axis-aligned bounding box from lesson 14: the rickshaw is 1.2 metres wide and 2.0 long, obstacles about 1.0 by 1.0. Because only objects near the rickshaw can collide and there are few on screen, a simple check of the rickshaw against each active obstacle and coin is enough; no broad phase is needed, a deliberate simplification. Hitboxes are made slightly smaller than the sprites so near misses feel thrilling rather than unfair, a classic game-feel choice. Touching a coin collects it; touching an obstacle ends the run, unless a short invincibility after a revive is active.

Spawning, seeds and pools: The spawner uses a seeded random generator from lesson 19, so a daily challenge can seed with the date and every player gets the same road. Obstacle kinds come from a weighted table that changes with distance, potholes common early, buses more common later, and a shuffle bag ensures coin lines appear regularly. With a visible road of about 60 metres and rows 8.4 metres apart at top speed, about 7 rows are visible, with at most two obstacles each, so a pool of 20 obstacles, from lesson 22, is enough and nothing is allocated during play.

Audio and juice: Audio follows lesson 20: a looping upbeat track whose drum layer joins after 30 seconds, a bicycle bell when switching lanes with small pitch variation, a bright coin sound, a horn warning when a bus spawns in your lane, and a crash sound with a short hit-stop and screen shake. Coins pop toward the HUD counter, which bounces. Settings offer separate music and effects sliders, reduced shake and a high-contrast mode for colour-blind players.

Saving and scoring: The score is distance in metres plus 10 points per coin: 1,000 metres with 25 coins scores 1,000 + 250 = 1,250. The save file from lesson 21 is small JSON with a version field: best score, total coins, unlocked paints, settings. It is written with the temporary-file-and-rename pattern after each run and when the app goes to the background. If a global leaderboard is added later, scores must be validated on a server, since local saves can be edited.

Performance targets: The target is a steady 60 fps on mid-range phones and 30 fps with reduced particles on the cheapest supported phone, with frame time, not average frame rate, as the measure. Profiling on a budget Android phone, from lesson 22, checks that garbage collection spikes are absent thanks to pooling, that draw calls stay low thanks to the atlas, and that the phone stays cool during a twenty-minute session. The download size is kept small with compressed audio and textures so it suits mobile data.

Playtest and analytics plan: Following lesson 25, the team runs five-player playtests at each milestone, recording where players crash in the first minute, whether they understand swiping without text, and whether they want another run. After a closed test, analytics track run length, cause of crash and day-1 retention. If most first runs end before 20 seconds, the starting speed or spawn interval is eased. Monetisation is ethical: free, with an optional rewarded ad to revive once per run and a one-time purchase to remove ads; no loot boxes and no timers.

Building it step by step: Build in vertical slices. Week one: a greybox prototype with coloured rectangles, three lanes, swiping and one obstacle type, to test whether dodging is fun. Week two: spawning, difficulty curve, collision and game over. Week three: art, atlas, audio, juice and HUD. Week four: menus, saving, settings and shop. Week five: performance, accessibility, playtesting and fixes. Keep the game playable at the end of every week, and cut features rather than delay, a lesson from Software Engineering that games teach again.

Extending the project: Once the base works, possible extensions use other lessons: a simple utility-AI traffic police officer who occasionally waves vehicles across lanes, from lesson 17; flocking pigeons that scatter as the rickshaw passes, from lesson 18; a two-player race with ghost replays stored as seeds and inputs, from lessons 21 and 24; or a 3D version with a chase camera, from lesson 23. Each extension should be playtested to check it adds fun, not just features.

Course recap, design and foundations: You began with what a game is: goals, rules, feedback and voluntary participation, and the MDA lens linking mechanics to experience. You balanced numbers, built loops and motivated players, compared genres and platforms, and built the game loop with fixed timesteps. You chose engines, organised objects with scene graphs and ECS, and used vectors, dot products and interpolation everywhere.

Course recap, systems: You rendered sprites, tilemaps and parallax, built cameras and input with coyote time and buffering, integrated motion and designed jumps, used physics engines carefully, detected collisions with AABBs, circles and SAT, scaled with broad phases, and resolved collisions with impulses. You built AI with state machines, behaviour trees and utility, moved characters with steering and A*, and generated content with seeds, noise and fair randomness.

Course recap, polish and shipping: You added audio, HUDs, menus and juice, saved progress safely with versions and atomic writes, kept frames within budget on real phones, stepped into 3D, connected players over networks with prediction and authority, and learned to playtest, monetise ethically and publish. Rickshaw Rush uses nearly all of it; your own game will too.

Final advice: Start small, finish games, and show them to players. A finished small game teaches more than an unfinished ambitious one. Join a game jam, build a portfolio on the web, read other developers' post-mortems, and keep playing games critically, asking why each design choice was made. Games combine computer science, art, psychology and storytelling; that combination is what makes them such a rewarding field to study and to build.
